Bagoly=Owl
BagolyLeiras=The [z]Owl[-] came to the aid of the island’s animals when they asked for help in restoring their home.\n\nNow it circles above the island, and whenever you complete an environmental / nature Impact-game with the animals’ help, it uses the collected trees, bushes, and leaves [z]to restore[-] the affected part of the island with its special abilities.\n\nAlong with the Squirrel, the Owl can also be chosen as a controllable character.\n\nThe Owl is controlled in the air [z]with mouse movement[-] in all directions, while [z]scrolling the mouse wheel[-] speeds it up or slows it down.

Mokus=Squirrel
MokusLeiras=The [z]Squirrel[-] is the game’s main character.\n\nBecause of its agility, endurance, and low needs, the animals entrusted it to explore the island in search of survival options and opportunities to reclaim their former habitat.\n\nWith its help you can discover the ruined, abandoned island and reach the places in need of restoration.\n\n[k]Special trait:[-] One of its favorite foods, the nut, can be used as a [a]Nut Shot.[-]\n\n[k]Restoration required to unlock:[-]\nThe Squirrel requires no restoration site—thanks to its minimal needs, it can survive for long periods even on the barren surface.\n\nThe Squirrel is moved with the [z]arrow keys[-] or the [z]WASD keys,[-] runs quickly when the [z]Shift key[-] is held down, and jumps when the [z]Ctrl key[-] is pressed.\n\n[z]Scrolling the mouse wheel[-] moves the camera closer to or farther from the Squirrel.\n\nIn the loaded game’s settings window, there is a [z]checkable option[-] (Player’s camera controlled only by mouse) which allows you to set whether the camera is controlled only by the mouse or also rotates automatically with the Squirrel.\n\nThe Squirrel [z]can also climb[-] thicker, straighter tree trunks—just jump onto the trunk.\n\nAlongside the Squirrel, you can also choose to control the Owl circling above the island.\n\nWith the [z]Owl’s help[-], you can view the island’s current state and the restoration sites from above.\n\nYou can switch back and forth between Squirrel and Owl with the [z]“C” key.[-]

Medve=Bear
MedveLeiras=The [z]Bear[-] embodies toughness and a massive appearance, while also being friendly by nature.\n\nIt loved that the island provided everything it needed: it could pick berries and fruits from bushes all day, satisfy its hunger with fish from the inner lake or the sea, and nap in the pleasant shade of the trees whenever it wished.\n\nThe new conditions on the island are unbearable for it: even the shelter of the cave is now far more welcoming than the barren surface.\n\n[k]Special trait:[-] Symbolizing its toughness, the Bear offers the [a]Stone Shot[-] among the available shots, giving it a chance to regain its former life.\n\n[k]Restoration required to unlock:[-] {0}\n\nAlong this path were the fruit trees and berry bushes the Bear loved so much, which are essential for it to be able to care for itself outside the cave.

Siraly=Seagull
SiralyLeiras=The [z]Seagull[-] once spent almost its entire life in the air and on the water: the coastal waters around the island were full of fish, and it could hatch its eggs undisturbed.\n\nNow it has nothing to eat, because the waters around the island have become polluted and the fish have disappeared.\n\n[k]Special trait:[-] The Seagull comes from the cold southern regions, where frozen seas are a natural sight.\n\nIt loved that place not only for the abundant food, but also for the beauty of its unique environment.\n\nIt was fascinated by the way sunlight sparkled on the floating ice, shimmering in brilliant rainbow colors.\n\nThen, to its dismay, everything slowly began to melt, the ice vanished, and with it the magical landscape.\n\nThe Seagull had to move on, and it was only by luck that it found such a wonderful new home on the island.\n\nMemories of its former home still live vividly within it, and because of this, it offers the [a]Freezing Shot[-] to help rebuild the island.\n\n[k]Restoration required to unlock:[-] {0}\n\nBecause of the fuel spilled from a truck that slid into the sea, the fish fled far away.\n\nThe Seagull no longer wants to search for another new home, because the island provided everything it needed.\n\nTo survive, it requires small fish and clean, fresh water.

Pok=Spider
PokLeiras=The [z]Spider[-] loved the little island: with its swamps and lakes, it was a true paradise, always providing it with fat, well-fed flying insects.\n\nIt spun its web, wrapped up its prey, and slowly consumed it.\n\nBut after the destruction of its environment, it can no longer spin its web, nor catch the already diminished number of insects.\n\n[k]Special trait:[-] To support the renewal of its environment, the Spider offers the [a]Vanishing Shot.[-]\n\n[k]Restoration required to unlock:[-] {0}\n\nThe Spider built its web in many places, but it was on the side of a kapok tree standing at the edge of the mangrove area that it found the most favorable insect routes.\n\nIt needs this tree, because only the insects caught in its web here can give it the best chance of survival.

Roka=Fox
RokaLeiras==The [z]Fox[-] greatly appreciated that the island met all of its needs: its primary food, the many rodents, scurried endlessly through the undergrowth, always at hand.\n\nAnd when it sought peace in the evenings, it could drift to sleep to the chorus of frogs bidding farewell to the sun and the crickets’ night song.\n\nMosquitoes loved the Fox, but the feeling was not mutual.\n\nIt hated them, and no matter how furiously it lashed out at them, it only attracted more.\n\nLuckily, the frogs brought order to the swarm of mosquitoes, and the Fox came to understand the true value of living in a community where animals not only care for themselves but also for one another.\n\nAfter its habitat was destroyed, the rodents it fed on vanished.\nOn the surface it found neither food nor shelter.\n\n[k]Special trait:[-] Its proud red fur now brings it no benefit, so the Fox gladly offers the [a]Fire Shot[-]—a symbol of its fiery coat and temperament—to help restore the island and bring back its favorite rodents.\n\n[k]Restoration required to unlock:[-] {0}\n\nWith the construction of the rocky road, the Fox’s den dug among the stones disappeared as if it had never existed.\n\nWithout its familiar, comfortable den, even the dark, damp cave offers better living conditions, for at least it provides shelter.\n\nRestoring the road’s original environment and its den is essential for the Fox’s life on the surface.

Vadkacsa=Mallard
VadkacsaLeiras=The [z]Mallard[-] spent most of his life in the marshy inner lake.\n\nEarlier he flew here from a distant peninsula, because there he was constantly disturbed and hunted.\n\nThe flashes and thunder of gun barrels still sometimes haunt his mind, reminding him of his terrible past life.\n\nOn this island, the peaceful environment, the many aquatic plants, duckweed, reeds, and the abundance of fish made him realize what a wonderful life he had—what a treasure he possessed.\n\nThe sight of the devastated island has utterly shattered him.\n\nWith his favorite lake polluted and its waters poisoned, he cannot return to his old habitat; only the cave remains as a shelter.\n\n[k]Special trait:[-] To regain his new life on the island, as a remnant of his wretched persecuted life on the peninsula, he offers a [a]Lightning Cloud,[-] able to release effective lightning against various cannons and batteries.\n\n[k]Restoration required to unlock:[-] {0}\n\nThe central big lake, the Mallard’s favorite spot, thanks to the inflowing stream and outflow channels, used to supply the animals with constantly fresh, oxygen-rich water.\n\nDuring logging, a tree fell into the main outflow and was left there, making the water stagnant and foul. Small fish and insects vanished, and aquatic plants began to rot.\n\nUntil his beloved lake is cleansed, the Mallard cannot return to his watery life.

FuvesUtMJNev=Littering
FuvesUtMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nAll over the world, conscious littering causes serious problems.\n\nIt clearly shows the carelessness and insensitivity of those who litter toward nature, and reveals much about their character as well.\n|{K203@Piles of trash disfiguring nature and polluting the soil}|\nBesides the sad sight of discarded items and heaps of waste, they also scar and disfigure the environment and may contaminate both the soil and its surroundings.\n\nThe concept of littering not only refers to the discarded waste itself, but also to the production of low-quality goods that turn into garbage in a very short time.\n\nDiscarded waste, illegally dumped trash, and decaying food leftovers pose serious dangers to animals, as they may eat or carry off the garbage, crawl into it, get entangled in it, and suffocate.\n\n|&K36&[p]Our littering destroys countless animals, and the enormous landfills ruin vast areas of high-quality, valuable soil.[-]|\n|{K204@Pollution of incomprehensible magnitude}|\nHow many times a day do you throw garbage into your bin? What kind of garbage do you throw away?\n\n|&K36&[k]Is there really nothing you can do with a single piece of your trash?[-]|\n\nLittering may seem like a tiny, almost negligible issue, yet it is one of the greatest environmental problems.\n\nIt is such a huge problem because the incomprehensible amount of products we constantly produce—along with their packaging—sooner or later all turn into waste (or garbage).\n\nAt present, we are far from being able to fully process it: partly because the countless types of waste pose enormous technical challenges, partly because recycling is expensive and not something we can (or want to) afford everywhere, and also because the sheer volume of waste generated is simply unmanageable.\n\n|&K36&[p]Humanity produces nearly 2 billion tons of municipal waste every year.[-]|\n\nThis staggering amount of waste—generated by households, hospitality, and businesses alike—could fill more than 800,000 Olympic swimming pools.\n|{K702@Each European produces on average 5.2 tons of waste, trash, and leftovers every year.| This staggering amount represents the waste generated by every single person among Europe’s 746 million inhabitants—and it comes out to more than 14 kilograms per person every day... How much waste is produced at your place daily and yearly?}|\nThe world’s total population keeps increasing, and the global range of products is expanding as well—which means the amount of waste generated is also growing—therefore, in the coming years there will be a great need to make global waste management more effective.\n\nWe are still far from being able to keep up with our waste.\n\n|&K36&[p]Over the course of a lifetime, one person produces about 600 times more waste than their own body weight [8].[-]|\n|{K403@When it comes to littering, there are no exceptions: beaches, streets, rivers, or just anywhere in nature...}|\n|{K407@After a running race—even our sporting activities are not free from waste. Although organizers usually collect the garbage, there could surely be other solutions (e.g., refillable, reusable bottles that can be carried, put down, or handed over) to quench thirst...}|\nUnfortunately, a big problem is that many of us do not realize the damage we cause with our waste—often discarded without sorting and therefore treated as communal garbage.\n\nThe huge amount of incinerated waste pollutes the air and contributes to global warming; while the piles of waste that end up in nature not only contaminate the soil but also poison lakes and rivers, and fill up the seas and oceans.\n\nBesides the litter that ends up in nature, why is waste incineration the worst-case scenario—even though in some power plants burning waste produces energy?\n\n|&K36&[p]Because it cuts off every possibility of recycling the waste.[-]|\n|{K506@A garbage truck collects and compresses our stinky mixed waste}|\n|{K108@An illegal dump site: infectious, burning, and polluting the air}|\n|{K603@Balloon releases are one of the most harmful holiday customs—when we let go of helium balloons, we also let go of the responsibility for the damage they cause to wildlife. According to an Australian study [1], balloons are the most dangerous type of litter for seabirds—but they are also dangerous to other animals. Animals eat the balloons (made of plastic or rubber, drifting an average of 70 km, but in some cases 400–500 km) or their burst remains, which slows their growth or even kills them—soft plastics can cause fatal intestinal blockages.  It can also be deadly if balloon strings get wrapped around animals, restricting their movement or breathing. This is equally true for so-called eco-friendly balloons [4]: the prescribed degradation time of biodegradable plastic is only guaranteed under special conditions—which do not exist in nature. In addition, we should conserve helium, as global reserves are quite limited and may run out in 25–30 years. Helium should be redirected to weather forecasting, ozone monitoring, and meteorological research balloons, rather than wasted on purposeless, polluting plastic balloons.}|\n|{K704@Many products (sometimes wrapped very attractively) contain too much packaging material, or their packaging is made of several different materials. Excessive packaging can be avoided (and perhaps more easily), but packaging made of multiple materials is more difficult for both us and recycling plants to deal with. We should tear packaging into separate pieces by material type and collect them separately for recycling. However, this is not always simple because of glue, staples, and other strong fixings. Another problem is that the types of materials are not always recognizable (e.g., many kinds of plastics, sometimes deceptive in look and feel, are used in packaging, and not all of them can go into selective recycling bins).}|\nThe only reasonable thing you can do against the mountains of waste overwhelming us is:\n\n|&K36&[a]###Reduce the amount of waste and garbage—of every kind—you generate in your daily life.[-]|\n\nBut this requires not only you, but everyone: producers, shops, and other consumers as well.\n|{K707@In front of stores, you can sometimes see  piles of waste like this (e.g., during selective waste collection). Yet shops could also help reduce waste generation by selecting their goods based on less and more recyclable packaging (all they would need to do is review their own generated waste), thereby encouraging both producers and consumers that change is needed.}|\nFrom a sustainability perspective, recycling causes problems because the companies that produce waste (e.g., packaging materials) have no motivating force to neutralize that waste, and since the place of production and the place of use are different, the responsibility falls on the state.\n\nThe profit remains with the companies that produce disposable packaging, while the cost of dealing with the waste does not—which is harmful to society as a whole, because the state must divert funds from elsewhere to finance recycling.\n\nThe great importance of recycling and selective waste collection lies in drawing people’s attention to the problem.\n\nSome forms of recycling are extremely cumbersome, requiring more energy and effort than can be saved by reuse—therefore they are not efficient and overall increase the burden on nature.\n\nBut this has also become the driving force of important processes: it encourages efforts to minimize waste and strengthens the “zero waste” principle.\n\nThese important efforts help reduce waste generation and therefore belong to the topic of prevention.\n|{K502@###What’s in your attic? Have you also experienced similar water shortages in your environment?}|\n|{K102@Plants fight to the very end against water scarcity and drought}|\nOne of the most serious challenges of the coming decades may be the lack of freshwater for humanity.\n\nMoreover, according to a joint report published in 2019 by UNICEF and WHO [5], this is already the present:\n\n|&K36&[p]Even now, every third person lacks access to safe drinking water.[-]|\n\nWhy? Because the growth of the Earth’s population, the skyrocketing demand for freshwater, and global warming are already causing serious water shortages in some regions—an issue only worsened by the unequal distribution of freshwater. The situation is continuously deteriorating, and the demand for water is increasing even more steeply than the population itself: between 1900 and 2014, the world’s population grew by 336 percent, while global freshwater demand rose from 671 billion cubic meters to 4 trillion cubic meters, which represents nearly a 600 percent increase!\n|{K706@Water tanks on rooftops in Cyprus.  Cyprus has been struggling with water shortages for a long time, and during the driest periods water is shipped in from Greece.}|\nClimate change is also continuously and significantly altering the water cycle, as higher temperatures increase evaporation. This means more severe droughts in some regions, while in others we can expect more sudden downpours and floods—and with rising average temperatures, increasingly less snowfall.\n\nWe must prevent a water crisis at all costs, because in addition to the geographically uneven distribution of freshwater, a growing population and the rising demand for food and energy will only worsen the shortages. By the middle of the century, more than half of humanity could be in a much more difficult situation.\n|{K908@The Oder lowlands near Fürstenberg, Germany, along the River Oder, suffering from recurring droughts and gradual drying.}|\n|&K36&[k]What are the possible causes of drought and desertification in inland areas?[-]|\n\nOne factor is the prolonged La Niña phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean basin, which brings cooling cold ocean currents. As a result, the cooler ocean evaporates less water into the tropics.\n\nAnother, even more serious factor is that unsaturated water vapor reaches inland areas. This is aggravated by the fact that water vapor has a very strong greenhouse effect and further intensifies warming.\n\nFor clouds and precipitation to form, water vapor must become saturated. However, this process can take a long time, since at higher temperatures more water vapor is needed for saturation.\n\nAnother factor is when cyclones shift northward and powerful anticyclones dominate the weather. These are characterized by cloud dispersal, which in summer is accompanied by heat waves.\n\nIt is also a problem when there is little moisture in the soil (for example after a prolonged drought), so not enough water returns to the atmosphere through plants.\n\nForests, wetlands, and river floodplains actively contribute to a wetter local climate through continuous evaporation.\n\nIf we cut down vegetation in these areas, drain or divert waters, reduce their size, and instead use the land for water-intensive agriculture, we accelerate the drying of the local climate (agroforestry has developed as a countermeasure, harmonizing agriculture with nature).\n\nIn addition to these drought-inducing factors, some regions are geologically predisposed to arid conditions. However, all of these conditions are intensified—negatively influenced—by climate change.\n\nClimate change accelerates warming and the melting of ice caps and glaciers, whose freshwater flows into the seas, adversely affecting (slowing down) ocean currents that also influence the climate.\n\nWith every additional degree Celsius of atmospheric warming, the air can hold about 7 percent more water vapor without becoming saturated. This not only makes precipitation formation harder and prolongs droughts, but also means that when warm, moisture-laden air suddenly cools and reaches the dew point, it can result in heavy rains and, in some cases, flash floods caused by torrential downpours. Neither extreme is good.\n\n|&K36&[a]###In addition to warming, climate change also negatively affects the water cycle.[-]| Help! Reduce your greenhouse gas emissions![-]|\n|{K302@Disappeared wetland: streambed dried up in severe drought}|\nThe equatorial rainforests of Amazonia repeatedly suffer from drought, and the increasingly frequent weather extremes do not spare the Amazon River—the richest in biodiversity on Earth—either, because prolonged dry periods may be followed by disproportionately heavy rainfall. By the end of 2023, the water level of the Amazon had dropped to a level not seen for more than a century.\n\nFor most of the year, the Amazon Basin, one of the wettest and rainiest regions on Earth, covers nearly half of the entire South American continent as its watershed—it is vitally important that the transported rainfall also reaches the lower parts of the continent.\n\nBoth sudden, heavy rainfall and the subsequent drought periods cause serious problems in the unique ecosystem and in human environments as well.\n\nAmazonian drought is a serious climate risk because plants absorb greenhouse gas carbon dioxide and incorporate it into their bodies, thereby helping to mitigate global warming.\n\nDeforestation and forest fires in the Amazon region threaten more than 8,000 native plant species and 2,300 animal species with a high risk of extinction.\n\nIn addition, the Amazon plays a key role in shaping the global climate and, through its evaporation, also contributes to the formation of rainfall.\n\nThe rainforest is a vital bulwark against climate change because of the carbon dioxide it absorbs and stores, therefore, in order to steer the global crises of climate change and biodiversity loss toward solutions, the fate of the Amazon region plays a central role.\n\nAlongside the Amazon, the fate of the Central African and Indonesian rainforests is also relevant, because frequent droughts (as well as deforestation and forest fires) have severely endangered the natural carbon dioxide absorption capacity of the equatorial rainforests of these continents.\n|{K205@The long-awaited rain came too late}|\nWetland areas are shrinking at an alarming rate worldwide.\n\nBetween 1970 and 2015, 35 percent of these particularly species-rich areas disappeared due to urban development near water, environmental pollution, and the negative effects of climate change.\n\n|&K36&[p]25 percent of the flora and fauna of wetlands are threatened with extinction.[-]|\n\nWe are receiving reports from more and more places that lakes are shrinking drastically due to the impacts of human intervention and/or climate change [24-28]. However, this process does not only mean local problems; it highlights a global environmental crisis.\n\nThe following lakes, listed as examples, were once significant, iconic representatives of their regions, but today they have receded and lost their precious natural value:\n\n- Lake Tuz (Turkey): The Konya Basin, where the lake is located, used to be the breadbasket of Turkey. However, alongside excessive agricultural irrigation, the region’s farmers drilled thousands of unauthorized wells. This, combined with the effects of climate change, led to the near-total depletion of the life-giving water resources.\n- Aral Sea (Central Asia): The largest human-caused ecological disaster in history. It was once the world’s fourth-largest lake, but the rivers flowing into it were diverted to irrigate cotton fields, which are extremely water-intensive. Today, the lake has lost more than 90% of its original surface area. Pesticides, fertilizers, and chemicals used on the cotton fields for decades have accumulated on the dry lake bed. The area has turned into a toxic desert, and the desert wind blows its salty, chemical-laden dust toward the surrounding population, causing various serious illnesses.\n- Lake Chad (Africa): Compared to the 1960s, it has lost about 90% of its surface area. This dramatic shrinkage was caused by a combination of severe droughts plaguing the area and the irrigation needs of a booming population, which has also led to serious humanitarian and political conflicts in the region.\n- Dead Sea (Middle East): Its water level drops by 1 to 1.2 meters per year. The main reason for this is that nearly 95% of the water from the Jordan River, which flows into it, is used for domestic and agricultural purposes in surrounding countries. Furthermore, the mineral extraction industry operating in the southern basin accelerates evaporation.\n- Great Salt Lake (USA): An iconic lake in the state of Utah, which closely resembles Lake Tuz. Due to climate change-induced drought and growing urban and agricultural water demands, it reached its lowest water level in history in 2022. Its area has shrunk to a fraction of its original size, threatening surrounding cities with toxic dust storms.\n- Lake Urmia (Iran): It was once the largest endorheic saltwater lake in the Middle East. Due to dams built on its rivers, illegal wells, and climate change, it has lost nearly 95% of its surface area in recent decades. Similar to Lake Tuz, it often turns red due to algae.\n- Mar Menor (Spain): Europe’s largest saltwater lagoon. Although it has not dried up completely, it has undergone an ecological collapse (oxygen depletion, mass fish kills) due to agricultural fertilizer runoff and rising water temperatures caused by climate change.\n- Lake Velence and Lake Balaton (Hungary): Vulnerable lakes of the Carpathian Basin. Although the water level of Lake Balaton is artificially regulated, prolonged summer droughts and high evaporation have created critical periods for both lakes in recent years. In 2022, Lake Velence sank close to its historical minimum, causing severe oxygen depletion and fish kills, and in 2026, it was directly threatened by drying out completely.\n\nThis list is by no means exhaustive (look it up), but it is highly eye-opening and highlights the environmental problems of the modern era.\n\nIn more and more places around the world, wetlands (among other ecosystems) are receding as a result of various irresponsible human interventions and rising temperatures, causing an ecological crisis in the affected regions. If we focused not on short-term, highly profitable, and resource-intensive activities, but on a harmonious coexistence that exploits nature less—and even restores it—we would also benefit, as our environment would remain livable in the long term.\n|{K606@Wetland habitats in urgent need of help—alongside restoration efforts, we must also examine the root causes to assess the scale of the problems}|\nAccording to some climate models, droughts will worsen in the future, and forest and bushfires will become more frequent.\n\nThis is also a very serious issue, because after forests burn, as much carbon dioxide is released back into the atmosphere as the forests had sequestered!\n|{K206@Prolonged drought can cause fires in nature}|\nExtreme heat and the increasingly intense UV (ultraviolet) radiation of sunlight, due to the thinning ozone layer (though hopefully this will stabilize), have very serious health-damaging effects.\n\nA generally accepted, important piece of advice is not to go out into the sun between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. in summer.\n\nIn the future, if we cannot stabilize the Earth’s climate and even make it worse, how will this advice change?\n\nDo not go out in the sun between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m.? It may contain soap residues, fats, oils, or paint residues, but with proper storage and treatment it can be reused in the household, though it is not drinkable.\n\nCollected rainwater is also considered greywater, because it gathers contaminants from the air and the gutter, but its contamination level is much lower than that of household greywater, and it can therefore be used even without treatment.\n\nHousehold greywater is thus recyclable (for example, for irrigation), but its composition must be examined—what contaminants it contains and to what extent.\n\n|&B28&[s]###You pollute greywater the least if you only use products made of natural ingredients for washing, dishwashing, laundry and cleaning—as well as cosmetics that contain only natural ingredients.[-]|\n\nIf we want to store greywater, we must collect, filter, and disinfect it separately in a greywater storage system.\n\nFiltration can be done, for example, with a root-zone treatment method similar to natural filtration. Before entering the tank, the collected rain- and greywater is filtered through a loose structure intertwined with the roots of plants (reed, sedge, cattail)—here most contaminants are filtered out, the organic matter content and heavy metal levels decrease.\n\nIf we do not have a greywater storage system, then the water must be used as soon as possible (within 1–2 days), because the bacteria multiplying in it can increase the risk of infection.\n\nAccording to experts, greywater can only be reused after filtration and disinfection, and only for specific purposes. Greywater containing detergent must not be used to irrigate food crops, only ornamental plants. OriasKapokFaMellettVezetoUtMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nOur wonderful Earth struggles with many great problems, including ever-increasing air pollution, to which kerosene-powered aircraft in air transport contribute an ever larger share [20].\n\nIn recent decades the number of flights has increased dramatically; as a consequence this sector’s greenhouse gas emissions are continuously growing, which—together with road-vehicle manufacturing—further deepens the climate and social crisis through polluting technologies [19].\n\nAccording to statistics, air travel is the safest and one of the fastest forms of transport, but also one of the most polluting, with an average emission of 285 grams of carbon dioxide per kilometer [15][23] (in the latter two respects only spaceflight exceeds it).\n|{K101@The aviation industry has clear contours. What do you think of this sight?}|\nThe sky-slicing contrails themselves—although short-lived compared to average greenhouse gases, yet still significant due to flight frequency—also contribute to global warming, because they reflect back toward Earth the heat energy heading for outer space.\n\nAt present, about 20 percent of people can afford (because it is accessible to them and they can pay for it) to travel by plane.\n\nAccording to 2024 data, there are 45,527 (identifiable from the air) airports on Earth [27] (one-third of them in the USA (!)), and their number is increasing year by year.\n\nBased on 2020 data, the total (passenger and cargo) aviation sector’s carbon dioxide emissions of 1 billion tons account for 2.5 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, but overall it contributes more to climate change because, through other warming side effects, it influences the climate in more complex ways [9].\n\n@###Ultimately, aviation, responsible for 3.5 percent of global warming, in addition to greenhouse gas emissions increases atmospheric ozone in the short term but reduces it in the long term, lowers methane levels, releases sulfurous and sooty compounds into the air, heats the upper atmosphere through fuel combustion, and creates long water vapor streaks (contrails) in the air that sometimes turn into cirrus clouds.\n\nThese environment-impacting components together produce a warming effect.\n\nAlthough most attention goes to carbon dioxide emissions, research shows that the additional warming effects—most notably contrails—contribute a larger share (about 2/3) to the warming.\n|{K404@###The comparison table shows the carbon dioxide emissions of different modes of transport per person per kilometer based on 2019 data [24]. SziklasUtMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nA volcano is one of the most intense and most dangerous natural forces.\n\nBesides the fact that an active volcano is very difficult to approach (only for professionals and researchers; everyone else should avoid it from as far as possible), it can cause extremely serious damage to both nature and human structures.\n\nThe activity starts from the magma chamber—these chambers are cavities in the Earth’s solid crust filled with molten rocks, created and driven by the Earth’s heat and, since primordial times, by the decay of various radioactive substances.\n\nUnder lithostatic pressure this melt moves along fault lines toward lower pressure (i.e., toward the surface), pushing apart, arching up, and absorbing the rocks above it—eventually forming a conduit (diatreme) through which the magma breaks to the surface [1][2].\n|{K101@At the beginning of an eruption of enormous power}|\nIt happens that the magma does not find a path upward and remains in the magma chamber for a longer time—then it begins to stratify and cool.\n\nDuring cooling, the silicate-bearing melt can hold less and less water in solution and releases various gases (carbon dioxide, sulfurous gases, etc.).\n\nThese gases continuously increase the internal pressure in the chamber, and when it exceeds the overburden pressure, the volcano begins its activity with a massive explosive eruption.\n|{K201@In some cases the ground itself splits open and the eruption starts from there}|\nA volcano is therefore a fissure through which the extremely hot molten rock material beneath the surface—magma—reaches the Earth’s surface.\n\nIf magma reaches the Earth’s surface, we call it lava.\n\nA volcanic eruption and the proximity of magma are signaled by escaping steam, sulfurous gases, earthquakes, and tremors.\n\nDepending on its type, an eruption is preceded by a series of explosions with a huge roar, after which the eruption column formed from the opened vents shoots the magma skyward like a fountain, and enormous pieces of molten rock rise into the air.\n\nMeanwhile, a fast-moving, all-devouring hot debris flow composed of rock fragments, volcanic ash particles, and gases (pyroclastic flow) rushes down the volcano’s flank.\n\nThis generally claims the most fatalities and, along with the lava, causes the greatest environmental devastation.\n|{K106@The fire-red glowing magma rises into the air with explosive force}|\nThe glowing rocks, the cascading hot torrent, the unbearably hot lava flowing down the volcano’s side, and the mudflows produced by the torrential rains that sometimes accompany eruptions destroy everything in their path.\n|{K206@Geysers and mudflows can also increase the extent of destruction}|\nThere is no effective way to stop lava; like water, it forces a path toward the smallest obstacle.\n|{K102@The glowing lava moves unstoppably down the mountainside}|\nThe smoke-like ash column rising during the eruption blankets the sky and, depending on the prevailing wind direction and wind speed, can travel thousands of kilometers.\n\nThe falling volcanic ash can cover a radius of 5–10 kilometers around the volcano in layers even a meter thick, thereby making all life impossible there.\n|{K302@The rising smoke and ash cover everything over a vast area}|\nThere are about 1,500 volcanoes on volcanoes, and even metropolises may be built near long-dormant volcanoes.\n\nHowever, because of the difficulties of forecasting eruptions, this can have unforeseeable consequences for the affected The research looked at electric vehicles registered in 2021 in India, China, Europe, and the U.S.—markets accounting for 70 percent of the world’s new-car sales—so the result is globally valid. For cars they assumed at least 18 years of use, and they took into account the energy sources used, current energy regulations, and the International Energy Agency’s projections as well.\n\nThe results: for a European car, electric vehicles emit 66–69 percent less; in the U.S., 60–68 percent less; in China (where there are more coal plants), 37–45 percent less; and in India (where coal plants dominate), 19–34 percent less harmful emissions compared to vehicles with internal combustion engines.\n\nManufacturing an electric car involves more emissions due to the large battery (battery recycling can improve this a lot), but this disadvantage can be offset by one year of use: after this time, the EV’s total life-cycle pollution becomes lower.\n\nGeorge Bieker, an ICCT researcher, stated [2]:\n\n|&B28&[a]“None of the vehicles with internal combustion engines can meet the targets needed to reduce the concentration of greenhouse gases in the fight against climate change. Our findings are globally valid, so we need to phase out internal combustion cars from the market worldwide.”[-]|\n\nThe study’s result is not surprising—by general consensus, one of the main drivers of global warming is the use of vehicles powered by internal combustion engines.\n\nThe European Union and several U.S. states have set the goal of phasing out internal combustion engines from 2035—their goals, actions, and results will be valuable and exemplary for the rest of the world.\n\n|&K36&[k]Why is this example-setting so important?[-]|\n\nOverpopulation comes with additional consumption, and people generally strive for convenience: therefore, in a very large share of households, acquiring a car is among the first plans.\n\nGiven that the pollution and climate-change-inducing impact of cars running on non-renewable fuels is very significant, that oil causes various environmental problems at every stage of its life cycle from extraction onward, and that we must expect a significant decline in oil within decades, the rapid transformation of the automotive industry has become a very important factor.\n\n|&K36&[a]On average, 80 million new cars are produced every year (a number the growing population is expected to boost further), and it makes a world of difference whether these cars run on fossil fuels and will keep polluting for decades, or on electricity, whose generation will become cheaper and cleaner year by year thanks to the rise of renewable energy.[-]|\n\nThe comparison of the environmental burdens of internal combustion and electric cars can also be expressed with numbers (thanks to vlogger András Horváth for the explanatory video [14]):\n\n1 liter of gasoline contains an amount of energy equivalent to 9.5 kWh of electricity. That means that filling 6 liters of fuel into an electric car with a 57 kWh battery—typically giving a 300–400 km range—would “fill” its tank.\n\nHow far can you go on 6 liters of fuel? 50–100 km? Perhaps 120 if you drive very economically?\n\nWhy is it that with the same amount of energy, electric cars go farther than internal combustion ones? Because the efficiency of electric cars is 72 percent, whereas that of internal combustion cars is 16 percent—and these values are measured from energy production all the way to its full use on the road (that is, from the power plant for EVs, and from the oil well to the moving wheels for ICE vehicles).\n\nBurning 1 liter of gasoline and 1 liter of diesel corresponds to 2.4 and 2.6 kilograms of carbon dioxide emissions, respectively (diesel contains more carbon atoms than gasoline) The reason more CO2 is produced than the weight of the fuel is that combustion requires oxygen—a lot of it (a carbon dioxide molecule consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms).\n\nThis means that a car with a 50-liter fuel tank turns a full tank of fuel (which a commuter can burn in as little as a week) into an average of 125 kilograms of carbon dioxide—and all of it goes into the atmosphere. 125 kilograms... that’s more than most people can lift; if it were a weight in front of us, we couldn’t even budge it... This amount of burned fuel already adds up to a combined 1-ton emission for just 8 cars, to which are added those toxic and smog-forming substances (carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, soot particles, etc.) that exit through exhaust pipes during imperfect combustion.\n\n|&K36&[p]Every time we burn a full tank of fuel (50 liters), we also decide to release 125 kilograms of carbon dioxide into the air, as well as toxic substances that can cause death within minutes in a confined space.[-]|\n|{K802@Carbon dioxide is a colorless, odorless, non-toxic gas. However, accumulated in the air it creates a greenhouse effect and becomes dangerous: it warms the Earth}|\nThe local (operational) carbon dioxide emissions of electric cars are zero, but there are still CO2 emissions whose amount depends on how much carbon dioxide is emitted to produce 1 kWh of electricity in the given country: in the case of nuclear power plants this is 10 grams, for coal plants 600 grams, and for solar (or other renewable-energy plants) almost 0, apart from their manufacturing.\n\nIn Central Europe, in Hungary, producing 1 kWh of electricity emits 200 grams of carbon dioxide—so if the energy does not come from solar panels but from power plants, then on average (for the above 57 kWh car and a 350 km range) 1 kilometer entails 33 grams of CO2, which means 3.3 kilograms per 100 kilometers.\n\nFor a similar-performance and similar-acceleration internal combustion car consuming 10 liters, carbon dioxide emissions are 25 kilograms per 100 kilometers.\n\n3.3 versus 25 kilograms of CO2—this is a huge difference even if we consider a very favorable 5-liter-per-100-km internal combustion car (then it’s 3.3 versus 12.5 kilograms of CO2).\n\nIn the aforementioned country of 10 million people (Hungary), 3.6 billion (3.600.000.000) liters of fuel are consumed annually, which means that 9 million tons (9.000.000.000 kilograms) of carbon dioxide are released into the air by all forms of road transport. If every road vehicle there were electric, then CO2 released into the air would be 2.2 million tons.\n\nIf you install solar panels on your roof (which, by the way, offset their carbon footprint in 3–7 months), and if the world also switched to renewable energies, then for you—and globally—this number would approach 0, because only the carbon cost of manufacturing renewable-energy plants (solar, wind, water, geothermal) would need to be considered.\n\nThe manufacturing of both internal combustion and electric cars has a carbon cost (on average 10 tons), to which for electric cars we must add the carbon emitted when producing the battery (which, for a larger 100 kWh battery, averages 5 tons).\n|{K803@We need every tool available to mitigate climate change—electric vehicles are among them}|\nIf, based on the above, an average electric car emits 4 times less carbon dioxide under average electricity generation and use, then (calculating with the EU energy mix) after 50,000 kilometers an electric car already recoups the extra carbon footprint from battery manufacturing compared to an internal combustion car. In a country that uses more alternative energy (e.g., Norway), this number drops to 15,000 kilometers.\n\nA quick calculation can reveal how long it takes an internal combustion car to catch up to the 5-ton carbon footprint of an electric car’s battery.\n\nAssuming an average favorable consumption of 6–7 liters/100 km, consider the previously mentioned commuter traveling 100 kilometers round trip on weekdays, who—with weekend driving—has to fill up their 50-liter tank once a week.\n\nBurning 50 liters per week results in an average of 125 kilograms of CO2; dividing the 5 tons by this shows that in just 40 weeks the “carbon advantage” of manufacturing the electric car’s battery is used up. Even if we halve the travel distance in the calculation, we still get only about one and a half years.\n\nAll things considered, over the entire life cycle from manufacturing, projected to 150–200 thousand kilometers, electric cars pollute roughly half as much (and only a small fraction of even that if the electricity is produced from alternative sources) compared to an internal-combustion car.\n\nIn everyday use—whether in the city, the countryside, anywhere—electric cars produce zero local air pollution, which significantly contributes to clean air in human communities and thus to healthier living conditions.\n\n|&K36&[k]What is the current position among manufacturers?[-]|\n\nCar and battery manufacturers have set out toward carbon neutrality; cobalt will be eliminated from batteries (LFP—LiFePO4, lithium iron phosphate—batteries already contain no cobalt), and both the production and reuse of lithium-ion batteries are getting greener: less water is used during manufacturing, and 95–98 percent are recycled, since the lithium and other raw materials they contain are practically treasure.\n\nNoticeable progress is also being made with carbon (graphene)-based and sodium-ion batteries, which likewise help make battery manufacturing more sustainable.\n\nGreater rates of recycling for cars and batteries will reduce our reliance on and dependency upon natural resources, the carbon dioxide emissions associated with mining, and the environmental damage that comes with it.\n\nIn addition, with technological progress, battery lifespans will increase—up to 20–25 years—and once expired, after recycling they can be repurposed for other energy-powered devices.\n|{K701@###Cleaner transport presents us with many tasks to solve in the areas of reducing environmental burdens, recyclability, and energy efficiency. If this balance is upset, the consequences can be very serious: entire species may go extinct, or multiply so much that the area can no longer support them.\n\nIt also happens that we irresponsibly release exotic pets or plants we’ve grown tired of (or they end up in nature by other means), which then proliferate or spread so extensively that they threaten native communities—and by then, getting rid of them becomes an extremely difficult task.\n|{K503@Common ragweed, Japanese beetle, brown marmorated stink bug, East African green shieldbug, and various slugs hiding in flowerpots and root balls that can endure long journeys. FeszerMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nSpace exploration is an extremely valuable endeavor, because it allows us to glimpse the past of outer space and can also provide answers regarding Earth’s future.\n|{K101@Our terrestrial beacons—cities and road networks}|\n|{K102@The sun rises and the Earth’s marvelous colors emerge from the darkness}|\nOur curiosity and desire for adventure directed toward outer space are immensely powerful.\n\nIn addition to feverishly searching for extraterrestrial life, we would also like to find a planet suitable for earthly life—somewhere we ourselves could relocate and expand.\n|{K203@Outer space is an exciting, mysterious adventure}|\nAlongside spacecraft that search for distant worlds or conduct Earth-observing research, we also launch many satellites that serve our comfort and communication needs: these are telecommunications and telecommunication satellites.\n|{K106@Earth is surrounded by an incredibly complex communications network}|\nThe tasks of communications satellites include message relay, multimedia broadcasting, providing internet services, and GPS positioning.\n|{K107@A rocket launch is an amazing sight up close...}|\n|{K108@...and from afar, too}|\nLike terrestrial services, services that use Earth orbit have problems as well as advantages—and we must face these too.\n\n|&K36&[p]Not only Earth’s land, seas, and oceans are polluted; unfortunately, space—Earth’s orbits—is no exception.[-]|\n\nSpace debris can be divided into several groups [1]: some are defunct or idle satellites, as well as burned-out carrier rockets and their fragments; another part is debris created and dispersed in Earth orbit as a result of collisions or explosions.\n\nIn addition, smaller and larger asteroid and meteoroid rock fragments captured by Earth’s gravity also reside in orbital regions.\n\nOver nearly seven decades, about 9,000 tons of space junk have accumulated, and they can be grouped into three size categories: larger than 10 centimeters (about 29,000), larger than 1 centimeter (about 670,000), and larger than 1 millimeter (about 170 million pieces).\n|{K302@Sadly, Earth’s orbits are littered too—let’s do what we can to keep outer space from becoming—just as a science- and sustainability-savvy journalist wrote [1]—a dumping ground for humanity’s cutting-edge technology...}|\nThe many millions of pieces of space debris orbit at speeds of at least 28,000 kilometers per hour (nearly 8 kilometers per second—speeds high enough to remain in orbit); even the tiniest fragments are dangerous to functioning satellites and spacecraft.\n\nFragments larger than 10 centimeters can tear a satellite apart; 1-centimeter pieces can disable a spacecraft or damage the shielding of the International Space Station; tiny, millimeter-sized bits can destroy subsystems of space hardware.\n|{K303@Like a gunshot—a piece of space debris punched a hole in the side of the spacecraft}|\nAs a result of our continuous development, more and more spacecraft and satellites are placed into Earth orbit—sometimes using more than 1 million liters of fuel (e.g., kerosene, a petroleum derivative with an inherently high environmental footprint).\n\nRocket emissions are off the charts: their fuels are toxic, and when burned they harm the environment—the combustion product, black soot, deposits in the stratosphere, where it can remain for years, thereby intensifying the greenhouse effect and damaging the ozone layer.\n\nReducing atmospheric pollution from launches and converting propellants to more environmentally friendly alternatives are vital tasks, because commercial launches will become increasingly frequent in the future\n\nModeling suggests that if the current number of launches were to increase tenfold by 2040, it would not only make the stratosphere busier but also ten times more polluted—amounting to about 10 million kilograms of soot dispersed.\n\nThis could increase the average temperature of the stratosphere by as much as 1.5 degrees Celsius, a change large enough to influence weather phenomena in Earth’s atmosphere—for example, it could alter the paths of storms and cyclones.\n\nFortunately, there are propellants planned/introduced that are more environmentally friendly: a methane–oxygen mixture, which burns efficiently and produces little soot, and hydrogen–oxygen propellant, whose exhaust is water—though it requires extremely costly technological infrastructure.\n\nHowever, these greener technologies can only be effective if they are extended to all space-service providers\n|{K307@It is an extremely urgent task to make rocket propellants more environmentally friendly. If this direction can be introduced at an affordable cost, it could also contribute to cleaner operations across the entire transport sector}|\nIn July 2020, 2,787 spacecraft orbited Earth; by the end of April 2022 there were 5,465, and according to the UCS Satellite Database [2], their number is steadily increasing—thousands, even tens of thousands (!) more are planned for the coming years.\n\nEighty-five percent of launched spacecraft are commercial; the remainder serve governmental, military, and civilian purposes.\n|{K306@The illustration highlights our astounding human capabilities: satellites communicating with each other and with terrestrial systems}|\nBecause of the multitude of spacecraft, the risk of collisions with space debris is growing, and the satellites we send will, in time, increase the amount of debris unless long-term, reliable solutions are found for cleanup.\n\nIn addition to the rising likelihood of orbital collisions, astronomers’ problems are also multiplying: satellites orbiting above 600 kilometers are the most disruptive to their work because they remain visible longer in the sky, and the thousands of satellites also complicate the work of the largest observatories.\n\nAstronomers have also warned that light reflected from satellites crowding the sky could erase the starry night, which has been part of human life since ancient times.\n|{K304@A long-exposure astrophotograph of the starry night sky}|\n|{K308@You yourself have a good chance of seeing a satellite with the naked eye [4] (or perhaps a larger piece of shiny-clad space debris) in the early evening sky. To do so, look up at the starry sky shortly after sunset—by then it is dark on the ground, but the sun still illuminates satellites orbiting high above. Satellites appear as white points moving across the sky at a steady pace; they have no light of their own: their bodies, mostly made of aluminum alloys, reflect sunlight. Unlike airplanes, they remain silent even when passing overhead and emit neither flashing nor non-white marker lights}|\nAstronomers understand that the spread of private satellite networks is part of the evolution of telecommunications; TaviOlajosHordokMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nSoil pollution is a global problem that affects the entire Earth.\n\nThis form of pollution primarily degrades soil quality, rendering it infertile.\n\nSoil (and groundwater) contamination is most often caused by landfills, but excessive agricultural fertilization and the use of pesticides also play a major role.\n|{K201@All kinds of trash burned—polluting the air and the soil}|\n|{K406@Animals rummaging around a huge, infectious dump}|\nAir pollution from industrial areas and places with heavy traffic also contaminates the soil—critically, in the form of acid rain.\n|{K302@The massive smoke pouring from a coal plant obscures even the sun}|\n|{K404@A landscape with fatal wounds}|\nWater pollution also falls within the topic of soil pollution when contaminants in the soil directly or via precipitation reach groundwater or nearby lakes and rivers—placing the organisms living there, including humans, in serious danger.\n|{K403@Algal blooms formed by fertilizer seeping into the lake endanger all aquatic life}|\nBut the reverse is also true: water pollution always pollutes soil as well, because toxins pass from water into the soil.\n|{K104@Saving this river requires immediate intervention}|\n|{K401@Oil derivatives that enter the water render both aquatic habitats and adjacent terrestrial habitats uninhabitable}|\n###Beyond pollution that directly affects the soil, deforestation; droughts resulting from the negative effects of climate change; washouts from heavy rains; improper tillage; improper storage of hazardous industrial waste; and irresponsible mining activities—all promote soil erosion and degradation.\n\nJane Rickson, a soil expert at Cranfield University in the UK, puts it plainly [9]:\n\n|&K36&[p]“The thin layer of soil covering the Earth’s surface represents the difference between survival and extinction for life on Earth. Only 3 percent of the planet’s total surface area—including oceans—is suitable for agricultural production, and every year 75 billion tons of topsoil are lost due to land degradation.”[-]|\n|{K208@Exhausted open-pit mining sites amount to an ecological catastrophe without restoration}|\nLaptop, tablet, mobile phone, game console, monitor, smart TV? Our everyday digital devices—you’ve likely used many of them.\n\nLead, cobalt, nickel, copper: among other things, these are the minerals obtained by mining that are needed to make them.\n\nThe impacts of mining activities on nature are immense: deforestation, soil erosion, soil, air, and water pollution, threats to biodiversity...\n\nKeep this in mind when you replace your digital devices—and therefore use them for as long as possible.\n|{K607@Every single digital device leaves a mark on nature}|\nIncreasingly frequent, prolonged heatwaves and droughts also degrade soil fertility, and wind easily sweeps away weakened, powdery soil.\n|{K203@Soil weakened by drought}|\n###Salinized soil—affecting 1 billion hectares worldwide (salinization is the salting of the soil’s upper fertile layer)—also causes enormous problems, because the accumulation of water-soluble salts (e.g., sodium salts), which plays a decisive role in its formation, reduces productivity and restricts 1.5 billion people in food production.\n\n###In addition to contributing to soil erosion, salinization degrades groundwater quality and adversely affects soil biodiversity, jeopardizing the global fight against hunger and poverty.\n\nMost saline soils are found in desert or semi-desert (or desertified) areas, and their formation often begins due to several factors at once, typically the following: deforestation; high groundwater levels (e.g., due to overirrigation); high sodium content in soil or groundwater; excessive and improper use of fertilizers; sea level rise (whose salty water infiltrates coastal soils and groundwater); irrigation with groundwater mixed with seawater; and climate change.\n|{K706@Saline soil can be restored through sustainable soil management. There are two main types of remediation: mechanical remediation, e.g., subsoil loosening, sand application (plowing in sand), more efficient water management; chemical remediation, e.g., liming, gypsum application, subsoil spreading, lignite powder spreading, and combined procedures thereof. To select the appropriate treatment, the extent and category of soil salinization must first be assessed (there are two salinization categories: if the accumulation of sodium salts is characteristic of the upper soil levels, it is solonchak; if it is deeper below the surface, it is solonetz) and the state of groundwater must be evaluated. To halt salinization and improve productivity, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has created a global map of saline soils [8]; however, salinization could be managed far more effectively by reducing or eliminating the causes that trigger it}|\nOf the salinization factors mentioned, (over)irrigation perhaps requires more explanation: irrigation often uses network (tap) water, well water, or river water, which are generally hard waters with high dissolved salt content and high mineral content.\n\nThus, if we water with such hard water, salt deposits will appear on the soil surface over time—this is salinization.\n\n|&K36&[k]###What is the natural solution against salinization?[-]|\n|&K36&[a]###Water with rainwater![-]|\n\n###Rainwater is distinctly soft water; it has no hardness—during evaporation from seas, rivers, and lakes, water does not carry minerals with it—the water evaporates and the salt stays behind. If it does contain a little hardness after all, it’s only as much as it gathers from the air while falling from the clouds.\n\n###Rainwater also has a low deuterium content (this is a natural variant of the hydrogen atom), which is advantageous from a health perspective—but rainwater still isn’t directly drinkable, simply because it can pick up a lot of pollutants from the air.\n\n###However, rainwater is excellent for watering, because first, compared to tap water it’s free, and second, it doesn’t ruin the soil; using it will make our plants more beautiful and yield better harvests.\n\n|&B28&[s]###Rainwater is of great value—don’t let it run off: for small backyard farming you can collect it, for example, in purchasable one-cubic-meter tanks, or even in old septic pits lined with pond foil (so the water doesn’t escape).[-]|\n\n###In large-scale farms, long ditches and canals created right next to, and separating, the agricultural areas can help capture rainwater, which later, in times of drought, will be a great treasure.\n|{K105@###Don’t let precious rainwater run off! Find a way to store it, whether it’s about your small garden or a large agricultural area}|\nBack to soil pollution: the greatest danger arises when it directly damages habitats, becomes accessible to living organisms, and enters food chains, thereby upsetting the ecosystem and nature’s balance.\n\n###In addition to deforestation, forest fires, habitat loss due to urbanization, the associated light pollution, and various water and air pollutants, the ever-expanding agricultural areas that replace forests, flower meadows, and wetlands; food scarcity; diseases; parasites; and mosquito-control and plant-protection chemicals sprayed into the air above and settling onto everything below are responsible for the disappearance of flying insects!\n\nThe situation of insects is further worsened by the fact that people often dislike them—and exterminate them in their immediate surroundings.\n\n|&K36&[p]###Over the last 30 years, the number of flying insects essential to life on Earth has dropped by one quarter worldwide, and by nearly three quarters (!) in Europe![-]|\n|{K101@Spraying of plant-protection chemicals (pesticides)}|\nFor example, in large-scale apple production, to achieve a marketable product it’s recommended to spray the trees at least 10–12 times—but in some places it may even be necessary up to 34 times [22].\n\nPlant-protection chemicals end up in the fruit, the soil, the groundwater, in insects, and in the bodies of the birds that eat them.\n\n|&K36&[p]###The biomass (living mass) of insects is decreasing worldwide by two and a half percent per year![-]|\n\nInsects are key to food chains, and bees and other pollinators are indispensable for maintaining agricultural productivity (and thus human nutrition) as well as for the reproduction of wild plants.\n\n|&K36&[k]How can the Earth get its insects back?[-][-]|\n\nThere are several important components to this:\n|&B28&[a]Global and climate protection factors:[-]|\n|&B28&[k]- Action against climate change (reducing carbon emissions): a warming climate and extreme droughts directly decimate insects. According to the conservation charity Buglife, cutting back on fossil fuels is key to stabilizing insect habitats.\n- Drastic reduction in pesticide use: phasing out synthetic insecticides and herbicides in agriculture is the most critical step to halting mass decline.\n- Preservation and restoration of natural habitats: protecting forests, wetlands, and wildflower meadows, as well as transforming intensive monoculture agricultural lands.\n- Transition to ecological and sustainable farming: supporting the adoption of chemical-free, biodiversity-friendly agricultural methods (e.g., organic farming, permaculture).\n- Creation of ecological corridors and green networks: protecting isolated areas is not enough; insect populations need interconnected, accessible "green corridors" across the landscape to migrate and breed.\n- Control of invasive species: introduced non-native plants and predatory insects displace native insect species, making the monitoring and control of invasive species essential.\n- Global mitigation of light pollution: turning off artificial night lights or using shielded, warm-toned LEDs, as light pollution disorients and kills nocturnal insects.\n- Stricter environmental regulations and political commitment: participating in local politics, voting for eco-friendly laws, and government funding for research.[-]|\n|&B28&[a]Community and local-level measures:[-]|\n|&B28&[k]- Planting native plants and wildflowers: introducing species into parks and gardens that provide food (nectar, pollen) for local insect life, instead of non-native ornamental plants.\n- Changing lawn management (mowing less): leaving wildflower bee pastures and unmown patches in cities and gardens instead of maintaining "sterile", weekly-mowed lawns.\n- Providing insect hotels and artificial nesting sites: creating nesting sites and shelters for solitary bees, wasps, and other beneficial arthropods.\n- Leaving leaf litter and dry branches: fallen leaves, decaying wood, and dead stalks provide critical overwintering sites and shelter for butterfly pupae, caterpillars, and beetles. Premature autumn or spring cleanups in the garden destroy them.\n- Providing safe water sources (insect waterers): insects also need water, especially during summer droughts. Muck or gravel and twigs should be placed in waterers so bees do not drown.\n- Conscious use of pet anti-parasitic treatments: tick and flea drops used on dogs and cats (e.g., fipronil, imidacloprid) are highly potent neurotoxins. When released into the environment (e.g., garden lawns or natural waters), even in tiny amounts, they kill a massive number of beneficial insects.\n- Promoting composting: compost piles not only enrich nutrients but also provide warm, safe shelter and food for larvae and decomposing insects during the winter.[-]|\n|&B28&[a]Individual consumer choices and awareness raising:[-]|\n|&B28&[k]- Buying sustainably sourced (eco/organic) food: shifting consumer demand toward products whose production does not harm insect habitats.\n- Environmental education and raising awareness of the role of insects: dispelling fears (e.g., about the appearance of insects or species mistakenly believed to be dangerous) and teaching the importance of pollinators and decomposers.[-]|\n\nInsects are vital to the ecosystem: besides pollination, they help recycle nutrients in the soil and break down organic waste.\n|{K106@Plant-protection chemicals kill bees individually... and in large numbers as well}|\nBecause of the decline in insect numbers, swallows, starlings, and other insect-eating birds are disappearing; in the absence of natural consumers, ticks, stink bugs, and mosquito invasions disrupt human communities, who then demand extermination.\n|{K506@Ticks, mosquitoes, stink bugs—pests that make our lives miserable. It is particularly important to understand how great these damages are and that our staple crops can only be produced in sufficient quantities under balanced climatic conditions. a 1 degrees Celsius increase in average temperature (we have already passed this) corresponds to about 300 kilometers.\n\nThat is why, for example, kiwifruit and fig orchards are multiplying in temperate climates (around the turn of the millennium these fruits survived only in Mediterranean climates), while large-scale production of apricot, peach, raspberry, or currant works less and less well.\n\nIn crop production, problems are caused not only by summer droughts, scorching sunshine, or flash floods, but also by spring frosts: rising temperatures mean that plants’ vegetation period starts earlier—sap flow can begin as early as February—so even a minor late spring frost can destroy the plant; the fruiting parts die and there will be no yield.\n\nTherefore there are crop species that must be let go, but there are also those whose cultivation cannot be avoided—wheat, corn, and globally rice—because they are among the most important food and fodder crops; here breeding can help.\n\nBreeding is already at the point where hybrids can be created that better adapt to dry, extreme weather, can take up moisture from deeper soil layers during drought, use that moisture more efficiently, and resist pests and various fungal diseases (the latter also reduces the use of plant-protection insecticides).\n\nHowever, for field crops it can take 8–10 years to create a new variety, which is a very long time compared to the speed of change.\n\nIt is also a question whether varieties produced with the most advanced biotechnological methods (for example, targeted mutation, which does not belong to GMO methods, yet was most recently classified as genetic modification in European regulation) will be allowed into commercial cultivation. These are precision breeding methods that can accelerate the development of new varieties. Their essence is that since we know the full genome maps of the most important cultivated plants, it is possible to intervene within a species precisely at the gene segment that is important to achieve the desired effect—for example, more favorable water uptake or better water use efficiency.\n\n|&K36&[a]We must adapt to the changes—and just as this applies to crop varieties, it also applies to soil cultivation.[-]|\n\nWhat tools can facilitate adaptation according to Csaba Gyuricza, agricultural engineer, soil science specialist, and rector of the Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences [29]?\n\n|&B28&[a]“The role of the press and public communication is very important. In consecutive years this may even require completely different cultivation strategies...}|\nIncreasingly dry seasons associated with climate change force farmers to adopt water-retention farming [14].\n\nThe essence of this is that wherever possible a larger proportion of precipitation must be retained, and water resources must not be allowed to run off.\n\nThis mode of farming seeks to prevent the rapid drainage of flood and inland waters (e.g., by channeling flood waves from rivers into reservoirs, or closing side branches of inland drainage canals), and it also gives rivers more room (regularly flooding floodplains also increases biodiversity and, by improving the microclimate, reduces irrigation demand).\n\nWater retention does not drain and does not bring under cultivation the deeper and poorer-quality parts of fields—where water regularly collects—but uses them to infiltrate moisture; and in water-poor, drier areas it does not necessarily continue arable farming but rather seeks to improve water retention, the microclimate, and biodiversity through grassland establishment, planting of tree rows, field margins, or forests of native tree species.\n\nBesides reservoirs, oxbows, canals, and small watercourses, soil itself can store a great deal of water and is often the largest reservoir in a given area.\n\nIn most places, however, intensive tillage with heavy machinery and chemicals has already degraded soil structure so much that it can store only a fraction of this.\n\nWhen soils are degraded, farmers can help themselves only by increasing the organic matter content of their fields or by switching to soil-regenerating cultivation.\n|{K1006@For agriculture it is crucial how much water can be retained alongside arable lands}|\nHumanity has been modifying and damaging the soil biota for millennia, upsetting the balance of soil fauna [16].\n\nThe real environmental problems, however, began when agriculture industrialized: with large machinery we became capable of bringing vast areas under cultivation, turning the soil multiple times and more deeply, and applying chemical fertilizers and pesticides—many of which are washed into the groundwater.\n\nTillage damages indispensable soil-dwelling communities in multiple ways: the plow slices earthworms; it turns over microbes with different oxygen demands living in various soil layers, killing a large proportion of them (they are then decomposed by organisms living at the surface, so their organically bound carbon enters the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, which drives climate change)—leading to a long-term decrease in soil organic matter content.\n\nPlowing greatly increases evaporation of water from the soil because it increases the evaporating surface and disrupts the harder top layer that protects the soil from drying out.\n\nPlow-based soil cultivation has other negative consequences as well: for example, when land is cultivated every year at the same depth, 15–20 centimeters. Here the soil compacts and does not let moisture pass, which cannot percolate down to the roots. This means that rainwater can only percolate that far; below it the soil remains dry, and during a rainfall inland water develops very quickly; the excess water remains on the surface and then evaporates.\n|{K1101@It has now become certain that with tillage-based agriculture we cannot maintain productivity in the long term. water becomes contaminated with toxic chemicals; and as the environment degrades, rainfall becomes increasingly rare.\n\nThere are very problematic plant-based raw materials such as palm oil, soybeans, coconuts, corn, rice, potatoes, and cotton.\n\nDemand for them is enormous, and their intensified production causes numerous major problems: due to land acquisition, their huge pesticide requirements, and basic production practices, they entail enormous environmental burdens and the exploitation and health damage of many people.\n\nTherefore, when we need such raw materials or products made from them, it is particularly important to act responsibly.\n\nWe do best if we choose those with organic certification from sustainable farming.\n\n|&K36&[a]###Seek connections with eco-farms: prefer their products and learn from them—they are at the forefront in applying sustainable cultivation methods![-]|\n|{K907@Syntropic farming is a sustainable response to monoculture. It returns to following natural systems and moves away from the damage caused by modern, chemical-laden monocultures. Its goal is to mimic the natural growth layers of forests, from groundcover plants through small understory shrubs to medium and taller trees. This form of farming can turn even a degraded area previously used for cattle ranching into lush forest while still producing food}|\n###Soil pollution, like other types of pollution, has many forms—and in most cases these are easy to recognize.\n\n|&B28&[s]###If you notice any environmental pollution—or, in more serious cases, environmental harm that causes lasting damage—report it to the competent authority according to its nature![-]|\n|{K307@Wherever we go, we leave our mark on the soil}|\n|{K301@Damaged or discarded household hazardous waste}|\n|{K402@Bromine and sulfur pollution extremely dangerous to soil, air, and health}|\n|&K36&[a]###Reporting environmental harm is not only a civic duty; by doing so, you also take part in the fight for your home and a livable Earth![-]|\n|{K207@###Soil often goes unnoticed—yet it is one of the most important components of life on Earth. The leaf litter covering the soil surface is also a very important component: besides eventually turning into humus, it shades and protects the soil (prevents excessive heating from the sun and protects against abrasion), retains and stores moisture like a sponge, which it then releases slowly to protect the soil from drying out; and it provides a home for many leaf-litter and soil-dwelling insects, beetles, and countless tiny creatures (microorganisms). Forest soils covered with leaf litter contain on average 15–35 tons of living organisms per hectare (bacteria, filamentous fungi, worms, insects, and other organisms), whereas on arable land this figure shrinks to 2–4 tons due to intensive agricultural production. This comparison also points to the need to better protect our arable land. One may argue that fertilizers can replace everything missing from the soil, but this is not so. We may produce large vegetables and nice-looking grain, but with ever less nutritional value. Moreover, soil conditioners and insecticides destroy soil life and reduce its regenerative capacity.}|\n|{K608@###In autumn—if possible—leave the fallen leaves under the trees in your garden (or if they bother you when scattered, rake them together under the trees around their trunks), because every leaf is valuable! By leaving the leaves, you improve the winter living conditions of many small litter-dwelling creatures, and you also protect the soil from wind and water erosion. By covering the soil with leaf litter, you ensure the replenishment of fresh, high-quality nutrients, which will be repaid with healthy, nutrient-rich crops. If for some reason you later decide to rake up the leaves, do it in spring: the withered leaves collected as green waste will take up only a tenth of the space in the bags}|\n|{K805@###You can make excellent use of raked leaf litter—or shredded bark (mulch) available in garden stores—in your garden: besides covering the soil, it provides a neat environment and an aesthetic appearance, suppresses weeds, lets rainwater through, reduces evaporation from the soil surface (thereby reducing the need for watering and saving water and energy), protects seedlings in beds and the roots and lower trunks of garden shrubs and trees from frost, and by slowly decomposing it becomes loose soil}|\n$|&K45&[s]Lesson[-]|\n\nIn agriculture, both “gazdálkodás” (stewardship) and “garázdálkodás” (reckless exploitation) occur.\n\nThe steward is careful and, with long-term goals, considers others as well; the reckless one keeps only their own short-term interests in view.\n\nThere are fundamentally well-intentioned activities about which only later do we learn whether they had beneficial or harmful effects on the environment—the following instructive story—which also fits the lessons of soil problems—is about river regulation.\n\nThe aim of river regulation is to provide more land for agriculture, make navigation easier, and enable rivers to carry away the large amounts of water that accumulate during thaws and heavy rains without extensive floodplains and overflows.\n\nBy cutting off meanders, regulation “straightens” the river, reduces its length and floodplain, but increases its gradient; consequently, the water flows faster, its current is stronger, and it deepens the bed—all of which increase bank-edge erosion (fortified with riprap) and lower the groundwater level.\n\nIn the end, this means that more water flows out at the lower reaches of the river than flows in with its catchments, because the deeper, accelerated river also carries away the groundwater.\n\nTherefore, logically, levees must be built along the regulated river to keep water within a much smaller area than the former floodplains (which can create disagreements where waters flow between countries).\n\nWe would need to produce on ever larger areas (which we do gain with regulation)—but since the spread of waters is missing, evaporation decreases and less rain falls—the lack of precipitation and the already declining groundwater due to regulation can have tragic consequences during droughts lasting weeks or months.\n\nIrrigation is necessary, but it is a very energy-intensive process and, over time, irrigated land becomes saline (river or well water has a significant mineral content, unlike rainwater, which is soft—i.e., without hardness or salt content).\n\nWhat does all this mean?\n\nThere will be more land for farming, but the local climate becomes drier, which entails greater water and energy use and arable-soil erosion; aquatic habitats shrink to a fraction of their original size; recurring drought weakens yields; and nature also struggles with water shortages.\n\nWhat is the solution? More water coverage is needed—even at the expense of agricultural land. Read back—this was the starting state before river regulation...\n\nIt is no accident that deserts now stand where irrigation-based ancient societies once were.\n|{K804@Regulated river sections: cut-off oxbows, bank-protecting riprap, and extensive agricultural areas}|\nRivers worldwide have undergone regulation and now flow between flood-protection embankments.\n\n|&K36&[a]Yet if we allow the natural outflow and return of water on floodplains, it beneficially regulates climate, food production, drinking water supply, and the functioning of ecosystems.[-]|\n\nWe increasingly obstruct this natural dynamic in many places—among other ways by regulating rivers, clearing floodplain vegetation, draining areas capable of retaining water, and building over and paving natural wetlands.\n|{K803@Unregulated, meandering river sections—let’s preserve and protect aquatic habitats, because they are indispensable natural systems that influence climate, precipitation supply, and thus human food security}|\nWhen you pass by parched, withered cornfields in forty-degree scorching heat and trees that shed their scorched leaves in summer, does it occur to you how vulnerable the planet is?\n\nWe have altered the Earth’s surface, and today we know what we should do: we should return more territory to its original steward—nature—and we would benefit too: we would gain a chance at cleaner air, water, and soil, and a more balanced earthly climate.\n|{K1005@Many of us, in our daily tasks and travels, see only the rows of roadside trees and the cultivated fields peeking out behind them.
