In this mixed, municipal form, it is indeed very hard to do anything with it, even though it may contain valuable raw materials suitable for recycling. Effective recycling requires not only producers and recyclers, but consumers as well: with conscious purchasing, do not add to garbage heaps; strive for less waste and do not toss it out mixed together—place it clean and sorted into collection bins, because only then can waste have a chance at recycling. If waste that could otherwise be recycled is burned or ends up in nature, it not only pollutes, but we also squander the energy that was used to make it back when it was still a product}|\n###To achieve results, we must let go of the “use and throw away” culture—which requires not only companies but also consumers: manufacturing and buying durable, high-quality products that generate less waste; expanding rental-based business models; reducing wastefulness (including the accumulation of unnecessary or superfluous items and food waste); and adopting an energy-saving lifestyle—all these foster more sustainable operation.\n\n###Transforming production into a circular system, scaling recycling up to meet production, and maximizing the reuse of materials produced—as well as ensuring the repairability of electronic and other products—will reduce raw-material use. Part of this is that single-use plastics must be banned worldwide, because their unmanageable quantities and low societal value cause serious problems for both human communities and nature.\n\n###To transform production, we should no longer rely on fossil fuels, but shift the energy transition toward green energy and equip every production sector with effective, innovative ideas and solutions focused on sustainability that help increase the use of alternative energy.\n\n###Transformation also requires that government incentives, grants, and calls for proposals not reward raw-material extraction, but the use of recycled materials, thereby making them cheaper.\n\n|&K36&[z]###The progress we make today on these tasks will have a huge impact on the lives of our children and grandchildren.[-]|\n|{K408@Although the illustration depicts the promise of decarbonizing industry, every sector without exception depends on hydrocarbons—therefore major changes are needed in every sector}|\n|{K506@Alongside the coronavirus, the warming associated with climate change and sea-level rise are also reshaping the corporate real-estate market, and it’s certain they will play an ever greater role in corporate decision-making. To avoid risks and expected extra costs in coastal areas due to rising sea levels, companies are relocating headquarters or building new sites in areas—far inland—they consider isolated from the effects of climate change. These companies already know exactly what climate change entails—therefore they are likely to set an example in mitigation as well through operations transformed to be sustainable}|\n$|&K45&[s]Lesson[-]|\n\nOnly we can solve the environmental problems we have caused.\n\nWe know the solutions, but they will involve serious sacrifices: we must reshape our lives—we must make them more environmentally conscious.\n|{K303@In the future, our technological agreements must also include environmental protection}|\nSome people question why a 1–2 degree Celsius rise in the Earth’s average temperature is a problem, since when they go outside they can’t even feel the difference.\n\nThe answer can be explained by the thermometer effect. At a 2 degree Celsius increase, a clearly febrile state exists, indicating an aggressive illness that requires immediate treatment.\n\n|&K36&[p]This is exactly the situation with the Earth—we have already crossed the threshold into a feverish state.[-]|\n\nThis is also indicated by the WMO’s data (from the mid-19th century) [11], according to which 18 of the 20 hottest years on record have occurred in the past two decades.\n\nIn Europe, 2020 was more than 1.2 degrees Celsius warmer than an average 19th-century year, even as the La Niña effect, which brings cold ocean currents, prevailed; globally, the year 2016 shares the title of warmest year with 2020 (based on 2021 data [10]).\n|{K304@We cannot expect outside help for our feverish Earth—only we humans can help it}|\nThanks to the enormous technological development of the last 20–30 years, our comfort, travel, and entertainment opportunities have expanded significantly—but this required the exploitation of the Earth, whose size and capacity have not expanded along with human demands.\n\n|&K36&[p]This short time was enough for us to reach the limits of the Earth’s tolerance.[-]|\n|{K207@In our accelerated world we fail to notice that the iceberg has also begun to move}|\nWe often hear the cliché “carpe diem”—seize the day.\n\n|&K36&[p]This unrestrained, wasteful life philosophy is why we must face more and more environmental problems that intensify year by year.[-]|\n\nThis selfish, all-consuming behavior makes our descendants’ inheritance uncertain.\n|{K206@###A fitting image—if you have a truly good idea, don’t keep it to yourself!}|\nJust because something isn’t banned by regulations doesn’t necessarily mean we should do it.\n\n|&K36&[a]We shouldn’t cut down trees without restoration, get into a polluting vehicle if there’s a cleaner alternative that’s acceptable in terms of time, buy plastics that immediately become waste, acquire things that are unnecessary for us and that we will never use or wear, or throw away any food when we know how many people are hungry.[-]|\n\nAnd this list could go on for a long time...\n|{K308@Excessive waste and overconsumption are driven powerfully by marketing. TeherautoMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nPetroleum (crude oil) is a naturally occurring mineral found in the Earth’s solid crust, a mixture of thousands of organic compounds formed over millions of years under high pressure through the decomposition and transformation of living organisms.\n\nCrude oil is a defining element of our development: as an energy carrier and as a petrochemical feedstock it represents enormous potential.\n\nBecause of crude oil—also called black gold—wars break out, its possession lifts societies into wasteful prosperity, while its absence drives societies into poverty.\n|{K401@Crude oil is an energy source formed from organisms that once lived on Earth}|\nCrude oil is a non-renewable energy source, and due to its increasingly intensive use we must expect its extractability to decline within a few decades, eventually leading to depletion (according to the www.worldometers.info 41 years of reserves left).\n\nBut we cannot wait until then, because climate scientists, environmental authorities, and the unusual changes observed in the climate of our own environment all say the same thing:\n\n|&K36&[p]Pollution from the extraction, processing, and use of crude oil—and of fossil energy carriers in general—places such a massive burden on the environment that it is pushing the Earth toward an ecological tipping point.[-]|\n\nSince the Industrial Revolution that began in the mid-18th century, with exponentially increasing consumption, in just under 300 years we have practically used up all the crude oil (and natural gas and coal are likely to share a similar fate later) that the Earth created over hundreds of millions—even billions—of years.\n\nThis also means that a few generations from now, people will no longer be able to count on crude oil and other dwindling fossil raw materials—therefore it is important that we pave alternative solutions today for future generations so that the hydrocarbon-free era does not arrive for them as a massive energy crisis.\n\n|&K36&[k]Why do we need to reduce our dependence on oil as quickly as possible?[-]|\n|&K36&[p]Because, in addition to the fact that its growing scarcity threatens a massive energy crisis, the dwindling supply of recoverable oil, combined with our insatiable appetite for it, will give rise to causes of social unrest and war—just as it is doing today.[-]|\n|{K308@We cannot wait until crude oil is depleted. Beyond the environmental damage caused by oil, we cannot wait for depletion because its absence would trigger a global energy crisis, and the possession of the remaining, still operating oil fields would generate causes for war. We can avoid these global problems only by switching to alternative energy sources that replace crude oil as soon as possible!}|\n|&K36&[k]What is (would be) the primary, indispensable role of crude oil and fossil energy carriers in general in the 21st century?[-]|\n|&K36&[a]To support building a circular economy and facilitate the green transition—in other words, to contribute to the development and rapid deployment of technologies and equipment for renewable energies.[-]|\n\nHowever, to achieve this we should not burn these valuable materials—needed to build a more livable, greener future—in our vehicles and power plants.\n\nCrude oil has numerous applications, but by no means do all of them cause problems: for example, plastic polystyrene building insulation brings significant climate benefits; effective thermal insulation can play a key role in fighting climate change and environmental pollution if we achieve very low (near-zero) energy demand for heating and cooling buildings (passive houses)—this could reduce the energy use of settlements by as much as 40–50 percent.\n\nThe problematic sides of crude oil are mostly in power generation, its use as a fuel, single-use plastic production, and accidents during its extraction and transportation.\n\nAmong the greatest environmental disasters are oil discharges into the sea due to negligence or accidents at deep-sea drilling rigs, or when an oil tanker runs aground or is otherwise damaged and the oil enters the sea [23][24].\n\nMarine and coastal life needs immediate help, because oil adheres to both animals and plants.\n\nThe soil, roots, and leaves of coastal plants also become saturated with toxic, photosynthesis-inhibiting water contaminated with oil, condemning them to slow death.\n|{K301@Oil spilled into water causes immediate damage to all aquatic life forms}|\nFish, birds, and other animals living on the coast become immobilized, soaked with oil, and their respiratory systems are fatally damaged.\n\nOil usually floats on the water’s surface, blocking oxygen from entering the water, but by adhering to sediment particles that enter the sea it can sink to the seabed and destroy the life there as well [19].\n|{K101@Oil spreads in the water and blocks the water from the air}|\nCrude oil contains numerous toxic compounds that can cause heart and immune diseases, developmental disorders, and even death.\n|{K202@The colors and smell of oil alike signal danger}|\n|&K36&[k]Many people have already asked why it is so hard to quit crude oil and other fossil energy carriers?[-]|\n\nBecause in recent decades we have become completely dependent on them.\n\nCrude oil is an excellent raw material and, together with coal and natural gas, (even today) readily available in large quantities; they are efficient energy sources, so economic sectors have built their technological development upon them.\n\nHuge sums have been invested in industrial manufacturing processes, all branches of transportation, and agriculture.\n\nTime also pressured manufacturers, because they had to serve a growing population that, besides housing and food needs, thirsted for comfort and responded well to technical innovations.\n\nIn recent years, however, we increasingly see that the explosive development enabled by fossil energy carriers cannot go on indefinitely.\n\nWe are extremely wasteful with energy; the drive to meet soaring consumer demand at all costs has blinded us—we focused on easily extractable earthly resources and neglected recycling.\n\nThe linear economy—in which living standards are guaranteed by consumption and continuous growth—comes with such high environmental pollution that it changes the Earth’s climate and threatens the functioning of natural systems.\n\nWe should change, but the development system we have built has enormous inertia.\n\nPeople have become accustomed to comfort, to the achievements of technological progress, to energy that seems limitless—and they do not want to give these up.\n|{K502@Is there no prosperity without destroying nature? Household-sized storage batteries are available, but this does not solve the problem for the industrial sector and grid-scale energy storage. Never pour cooking oil down the drain, but do not burn it or throw it in the trash either! (indeed, at the 2000 World Economic Forum in Davos, climate change was already called humanity’s greatest challenge) and the need to stabilize the composition of the atmosphere were living standards—which no country has yet been willing to forgo—this would only be conceivable if we could introduce energy-generation systems and industrial and agricultural production technologies operating on radically new principles different from current technologies that do not emit greenhouse gases.\n\nWe do have hopes for this (many global companies are carrying out such technology developments), yet for now our goal must be to use every possible current tool to reduce the carbon-dioxide emissions of the production processes we employ and to increase carbon sequestration, because we have already emitted—and still emit—such enormous quantities of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere that we will not be able to remove them any time soon.\n\n|&K36&[a]###Worldwide, more and more people—many of them young—understand how greatly climate change will affect their future and are demanding firm climate-protection measures from decision-makers.[-]|\n\nThe global “Fridays for Future” [4] movement was created inspired by Greta Thunberg, the famous environmental activist, and among other things demands that we limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.\n\nAll over the world the movement draws attention through demonstrations that only radical, system-level changes can stop the destruction of nature and the escalating climate crisis.\n|{K504@###“Fridays for Future” activists urge everyone to act against the climate crisis—and to join them.. Their goal is to exert moral pressure on decision-makers to listen to scientists and take decisive steps to limit global warming}|\nThe initiative is impressive, but the desired system-level change is enough only to postpone the natural disaster by one or two generations, because Arctic ice is melting, permafrost is thawing, extreme weather ignites hellish wildfires, and huge storms and rains flood settlements.\n\n###The solution is not in slowing environmental pollution and achieving climate neutrality, but in uncovering and eliminating the causes that trigger climate change.\n\n###One key element of this is relieving the burden on nature (reducing fossil-energy use, raw-material demand, and waste generation) by building a sustainable circular economy; another is removing carbon dioxide (and methane) accumulating in the atmosphere and causing warming.\n\n|&K36&[z]###An ideal circular economy needs only energy, no new raw materials, thus realizing the perfect circulation of materials.[-]|\n\nThere is a principle called “cradle to cradle” (whose founders are Prof. dr. Michael Braungart, a process engineer and chemist, and architect William McDonough), which is based on nature [14]—in nature, biological cycles leave no waste behind.\n\nThe currently still dominant linear economy espouses the cradle-to-grave principle, which always requires new raw materials and at the end of the process the products end up in the trash.\n\nHowever, raw materials are only available in finite quantities, and the resulting waste pollutes the environment.\n\nThe cradle-to-cradle principle is the opposite of the linear economy: it does not squander the valuable resources used in products, but recycles them through environmentally friendly production and the use of renewable energy.\n\nThis requires designing products to be fully recyclable through chemical and physical processes, and manufacturers must take products back to recover raw materials—therefore products would not be purchasable, but obtainable via deposit, rental, or leasing.\n\n|&K36&[z]The result in the ideal case is a world without waste.[-]|\n\nIn a circular economy that seeks to imitate the functioning of nature, the resources used therefore remain in the system for longer and through many more cycles, thereby reducing the amount of raw materials used and waste generated (bearing in mind that a worn material—e.g., rusted iron—can never be reused fully).\n\n###Up to the Industrial Revolution, the operational model of human society conformed to nature and to a circular economy—the fossil energy carriers started the process that knocked humanity out of nature’s circularity.\n\n###It is beyond doubt that the release of quantities of energy previously unimaginable also had very serious benefits, as we owe to it our development to levels that seem almost unbelievable even today.\n\n###By now, however, we have reached a technological level where we are capable of returning to a circular economy, but we must implement it differently than before, because a system entirely different from today’s can no longer align with consumerist incentives and continuous growth.\n\n|&K36&[a]###We must switch to a model that manufactures less but in exchange provides more services and more maintenance: repair, refurbish, and operate.[-]|\n\nWe will still need the service of a given object in the future (whether a bicycle, printer, or angle grinder), but we must imagine two things differently: products must be designed to be durable, long-lived, and repairable; and for many products renting is sufficient—there is no need to purchase and own them, as these merely increase raw-material outstandings and generate further production and consumerist incentives.\n\nWith less manufacturing, workers will not end up on the street, because the workforce will shift to the service sector.\n\nToday we defend jobs tooth and nail from animal husbandry to car manufacturing—but if people were provided with the knowledge that enables them to participate actively in the transformation, then they could decide their fate themselves—so that the transformation does not just happen to them.\n\nIt is certain that in the transformation, states and market actors that define the business sphere will dominate, but let us not forget that the basis of all production and services is the user (i.e., the buyer), who through conscious purchasing—thus with their money—can exert significant influence on how the circular economy develops and turns out.\n\nConsumers who participate actively in the transforming economy must be offered alternatives that are better—and more sustainable—than before; to do this we must step one level above the consumer and review the business model: for example, how people could commute to work or take their children to school without a car; how to create favorable conditions and benefits to make their homes more sustainable.\n|{K503@###One of the most important tasks for the engineers of the future will be to design machines and production processes that, while generating no waste, are climate neutral—or even climate positive}|\nIn parallel with building a circular economy, we must also fulfill another indispensable requirement to stabilize the Earth’s climate: we must remove the greenhouse gases we have pumped into the atmosphere.\n\nHowever, this can succeed only if we manage to curb further greenhouse-gas emissions from human activities as well.\n\nPart of carbon-dioxide removal (CDR) from the atmosphere would be entrusted to nature through projects aimed at protecting and restoring natural carbon sinks—the oceans, forests, and soils [22]—which would also advance the handling of the worsening environmental and biodiversity crises; and at present we do not know of better solutions than these for removing CO2 from the air.\n\nAnother—artificial—means of removing carbon dioxide is DAC (Direct Air Capture) technology: air is moved through turbines and CO2 is filtered out of it.\n\nDAC, which is under continuous development, is expensive and at present can remove only about 0.1 million tons of CO2 per year worldwide (human activities emit nearly 40 billion tons annually—four hundred thousand times more), but according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), together with advanced batteries and hydrogen electrolyzers it will help the transition to a net-zero-emission energy system.\n\nThere is also CCS (Carbon Capture and Storage) technology, a CO2 capture, storage, and utilization technology primarily used to reduce emissions from factories and power plants.\n\nCaptured carbon dioxide must be stored; one solution is deep geological storage: liquefied CO2 is pumped deep into the ground, into rock cavities or the depleted porous geological media of oil and gas fields.\n\nWe are still far from a breakthrough for CCS technology, because it is primarily fossil-fuel power plants that use it (of the 36 million tons of CO2 captured by CCS, a significant share is related to coal- and gas-fired plants), and due to the high cost of the technology, developments are often suspended on the grounds that they are not economically viable.\n\nCCS is also hampered by the lack of targeted state support for its development and deployment, and by a CO2 price that is too low—thus it is not worth investing in expensive technologies.\n\nAccording to research by geological experts, deep storage of CO2 can be considered geologically and technically safe, because well-chosen storage sites can retain the injected gas for spans measurable on a geological timescale.\n\nHowever, no one can answer what will happen to future humans if, for example, due to an earthquake, the vast quantities of CO2 sealed in long-forgotten underground cavities are released by then...\n|{K508@###For now we know of no technology as effective in capturing and binding carbon dioxide as a tree}|\nEnvironmental activists are also skeptical of CCS technology, because the currently affordable technology would be introduced at power plants that already harm the environment—this could greenwash coal plants, but the environmental destruction and air pollution from mining and burning would remain alarmingly present.\n\nAt present there is no human technology that can effectively combat our astronomical CO2 emissions.\n\nMoreover, fossil energy carriers—primarily responsible for greenhouse-gas emissions—are forecast to remain indispensable to energy supply for decades to come.\n\nThe far more effective solution than any other would be to reduce their use to the lowest possible level as soon as possible.\n\nThis would be effective and cost-saving because, per kilogram of CO2, curbing emissions costs much less than using negative-emission plants that remove CO2, and the environmental damage caused by emissions is already so great that it cannot even be measured in money.\n|{K606@###Today, one of the most urgent issues concerning climate change is curbing carbon-dioxide emissions; however, to meet climate-neutrality goals, surplus CO2 must also be removed from the atmosphere. From time to time, startup programs are announced that help realize good ideas with business, professional, and financial support}|\nSome believe that climate change has already run amok and that more drastic solutions are needed to mitigate the climate crisis and reduce economic damage.\n\nTo this end, geoengineering [17][18] has emerged, with two branches: increasing outgoing energy (the already mentioned CDR technologies) and decreasing incoming energy (SRM—Solar Radiation Management—solar geoengineering).\n\nSRM technologies are intended to reduce the intensity of sunlight reaching the Earth that warms the surface.\n\nThis includes space-based shading, cloud whitening, foaming the ocean surface, or injecting light-reflecting sulfur dioxide or chalk dust (calcium carbonate) into the stratosphere.\n\nStratospheric concepts are based on volcanic activity, as materials ejected into the upper atmosphere during eruptions can, on average, trigger up to a 1 degree Celsius drop in global temperature for a few years.\n\nIt’s clear that SRM technologies are uncertain emergency measures that would significantly interfere with the planet’s life by disrupting atmospheric processes and manipulating sunlight essential for life on Earth.\n\nNumerous university and institute scientists [5] emphasize that the potential downsides of solutions aimed at reducing the impact of solar radiation far outweigh the benefits, and therefore urge that all experimentation related to SRM technologies be terminated through an international agreement.\n\nThere is currently no global regulation—anyone could start experimenting with the technology (if they have the funds) if they feel that warming threatens their enterprise or profits.\n|{K601@SRM technology would reduce the intensity of sunlight reaching the Earth—the natural world does this with clouds}|\nGeoengineering solutions that intervene in our planet’s energy balance can be considered extremely risky, uncertain, symptomatic treatments that mask the real problem instead of solving it.\n\n|&K36&[k]###What is the real problem?[-]|\n\n###Our mind-boggling greenhouse-gas emissions.\n\n###Let’s reduce our emissions and use and develop safe technologies for carbon removal and sequestration, because only these can lead to outcomes that don’t destroy life on Earth.\n\nFor countries, there are three concepts related to stopping global warming that limit emissions.\n\nCarbon neutrality does not require emission cuts (emissions may even grow), but all emissions must be offset (through investments in CO2-absorbing environmental projects and by purchasing carbon credits).\n\nWith net-zero emissions, emissions actually decrease, and the country emits only as much greenhouse gas as it absorbs, while also investing in offset projects.\n\nWith zero emissions there are no harmful emissions at all.\n\nThe latter is still a very distant goal for every country.\n\nThese concepts apply not only to countries, but to their citizens as well.\n\n|&K36&[a]###Strive for net-zero—or better yet, zero—emissions![-]|\n\n###By doing so, you not only make your country’s enormous task of reducing emissions easier, you also help the environment!\n\nEASAC (the European Academies’ Science Advisory Council) highlighted in its 2018 report [7] the slowness of climate measures, a delay that rests in part on the belief that technology will solve the problems in time.\n\nThe report also explained that the public and political decision-makers are unaware of how significant a CO2 reduction is needed to meet the goals of the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement—essentially, to keep warming definitely below 1.5 degrees compared to the pre-industrial level.\n\nTo this end, EASAC analyzed a number of negative-emissions technologies, including the following:\n\n|&B28&[k]- Afforestation and reforestation;\n\n- Maintaining and increasing soils’ carbon-sequestration capacity, carbon-sequestering agriculture;\n\n- Biomass utilization (power generation) coupled with CO2 capture and storage technology (BECCS);\n\n- Geochemical carbon-dioxide-binding processes (e.g., rock weathering);\n\n- Direct air capture of CO2 coupled with CO2 storage technology;\n\n- Increasing the oceans’ CO2-absorbing capacity.[-]|\n\nTo mitigate (indeed, to stop) warming, we will likely need to consider all atmospheric CO2-reduction technologies, while we cannot rely on them alone—first and foremost, all of us must reduce our emissions.\n\nIn the end, the development and application of CO2-sequestration technologies are absolutely necessary, but calculations suggest [8] that we would need 30,000 large, mind-bogglingly expensive CO2 capture plants (involving $15 trillion of investment) to neutralize our current annual global CO2 emissions.\n\nIf we wanted to remove only one quarter of that (10 gigatons—i.e., 10 billion tons), it would require as much energy as one-sixth of humanity’s current total use—and to this we must add the enormous raw-material demand required to build the system.\n\nSome CDR technologies can bring major benefits and co-benefits, while others involve trade-offs—environmental risks, food-supply, or energy-efficiency issues.\n\nThe weathering of rocks and silicates is one of the Earth’s thermostats—an important feature is that it removes CO2 from the atmosphere. Naturally it works like this: the more CO2 in the atmosphere, the warmer the climate and the faster the water cycle, but the greater the weathering too, which reduces CO2. However, this works only over longer timescales (on Earth’s timescale)—if the input is larger, the removal is larger as well. Experimenting with accelerated rock weathering is worth pursuing—every solution that can help reduce atmospheric CO2 concentration is needed.\n\nAll things considered, the more and the longer the Earth’s average temperature exceeds 1.5 degrees Celsius, the more we will later have to rely on these CO2 removal methods.\n\nSkeptics fear that the promise of CO2-sequestration systems could obstruct the fight to cut CO2 emissions—this is a trap humanity must avoid at all costs.\n\n|&K36&[a]We cannot wait for technology to solve the ever-growing problems that accompany warming year after year. To limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, the most reliable solution is drastic emission cuts—as soon as possible.[-]|\n$|&K45&[s]Prevention[-]|\n\nThe explosive technological development seen in recent decades in industrial, agricultural, transport, and household sectors is undeniably due in part to the multifaceted uses of crude oil.\n\nBut unfortunately this development has a dark side, because every life-cycle stage of crude oil involves environmental pollution: its extraction, refining, and use (transport, energy industry, plastics manufacturing, petrochemicals) alike.\n\nBesides oil pollution entering nature, its storage, transport, and end-of-life disposal (e.g., used motor oil) are also serious environmental burdens.\n|{K403@Oil is dangerous in every form when it enters our environment; we should take much better care to contain it}|\n|{K307@Oil refining (fractional distillation of crude into components) is an air-polluting industry}|\n|&K36&[a]###The time will come for all of us when—for the sake of protecting life on Earth—we can no longer depend on fossil fuels.[-]|\n\nOr, from another perspective:\n\n|&K36&[a]###Humanity can win the fight to restore the climate only if it gives up its dependence on fossil fuels.[-]|\n\nThe sooner this happens, the greater the chance that we will be able to heal the terrible wounds we have inflicted on the Earth.\n\nEnding our dependence on fossil fuels would not only benefit the climate, it would also ease violent rivalries by removing a major trigger.\n|{K207@Abandoned ships are serious environmental burdens too. Metal alloys, paints, oily and greasy parts, plastic compounds—life-threatening substances in the water}|\n|{K506@A sunken fishing vessel polluting the Baltic Sea coast}|\nAchieving results requires, first and foremost, an environmentally conscious mindset, persuading others, and supporting influential individuals and organizations that prioritize environmental protection and the preservation of wildlife.\n|{K105@###Environmental protection needs far more support to have a fighting chance against pollution and its root causes}|\n|&B28&[s]###You are already supporting the reduction of hydrocarbon use if you travel by bicycle, buy an electric car and power it from rooftop solar, and upgrade your heating system to a heat pump.[-]|\n|&B28&[s]###If you are thinking of building a new house, apply practices that have already proven themselves in many places. These include, for example, passive houses, active houses, or even the more nature-friendly Earthship approach.[-]|\n|&K36&[a]###Passive houses—buildings that operate without conventional heating or cooling technology—can be realized in every climate zone, for every building type, both for new builds and renovations.[-]|\n\nA passive house is a building standard aimed at minimizing a building’s energy loss, therefore it places special emphasis on good insulation, airtightness, and suitable windows [29]. The relatively small amount of heat needed to achieve the desired temperature is supplied primarily by solar radiation from outside, while a significant portion of internal heat comes from people and electrical appliances. In passive houses, energy efficiency is achieved by controlling the indoor environment—for example, regulating indoor temperature and ventilation, i.e., post-heating or post-cooling the air mass moved to keep the air fresh. A passive house offers numerous advantages, such as low heating and cooling costs, environmentally friendly operation, and high indoor comfort. Its construction cost is generally higher—and pays off only in the longer term—but due to its sustainability it counts among forward-looking house-building methods.\n\nAn active house represents a further level of energy efficiency compared to a passive house. In active houses, renewable energy and energy recovery are also integrated into the building’s system [30]. For example, they can use solar panels or wind power to generate electricity, as well as heat pumps, solar thermal collectors, or geothermal energy for heating and cooling. The goal of active houses is to achieve the building’s energy independence—that is, to be self-sufficient and consume little or no grid energy. This usually results in higher upfront investment but can yield significant long-term savings. Because of their environmentally friendly heating/cooling techniques, like passive houses their spread helps mitigate global warming.\n|{K701@A passive—and, thanks to the solar panels—an active house under construction}|\nAn Earthship is a self-sufficient, sustainable dwelling that significantly reduces energy consumption and operates in an environmentally friendly way [28]. They typically use recycled and natural materials, such as old tires, glass bottles, tin cans, and other waste. These wastes are built into the walls during construction, exploiting their insulating and heat-storage properties.\n\nHow do Earthships become self-sustaining buildings?\n\n|&B28&[k]- Self-sufficient energy: They use wind systems and solar panels to generate electricity—the roof-mounted solar panels collect solar energy, which is stored in batteries to provide power at night and during cloudy periods.\n\n- Natural heating and cooling: Their design prioritizes passive heating and cooling—the placement of buildings and the arrangement of windows are oriented to harness natural solar energy and minimize heat loss.\n\n- Water collection and use: Rainwater harvesting systems collect precipitation into appropriate storage, then use treated water for irrigation and other household activities.\n\n- Biologically treated wastewater: Biological treatment systems process wastewater so it can be reused for irrigation or released into the natural environment.\n\n- Food production: They often include greenhouses or indoor gardens where residents can grow their own food, aiding self-sufficiency and self-reliance.[-]|\n\nThe Earthship concept is applied in many places worldwide and is an increasingly popular choice in environmentally conscious and sustainable architecture. These buildings are excellent examples of how human creativity and innovative thinking can combine with eco-conscious design to reduce buildings’ environmental impact.\n|{K702@Earthship houses built in a desert area. In deserts, everything besides sunlight is scarce and there are no utilities—therefore houses built in such places must be self-sustaining}|\n|{K206@Hobbit houses (earth-sheltered homes) are also proven examples of nature-friendly, eco-conscious building. Because they are thickly covered with soil, they are much more resistant to extreme weather—they cool and heat much more slowly. The thick soil layer acts as a thermal buffer, resulting in a more even indoor temperature}|\nTruly energy-conscious homebuilding does not start with purchasing materials and equipment, but with choosing the right plot, taking orientation and topography into account.\n\nA southern orientation and many south-facing windows mean more captured solar energy; in hilly regions a south-facing slope likewise brings more sunshine and also dampens the strength of the north wind.\n\nGreening the garden logically is also important: from the north, it’s advisable to plant evergreens that keep their foliage in winter and protect against the cold north wind, while on the south side large-canopy, deciduous trees are practical—they soften the summer heat with their shade, while in winter the warming sun shines through their bare branches.\n\nIt’s not only passive houses that point to the future, and similar to Earthships there are other homes made of natural or recycled materials, designed in an eco-friendly way, powered by renewables, and livable with minimal environmental burden, which—besides being earthquake-proof—help reduce our environmental footprint.\n\n|&B28&[s]###Look into the houses built from PET bottles in Panama [25], the HOPEone buildings [26], and the Lifehaus house [27]![-]|\n\nIt’s not only passive houses that can be operated efficiently in a natural way—orientation, siting, and shading matter for every home.\n\nOrienting the apartment/house to the south and designing larger transparent (glass) surfaces lets a lot of solar energy into the living space.\n\nTo counter excessive summer heating, large-canopy trees, less frequent mowing of greenery (e.g., grass), and various shading solutions can provide relief.\n\nEnergy-saving solutions can be combined. There’s no need to wait for “the perfect solution.” Take small steps—but take them regularly!\n|{K104@###How energy-efficiently do you live?}|\n|{K103@###Reduce environmental burdens by using electric transportation vehicles}|\n|&B28&[s]###Plastic is made from petroleum. Plastic waste is an unnecessary, enormous burden for us and for nature!}|\nIn most developed countries, there has been a clear move toward sustainable, renewable energies.\n\nIn developing countries, however, the transition is far from simple, because their modernizing regions are only now reaching the level where they can access basic technological tools (e.g., transportation) and afford a more comfortable lifestyle.\n\nThey will not be able to afford modern renewable technology (and it would have to be built out), so they are likely to turn to well-established fossil energy.\n\n|&K36&[k]What can be done?[-]|\n\nAlongside exemplary individual eco-conscious attitudes from citizens of developed countries, the governments of developed countries must support developing ones in transitioning to renewables as quickly as possible, since climate change and the accompanying warming affect every country equally.\n\nResearchers at the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), in their 2021 report [6], are far from optimistic: in their view, the global oil, gas, and coal industries could continue to expand for decades, and even by 2050 the use of fossil energy and emissions are not expected to peak. Perfect combustion of natural gas produces carbon dioxide and water, without smoke, soot, ash, and with very low harmful byproducts (carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides). However, the CO2 released by burning natural gas imposes such an extra environmental load on the atmosphere that vegetation cannot offset it. For this reason, the burning of natural gas—considered cheap (setting aside gas shortages and price rises due to the war in Ukraine)—should be curtailed, which is anything but simple, because coal and wood are not good alternatives (their combustion produces more harmful substances and also CO2 emissions), electric heating is expensive to install and maintain (though while a heat-pump system is costly to install, its operation requires much lower expenditure), and hydrogen technology is likewise expensive and still has much development ahead of it. best}|\nA new energy carrier has also appeared on the market: hydrogen, which many regard as the missing link in the energy transition [20][21].\n\nThere are three types: green hydrogen (during production, a sustainable power source splits water into hydrogen and oxygen via electrolysis, with the electricity coming from renewable sources), gray hydrogen (produced by steam reforming the methane that makes up natural gas), and blue hydrogen (also a natural-gas-based technology—methane steam reforming or pyrolysis—but it does not lead to greenhouse-gas emissions because the process is combined with carbon capture and storage, CCS).\n\nHydrogen can be used in transport (fuel-cell hydrogen vehicles), in industry (to facilitate conversion to low carbon intensity), and since heat can be obtained from it without greenhouse-gas emissions—and its applications in many ways resemble those of natural gas—it offers a suitable alternative to fossil fuels (thus it can also be used in various power-generation solutions).\n\nHydrogen has good energy-storage capabilities (the same amount contains three times as much energy as gasoline), which can bridge the problems of electricity storage (battery storage efficiency, and the scarcity, weight, and costs of the raw materials needed for their manufacture).\n\nTransporting hydrogen is much cheaper (5–10 percent) compared to transmitting electricity, and existing gas pipelines can also be adapted to carry it.\n\nEnvironmentally friendly hydrogen (its use releases no harmful substances into the environment, as only water is produced) helps the energy transition and supports renewables (e.g., hydrogen produced from renewable sources during the summer can help meet heating needs in winter—when less renewable energy is available).\n|{K602@Hydrogen, by supporting renewables, can help the green energy transition}|\nBy 2050, hydrogen’s share of the EU’s total energy mix may reach 13–14 percent, showing that the energy economy is completely built on them, it favors hydrogen produced from fossil fuels—which is cheaper to produce compared to green hydrogen (and this maintains the practice of exploiting natural resources).\n\nThus, the EU seeks to promote the spread of hydrogen regardless of its source, assuming that renewable-based variants will gradually replace fossil-based ones.\n\nHowever, the spread of hydrogen must also be supported by end users (industrial processes, vehicle owners, and households) by investing in costly hydrogen-based technologies and appliances.\n\nIf, in the future, hydrogen can be spread globally across all economic sectors and its production shifted toward green pathways, it will benefit not only us but the environment as well.\n\nFor this, the technologies that produce and use hydrogen must become cheaper, and it must also be solved that hydrogen does not leak (the hydrogen molecule is very small, so traditional seals do not work)—and thus enter the atmosphere—during transport, at end users, and from tanks during storage under high pressure or in liquid form.\n\nThis is a concern because, over a 100-year interval, hydrogen is 11 times worse for global warming than the same amount of carbon dioxide, as it reacts with various atmospheric gases and indirectly multiplies the greenhouse effect.\n|{K405@The tasks enshrined in UN agreements will affect not only economic sectors but everyday people too—everyone is needed if we are to master these challenges}|\nWe must wait for the promised results, but according to climate experts we can already take it as a fact that we will reach 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming by 2030 at the latest, with all its consequences.\n\nIndeed, according to the WMO (World Meteorological Organization) 2022 report [11] and a 2022 analysis in The Guardian [12], there is nearly a 50 percent chance that we will cross the 1.5-degree threshold by 2026.\n\nAnother expert view [13] shows the same: according to authoritative estimates, the carbon budget associated with 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming will last for about 6 years, and for 2 degrees Celsius about 24 years—this is the time we have until we hit those notable warming thresholds.\n\nThe WMO emphasizes that reaching 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming does not yet mean sustained warming; cooler years may still come, but we must act very quickly.\n\nIf, without a significant reduction in carbon emissions, we also surpass a 2-degree Celsius increase, we will have to reckon with very severe consequences.\n\nHalf a year after the 2021 climate conference in Glasgow, representatives of more than 40 countries gathered in Copenhagen to discuss results achieved since then. What did they conclude? That there are still no signs that countries are fulfilling their commitments.\n\nThis is also supported by the fact that EU emissions have returned to pre-pandemic levels: in the fourth quarter of 2021 (over 3 months) the economy’s greenhouse-gas emissions were 1,041 million tons, which not only reached but already exceeded the pre-pandemic period’s emissions...\n\nThe 2022 COP27 conference held in Sharm el-Sheikh [31] did not deliver a breakthrough either: alongside the climate targets set for 2030, the world is still—counting optimistically—heading toward 2.5 degrees Celsius of global warming by the end of the century, and temperatures will continue to rise in the next century as well.\n\nConsequently, considering the current emissions intensity arising from the use of fossil fuels, holding the 1.5-degree threshold already falls into the “not feasible” category, and even the most optimistic scenario (if countries were to implement their official pledges along with their long-term net-zero-by-2050 targets) would mean an average temperature increase of 1.8 degrees Celsius.\n\nNearly 200 states did agree to provide financial support to developing countries to address the losses and damages caused by climate change, but experts rated this only as symptomatic treatment.\n\nOn the main causes of climate change—phasing out coal, oil, and natural gas—no substantive progress was made; only efforts toward the gradual phase-out of coal made it into the final document.\n\nClimate protection can be realized only through effective, compromise-ready cooperation between countries and governments; without this, our task will be very difficult.\n\nThe results of the 2023 COP28 conference held in Dubai finally give some reason for optimism: nearly 200 countries agreed on moving away from the use of oil, natural gas, and coal, and agreements were made to increase renewable energy capacity, accelerate the green transition, and support adaptation to climate change.\n\nThese agreements provide a clear direction for national-level decision-making, regulation, and economic actors; however, they do not mean a complete phase-out of fossil fuels and do not impose obligations regarding reducing their use.\n\nEverything depends on actual, practical implementation, because the world’s 2030 climate goals are still insufficient to curb climate change.\n\nTo be able to counterbalance the effects of climate change, beyond the climate-friendly goals set out in the agreements, we also have many other tasks on which we must likewise make progress:\n\n|&B28&[k]- In addition to forest protection, we must suppress forest fires, restore the quality of natural waters and soils we have damaged, and prevent further pollution.\n\n- We must reduce the plastic—and many other materials—waste we release into the environment, develop reuse, and clean the oceans of the enormous floating garbage patches.\n\n- We must stop the 6th wave of extinction by restoring destroyed natural habitats, increasing and preserving biodiversity, protecting ocean life, and safeguarding endangered species.\n\n- We must transform agriculture to focus on feeding people rather than feeding livestock—and return the areas thus freed to nature.\n\n- For the sake of our health and a livable future, we must modernize our daily lives—make them cleaner and more energy-efficient.\n\n- We must solve our overpopulation problem.\n\n- We must support underdeveloped regions in their unequal struggle against climate change, and provide information and education for all inhabitants of the Earth so that everyone understands what climate change means and what role they must play in reducing and averting it.[-]|\n|{K204@###We have a great deal to and because, according to the FAO, fishing and the industries built upon it are key factors in the fight against hunger and malnutrition.\n\nSince 1961, annual fish consumption has grown at twice the pace of the world’s total population, and with the growth of the global population, by 2030 we will eat 20 percent more fish—therefore fish farms will play a defining role in the sustainable food industry (already half (!) of the fish consumed comes from these farms), as the amount of fish caught in their natural environment has hardly changed since the late 1980s due to intensive fishing.\n\nThe FAO seeks to mitigate losses by cooperating with developing countries—for example, assisting with drying animals caught from Lake Tanganyika, or offering better technology for catching crabs in the Indian Ocean—in the former case they reduced damage by 50 percent, in the latter by 40 percent.\n\nIn addition, reducing illegal fishing is also among the goals—though among long-term goals—partly because it is currently very difficult to estimate the amounts actually caught, and partly because one of the basic conditions for preserving global fish stocks is to operate fishing under continuous supervision.\n|{K203@###How will we be able to supply an ever-growing population with ever-shrinking earthly resources? Data published by oceanconservancy.org and sourced from Statista [10] clearly show that plastic entering nature, after fragmenting into microplastics, also gets into our food, drinks, and air}|\nIn addition to fragmented microplastics, small lens-sized plastic pellets (plastic processing feedstock containing mixtures of various chemicals and fossil fuels—typically polypropylene, polystyrene or polyvinyl chloride) are also very serious hazards and persistent pollutants in natural waters—causing at least as much damage as oil spills.\n\nSeabirds, fish, turtles, dolphins, whales and other wildlife often mistake these substances—which also act like toxic sponges by attracting other chemical pollutants in the water—for food and ingest them, and they usually die from them—causing immeasurable damage to the seas and to the fishing industry.\n\nPlastic pellets circulate in the ocean with the currents for decades before washing ashore; GazTartalyMJNev=Methane gas swamps
GazTartalyMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n|&K36&[k]What is climate change and the greenhouse effect?[-]|\n\nThe main cause of climate change is the increase of the greenhouse effect [3].\n\nThe acceleration of temperature rise can also be caused by natural effects, but it is human activities that are largely responsible for it.\n\nSince the Industrial Revolution, year after year we have been releasing greenhouse gases into the atmosphere continuously and in increasing amounts, which raise the temperature of the lower layer of the atmosphere (the troposphere).\n\nThe energy from the sun and the greenhouse effect are indispensable for life on Earth; however, human-made greenhouse gases trap a large part of the heat energy that enters the atmosphere (approx. half reaches the surface through the air and clouds), then is radiated back from the surface in the form of infrared heat (approx. 90 percent is absorbed and re-emitted), thereby slowing heat loss to outer space.\n\nThe greater the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, the longer the sun’s heat energy warms the Earth, thus the higher the temperature will be.\n\n|&K36&[k]Which greenhouse gases most intensively trigger warming?[-]|\n|&B28&[k]- water vapor: the most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, and as the Earth’s climate warms its concentration also increases; however, it is not directly the cause of warming (the warming oceans also increase its amount in the atmosphere), but it amplifies the climate change already underway;\n\n- carbon dioxide: a very important component of the atmosphere (e.g., necessary for plant photosynthesis), it also enters the air naturally (e.g., volcanic eruptions), but over the past century it has been the main driver of climate change due to human activities (e.g., burning of fossil fuels—coal, natural gas, oil—deforestation, forest fires, improper use of soil). Since the Industrial Revolution its atmospheric amount has increased by 50 percent.\n\n- methane: it can be produced naturally (e.g by the decay of organic matter in wetlands) and by human activities (e.g., landfills, rice cultivation, livestock breeding, their manure, leaks from the production and transport of fossil fuels). Molecule for molecule methane is a much stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, but it occurs much less frequently in the atmosphere. Since industrialization its concentration has nearly tripled.\n\n- nitrous oxide: a powerful greenhouse gas; the increase in its atmospheric concentration (it has risen by 18 percent in the last 100 years) is primarily due to agricultural practices (organic fertilizers, soil fumigants), nitric acid production, the burning of fossil fuels and biomass fuels.\n\n- halogenated hydrocarbons (Chlorofluorocarbons—CFC gases): artificially produced compounds that were used as refrigerants, solvents, and aerosol propellants. The international agreement “Montreal Protocol” regulates CFCs, because in addition to their greenhouse effect they also damage the ozone layer.[-]|\n|{K106@Solar energy + atmospheric greenhouse gases = increase in the greenhouse effect}|\nIn the perennially frozen (permafrost) regions of North America and North Asia there are vast expanses of methane gas swamps.\n\nThe main problem with methane gas is that it is an extremely strong greenhouse gas.\n\nAlthough after its emission it remains in the atmosphere for a shorter time—10–15 years—compared to carbon dioxide, which can warm the Earth’s climate for up to two hundred years, the greenhouse effect of methane gas is 28 times stronger.\n\nNo one knows for sure what effect the melting of contiguous permafrost areas would have (will have), but experts predict a tipping point [9].\n\nIf the methane (and carbon dioxide) deposits beneficially trapped by Canada’s and Siberia’s permanently frozen regions—which make up 22 percent of the Northern Hemisphere—were to be released into the atmosphere, they would increase the Earth’s average temperature by half a degree Celsius in a very short time.\n\n|&K36&[p]Permafrost areas have already started to melt.[-]|\n\nMoreover, as a result of the Siberian warming in 2020 and 2021, the melting of both permanent and seasonal permafrost has accelerated.\n\nConsequently, methane formation has also accelerated, because microbes that decompose organic matter also release methane; as temperatures rise, they are able to break down the large amounts of undecomposed animal and plant remains found in the thawing soil, and methane is released in the process.\n\nA self-reinforcing process can also start: more and more methane and carbon dioxide trapped in ice enter the atmosphere, which further accelerates global warming, and as a result the melting also speeds up.\n\nMelting raises other problems as well [11]: from the thawing layers of frozen soil, pathogens dangerous to humans—microbes and viruses—can emerge from shallow human or animal graves long buried (it is not possible to dig deep graves in permanently frozen ground).\n\nMore and more people may migrate to the thawing landscapes to mine mineral resources, and any infection acquired there could be spread around the world.\n\nDue to melting and the warming weather (beyond the Arctic Circle the environment is warming three times faster than elsewhere), forest fires are also becoming more frequent, which in turn destroy the peat essential for the persistence of permafrost.\n|{K206@Melting permafrost area}|\n|{K208@Fragmented remains of a tidewater glacier}|\n|{K204@Mossing-over alpine tundra zone}|\nMelting permafrost affects not only the climate, but also the Arctic human infrastructure and future construction projects.
