WCMJNev=Extreme cold|Extreme weather
WCMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nIn some places on Earth, unbearable heat tests nature, elsewhere extreme cold does.\n\nNowadays, unusually cold weather strikes even places where it was not typical before.\n|{K103@Unidentifiable vehicles, paralyzed transportation}|\n|{K301@The sudden severe cold froze the air’s humidity as rime onto the trees}|\nNeither the people living there nor the animal and plant life are accustomed to the great challenges posed by extreme cold.\n\nIn a bitterly cold environment, crops cannot be grown, waters freeze, and everything lies dormant as long as it can endure the extreme conditions.\n\nHowever, it is not only truly severe cold that counts as extreme; it is also extreme if, in a tropical or Mediterranean area, the temperature suddenly drops by several tens of degrees and the locals have to face a completely different kind of weather.\n|{K206@The processes of nature go dormant—it is as if time itself stands still}|\n|&K36&[p]What might be behind extremely cold weather?[-]|\n\nThe answer is to be found in the polar vortexes.\n\nThese are gigantic cyclones (low-pressure, cold-air areas) the size of five Europes forming above the North and South Poles between November and March, which rotate counterclockwise in the north and clockwise in the south due to the Coriolis force.\n|{K105@Huge, rotating cyclone—the northern polar vortex}|\nThese cyclones keep cold air over the poles and protect them from melting, while shielding more distant areas from severe frosts.\n\nIn average winters, less solar energy results in cooling of the polar regions.\n\nAir currents encircle these cold regions and form a stable polar vortex, which, in cooperation with the associated stable jet stream, does not allow the cold to escape (the jet stream is a several-thousand-kilometer-long, several-hundred-kilometer-wide, kilometer-thick, swirling, fast-flowing layer of air in the planet’s upper atmosphere).\n\nThe occasional cold outbreaks beyond the polar circles and the melting of the polar ice sheets are linked to the operation of the polar vortex, more precisely to its weakening [2].\n\n|&K36&[p]According to some research and observations, the vortexes are clearly weakening due to global warming.[-]|\n\nA weak vortex develops when warmer-than-usual air circulates over the poles, because in this case a smaller temperature and pressure difference develops between the cold polar air and the warmer air further south.\n\nIf, after a sudden stratospheric warming in winter, the behavior of the jet stream changes, it can affect—i.e., weaken—the polar vortex, which in a chain reaction also feeds back on the jet stream, further disrupting (weakening) its usual operation.\n\nIf the jet stream weakens, warmer southern air can break north and colder polar air can break south.\n\nIn such a case we can experience unusual winter weather—instead of seasonally appropriate conditions, extremes; for example, extremely cold air flows from the Arctic into mid-latitude continental European or North American regions, while record-breaking heat is measured in parts of the Northern Hemisphere.\n|{K302@Have you ever experienced what a truly “bone-chilling” cold is like?}|\nAnother important topic influencing the Earth’s climate is ocean currents.\n\nThese currents are constantly in motion: the Earth’s rotation, prevailing winds, underwater topography, and the position of the continents influence the direction and speed of the water’s movement.\n\nOcean circulation systems driven by differences in temperature and salinity, with tremendous power, help equalize the temperature of the oceans and sustain the marine ecosystem.\n\n|&K36&[p]In recent decades, the circulation of the oceans appears to be changing, and this is true for the Atlantic’s slowing AMOC and Gulf Stream as well.[-]|\n\nThe AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation—of which the Gulf Stream is a part, i.e., the AMOC is practically the continuation of the Gulf Stream) brings warmer, less dense surface seawater that, due to the consequences of global warming, is unable to cool adequately upon reaching the polar regions and thus cannot sink deep enough to continue its return flow southward, maintaining the circulation.\n\nAs a result, both horizontal and vertical currents slow down.\n\nBesides affecting the weather, the slowdown of the circulation system results in cooling along the Atlantic coasts due to the loss of the warm current; and because it does not remove heat from the air, it may also promote climate change.\n\nClimate change does not only mean warming, but also an increase in the intensity and number of extreme events.\n\nMuch of Europe’s weather is regulated by two airflows: the more predictable, less variable zonal flow, and the wild, north–south meridional flow.\n\nLately, the meridional flow responsible for weather extremes has become increasingly dominant [9].\n\nThe reason is that the huge amounts of cold freshwater from melting Greenlandic ice mix with the warm water of the northbound Gulf Stream in the ocean, diluting it and hindering its further flow.\n\nThe warm water is unable to continue flowing north; the circulation slows, and because of its underperformance, the atmosphere must take over its role (since temperature differences prevailing on Earth must be equalized)—however, the difference in specific heat between air and water is several thousandfold, which intensifies the north–south meridional airflow.\n|{K202@Although ocean currents are hidden from us, they can be imagined like the jet streams on the planet Jupiter in this artistic depiction}|\nThe Gulf Stream is driven by the Coriolis force arising from the Earth’s rotation, while the AMOC is driven by thermohaline circulation [10].\n\nThermohaline circulation operates based on two fundamental physical facts: salt is heavier than water, and warm water is lighter than cold water.\n\nIn the tropics, ocean seawater is saltier than in the polar seas because the ocean is warmer in the tropics and thus evaporates more, but the salt cannot evaporate; it remains in the water because it has greater weight.\n\nTherefore, salty, warm seawater with buoyancy due to heat sets off northward, but after a while the environment cools the water, eliminating its buoyancy, and the saline water mass begins to sink due to its weight, then turns back southward in the deeper layers of the ocean.\n\nThis sinking and turning back occurs in the huge, several-million-square-kilometer downwelling zone of the Icelandic region.\n\nThis worked well for millennia, but now Greenland is melting rapidly and this disrupts the functioning of the entire system.\n\nBetween Canada and Greenland, the meltwater entering the sea collides with the circulation system and begins to sink the ocean water, so thermohaline circulation no longer begins at Iceland, but has shifted much farther southwest, and this also affects the Gulf Stream, slowing it.\n\nSince the AMOC is practically the continuation of the Gulf Stream, if it slows greatly or stops, the warm water will pile up where it should take over the transport function, and the sea will overheat.\n\nThe result is occurring before our eyes: this caused the extreme Florida heat wave of 2023—the water warmed to 38 degrees Celsius near Florida because the Gulf Stream’s warm water is piling up and not being transported toward the Arctic.\n\n|&K36&[k]Can the AMOC stop?[-]|\n\nYes. Earlier research put this at less than a 10 percent chance for the 21st century, pointing more to the 22nd century; however, a study by researchers at the University of Copenhagen, published in Nature in July 2023 [8], defines a much earlier time interval: with 95 percent probability between 2025 and 2095.\n\nIn scientific circles, the study publicizing the grave conclusions is criticized for its logical particularities, its broad time interval, and its focus on a single main factor—the burning of fossil fuels—while many other factors influence the extremely complex climatic changes.\n\nThe latter is undoubtedly true; however, it is also beyond doubt today that the already high and still continuously rising concentrations of greenhouse gases have an ever-increasing influence on the entire natural ecosystem—which this research ultimately also confirms.\n\nWhat did the researchers start from?\n\n|&K36&[p]From the assumption that humanity will not be able to drastically reduce its pollution that causes the greenhouse effect.[-]|\n\nThe significance of the research lies in the fact that it points out:\n\n|&K36&[a]###The serious, dramatic turning points of climate change will not happen in the distant future, but in the present, before our eyes, so we must act against them now.[-]|\n\nLászló Molnár, a meteorologist who graduated from the Faculty of Science at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE-TTK) in Hungary and researches long-term forecasts, said the following in a 2023 interview [10]:\n\n|&B28&[a]“There are still no signs of the sustainable transition that would curb climate change and might help us avoid the shutdown of the AMOC, and we know of no technologies with which the current civilization could be maintained without further increases in emissions.\n\nEnergy use also has its own evolution: for tens of thousands of years we used wood, then for several hundred years coal; we have used oil for roughly a hundred years, gas and uranium and hydropower for a few decades, and solar and wind power only this intensively for a few years.\n\nThese cycles are getting shorter and shorter, and it is not the case that we have switched from one to another. We still burn wood, only in larger volumes. We are not coming off any energy source; we are stacking them on top of each other, while even now there is not enough recoverable oil.\n\nThe fewer our resources—whether energy or raw materials—the more insanely we use them, and it is not difficult to predict that the point is near beyond which this will no longer work.\n\nThere is no reassuring solution, there are facts. Although scientific consensus is 98.4 percent regarding what causes climate change and what its consequences are, there is also research showing that only 6–7 percent of people are aware of all this.”[-]|\n|{K104@Even pine trees are immobilized by sudden cold snaps}|\nAccording to researchers [3][4], global warming also affects the oceans’ capacity to absorb carbon dioxide: the oceans absorb a third of atmospheric carbon dioxide, but as the water cycle changes, this amount decreases.\n\nWith slowing currents, the slowing supply of nutrients can upset marine life first and then terrestrial life as well.\n\nIf, alongside the melting of the Arctic ice sheet, the Greenland ice—which accounts for 10 percent of the Earth’s freshwater—were also to melt, then in addition to further sea-level rise inundating hundreds more coastal cities, the dilution of the oceans would change ocean currents and, as a result, the weather as well.\n|{K201@We must take great care of Greenland as well}|\nAfter the ice sheets melt, rapid warming would slow the prevailing winds (they have already noticeably slowed over the past 30 years), which would further affect the atmospheric jet streams of the continents: we could expect further heat waves, or conversely, sudden cold snaps and other unusual, unpredictable weather extremes.\n|{K208@Formation of a huge storm cloud from above}|\n$|&K45&[s]Restoration[-]|\n\nPolar vortexes and ocean currents are giant autonomous systems that have been performing their tasks without external intervention since the beginning of the Earth’s history.\n\nNow, however, our harmful human activities seem to influence these processes, without understanding their consequences.\n|{K101@Thinning forest—we do not always see or understand the causes. Behind the scenes there may be river regulation, or a drier local climate and falling groundwater levels resulting from the clear-cutting of a more distant forest, but a migrating/introduced invasive species can also cause serious damage. Before intervening in nature, we should understand how natural systems work so that the environmental damage caused by our activities is as small as possible}|\nWe cannot accept such uncertainty when we know for sure what we must do to avoid it: we must reduce the human-caused drivers of climate change as soon as possible.\n|{K108@Increasingly powerful, huge cyclones over the Atlantic Ocean}|\n|{K304@Let us hear and understand each other’s words: let us help protect nature, because in doing so we also help ourselves!}|\n$|&K45&[s]Prevention[-]|\n\nLike polar vortexes, ocean currents are extremely complex, sensitive systems.\n\n|&K36&[z]Wonders of the creative power of nature.[-]|\n\nWe cannot directly “nudge” these robust, global systems into optimal operation, but we can do so indirectly: for these perfect and refined phenomena to continue to contribute to sustaining life on Earth, we also have tasks: reduce the disturbing burden on them—live in an environmentally conscious way.\n|{K303@Environmentally responsible behavior = a smaller footprint we leave behind}|\n|{K207@Let us get closer to nature and lead our children on this path as well!}|\n$|&K45&[s]Lesson[-]|\n\nWe still have to wait for the results of long-term research on polar vortexes, but it is likely that the Earth’s warming is disrupting the stable operation of these phenomena.\n\nLet us act to ensure that these giant cyclones do not become capricious and unpredictable in the future!\n|{K205@After completely unexpected, torrential rain, everything has gone underwater}|\nThe AMOC and the Gulf Stream exert an intense influence on the weather across the entire Earth and on its entire ecosystem.\n\nTheir persistent, continuous slowdown—or—may it never happen—their shutdown would have consequences that would change the Earth’s climate.\n\nSome say it would reinforce global warming; others say an ice age would begin.\n\n|&K36&[a]Let us do everything to ensure that neither happens![-]|\n\nThe IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change of the UN) introduced the concept of tipping points two decades ago, according to which after a certain level of warming, such critical, irreversible changes can begin in the Earth system (climate, ocean currents, biosphere) that humanity—according to our current knowledge—will be unable to influence.\n\nSuch points include the melting of the Arctic and Antarctic and the subsequent sea level rise; the slowing and stopping of the AMOC; the destruction of northern boreal forests by wildfires and pests and their transformation from carbon sinks into carbon sources; the irreversible melting of permafrost (permanently frozen ground); the transformation of the Amazon rainforest into savannah due to warming and tree loss; and changes in the marine biosphere due to ocean acidification and pollution entering it (e.g., the collapse of fish populations in masses due to the disappearance of corals).\n\nThese tipping points greatly influence the Earth’s biodiversity and human food security, make the weather more extreme, and further intensify climate change, which can trigger new effects or even chain reactions.\n|{K401@Let us not wait idly for the point when we can no longer intervene!}|\nCurrently, the costs of these risks are not reflected in the world economy, even though it is certain that crossing the tipping points will entail economic losses.\n\nThese points can still be avoided if we reduce the emissions that cause global climate change as soon as possible and invest in a low-carbon economy.\n\nOur climate-friendly transformation will be expensive, but if we do not act in time, the costs of climate-related damage will be much higher.\n\nScientists, backed by millions of measurements, warn us to make changes as soon as possible: reliable data speak for themselves; there are no versions in facts (just as there are none in the truth).\n|{K102@A beautiful autumn—but what can we expect in winter—and next summer? It is becoming increasingly difficult to predict weather extremes...}|\nSkeptics argue that there is still nothing wrong, since the climate constantly changes—cyclically warming and cooling—and the increasingly frequent weather extremes also fit within the fluctuations of weather. In their view, global warming is a cyclic, geological event, the climate changes because of solar activity and variations in the Earth’s orbit, and humans have no influence on it.\n\nOthers also claim that it is not humans but the seas that cause the rise in carbon dioxide. The continuously dying masses of plankton sink to the ocean floor, undergo anaerobic processes in an oxygen-deprived environment, and after slow decay turn into rotting sludge. Then, if this sludge enters an oxygen-rich environment due to a deep-sea earthquake, tsunami, or other effect, rapid oxidation occurs and large amounts of carbon dioxide are released in the process.\n\nThere is scientific logic in each statement; however, today’s changes are hundreds to thousands of times faster than anything the Earth has ever experienced before!\n\nThroughout Earth’s history, warmings and coolings alternated; of the periods resulting from the axis tilt and orbital variations that change the amount of solar radiation reaching Earth, the shortest is 20,000 years, but there are also several-hundred-thousand-year ones [11].\n\nSmaller cyclical temperature changes have also occurred in human history: such was the Medieval Climate Optimum about a thousand years ago, associated with significant warming, or the Little Ice Age between the 13th and 18th centuries.\n\nHowever, the warming associated with the Industrial Revolution and the period since then—linked to human polluting activities (which, through greenhouse gas emissions, drastically change the composition of the atmosphere)—differs from all previous ones: it is extremely intense, continuous, seemingly unavoidable, and has a very uncertain outcome. According to the IPCC’s scientific estimate, by the end of the 21st century the global average temperature will rise by 1.1–6.4 degrees Celsius compared to that measured at the end of the 20th century.\n\n|&K36&[a]It is a scientifically indisputable fact that carbon dioxide, as a greenhouse gas, controls the Earth’s climate, to which the sun’s radiation provides the heat and the greenhouse effect of carbon dioxide keeps it here. So carbon dioxide is indeed necessary—but not with such high emissions and not at such high concentrations.[-]|\n\nOn the graphs, natural warming is a very flat, slowly rising process, whereas climate change driven by humans since the Industrial Revolution—when measured on a similar time scale—is a suddenly appearing needle point.\n\nFrom the perspective of ecological systems, accelerated climate change is a very rapid change to which species cannot adapt.\n\nFor example, to a slow climate change taking place over 10,000 or 100,000 years, the oak tree can adapt, because due to the warming coming from the south it (scientifically proven) instinctively drops its seeds to the north and the forest migrates that way.\n\nBut with a change occurring over 150 years, the tree has no time, because this time corresponds to only 1–2 tree lifespans, and the tree remains in place, becomes sick, and dies [7].\n\nThe Medieval Climate Optimum and the Little Ice Age occurred at a time when humanity still lived in harmony with nature, and the planet still had the strength to weather the trials and heal itself—today it is by no means certain that this will occur.\n\nSo let us not rely on that, but on the fact that the damage caused by humanity must be repaired by humanity.\n\nThis perspective is crucial for us, because the Earth will certainly survive the climate crisis in some form and will later regenerate itself; the question is whether humanity can save itself in the meantime.\n\nWe cannot solve the problems with technology alone; we also need the health of ecological systems to survive.\n\nWhat the actual global average temperature will be by the end of the 21st century depends solely on how capable we are of giving up fossil energy carriers, how capable we are of transforming the “use and throw away” linear economy and switching to a more nature-friendly, sustainable circular economy, and whether we leave enough undisturbed space for nature’s ecological systems to maintain life processes and renew themselves.\n\nHowever, to achieve this, we would need to convince everyone that the climate crisis is a real threat and that the protection of the future of nature and humanity should be placed ahead of material goods.\n\n|&K36&[p]What more will it take for the doubters to be convinced?[-]|\n\nIt is bizarre to think about things like climate change or that life on Earth is in danger.\n\nAfter the emergence of humans, none of our ancestors dealt with such topics, and indeed not even our parents when we were children.\n\nBy doing so we would be probing and questioning things like the origin of life or the meaning of life.\n\nThese are concepts we have never had to interpret; we have never had to explain them. We simply accepted it, since it is the basis of all life on Earth.\n|{K203@The meaning of life or the origin of life are abstract concepts—everyone interprets them differently}|\nThen we grew up and involuntarily noticed changes. Changes that 20–30 years ago were almost imperceptible—or did not exist at all.\n\nWe experienced that, unlike before, the sun now burns, summer heatwaves have become drier, hotter and harder to bear, winters have become much milder, the seasons have shifted, non-native species have invaded our environment that we did not even know before, and we feel on our own skin—or learn from the news—about the increasingly frequent and ever-stronger natural and environmental disasters.\n\nSo we don’t even need to dig up stories from people of the past to see the changes: anyone who was in their teens or twenties in the 1990s can clearly see how different, how much more livable the climate was then than now.\n|{K306@In Central Europe (the temperate zone), 20–30 years ago on the hottest summer days the temperature rarely exceeded 30 degrees Celsius, and being outdoors all day caused only a slight redness on uncovered skin. At present we already reach 30 degrees in May, even exceed it, and in summer temperatures of 38–40 degrees (or even surpassing these(!)) are not uncommon. Being outdoors in the blazing sun during the day is not recommended for more than half an hour to an hour even for those with normal skin, let alone sensitive skin, because they risk serious sunburn and, with it, various skin diseases...}|\n|{K307@The same Central European temperate climatic zone before the turn of the millennium in winter: apart from short periods, the frost did not relent for months and abundant snowfall occurred; in the present, it often does not freeze even on New Year’s Eve, almost no snow falls all winter (or if it does, it melts in days), whereas the vegetation period of plants starts earlier and the sap flow of plants can begin as early as February, which makes them more vulnerable to spring frosts: in March and April, frequent warm days lure out the buds and blossoms of fruit trees, which the returning frosty nights destroy, damaging the annual yield and the plant itself}|\n|{K305@With the ever-stronger shift of the seasons, milder autumns and winters, and generally drier weather regardless of season, climate change disrupts the life cycle of crops and plants in general, which weakens them and makes them more defenseless against pests. Native plant species are pushed into the background, while non-native vegetation that can tolerate a warmer climate gains advantage. Moreover, warming supports pests and pathogens too, promoting their spread and their survival over winter.}|\n###Climate change and the increasing frequency of weather extremes can be felt everywhere in the world, but they manifest differently in each climate zone—among others, those living in Central Europe, in a temperate climate, feel and experience that:\n\n|&K36&[p]###As a dark side of our unbridled development, due to environmental damage and pollution, within a few decades the cold winter with abundant snow has disappeared, and summers have become drier and scorching hot.[-]|\n\n###All over the world many took the trouble to look for explanations and wanted to understand what is happening to nature—the very nature that we never even had to think about before, because it simply “existed” as it was.\n\n|&K36&[p]###The answers to the questions shocked everyone, because they pointed to us humans—we are the cause.[-]|\n\nEveryone reacted differently to this.\n\nSome say there is no problem and “bury their heads in the sand”—for if they admitted the opposite to themselves, they would also have to assume responsibility.\n\nOthers understand that there is a problem but do not know what to do, so they remain indifferent.\n\nStill others think that we are already late; they fall into lethargy and are tormented by climate anxiety.\n\nThose who deny climate change and its human origin do not take into account that since the 1750s, since the Industrial Revolution, we have been constantly burning: gas, coal, and oil.\n\nThis did not happen before, and as a consequence there has not been as much greenhouse gas in the atmosphere in the last 150 million years as there is now.\n\n|&K36&[a]With many people, it feels as if they are just waiting for top-down orders regarding mitigating climate change, as if regulations would solve the problems. MangrovemocsarMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nThe South American rainforest along the equator, the Central African, and the Indonesian rainforests are all struggling with a very serious problem.\n\nDue to deforestation, truly untouched wilderness has shrunk to just one-third of its original area and continues to decline.\n\nThirty-four percent of Earth’s ancient tropical rainforests have disappeared, and a further 30 percent is so degraded that it has become vulnerable to fires and future destruction—primarily because of logging for agriculture and land conversion [1].\n|{K106@There used to be rainforest here}|\n|&K36&[p]As a result of clear-cutting and other logging, we cut down 15 billion (!) trees every year.[-]|\n\nThis number is almost unimaginably large—so large our minds can barely grasp it.\n\nAs if each inhabitant of Earth (and there are many of us...)—from infant to elder—cut down two vigorous big trees every year.\n\nOr put another way: the vast Amazon rainforest holds roughly 400 billion trees [11]—if logging were concentrated there alone, in less than 27 years the enormous area would be stripped bare like a desert.\n|{K208@A hurried, quickly executed deforestation}|\n|&K36&[p]Between 2001 and 2020, Earth lost 411 million hectares of forest.[-]|\n\nThis area is more than four times the size of Egypt.\n\nWhere primary forests disappeared, the work of nature spanning hundreds—sometimes thousands—of years was destroyed; their loss thus has a very serious impact on biodiversity.\n\nWhy? Because biodiversity thrives most in tropical rainforests—which cover 6 percent of Earth’s surface—where two-thirds of all species live (around 1.7 million animal, plant, and fungal species have been identified so far on Earth).\n\nMost deforestation is illegal, and felled trees are not replaced with planting.\n|{K603@This tree may have been over 100 years old—will it be replaced?}|\nNatural erosion (wind, precipitation) dries out or washes away the now-exposed arable land, which is often used simply as pasture; thus the stubble’s fertility is significantly reduced.\n\nMoreover, rainforest soil is inherently poor, as frequent rains leach out nutrients and microorganisms fully decompose organic matter.\n\nThe vulnerable thin humus layer of soils in cleared forests is washed away by rainfall within a few years; the remaining red soil—terra rossa clay—turns rock-hard under the scorching sun.\n\nTherefore after clear-cutting or burning, farmers can usually cultivate the land for only a few years, which brings them only short-term profit; then they are forced to move on because the soil is so degraded.\n\nEven after decades of resting, only some pioneer vegetation can return to such exhausted, abandoned areas; once cleared again, the capacity will be far from enough to feed the fast-growing population.\n|{K301@If only extraction were followed by restoration...}|\nDeforestation is an ideal example of the total exploitation of the natural environment: to meet our economic and food needs, we completely ignore the integrity of forest habitats and the health of the environment, leaving behind a stripped, dried-out, destroyed area instead of a living, breathing, oxygen-producing environment.\n|{K206@Clear-cutting kills trees—the ones felled years ago have been impossible for nature to restore}|\n|&K36&[p]At the center of systematic deforestation lies our unsustainable lifestyle.[-]|\n\nAlmost all major industrial sectors—logging; Drought threatens intact forests further from and adjacent to deforested areas too because it fosters forest fires that are almost impossible to control, and heat causes further degradation.\n\nThis is the level at which a previously healthy, densely forested area becomes a net emitter of carbon dioxide rather than a sink because of deforestation and fires.\n\nDeforestation and fires thus open a vicious circle: with less rainfall, the climate becomes drier; there are more fires and natural die-offs; thus there are fewer trees to induce rain...\n\nAmazonian deforestation and burning are a textbook example of this drought-inducing vicious circle [11]: the rainforest creates its balanced, humid climate—including by recirculating moist, cooling air flowing in from the Atlantic Ocean. Pastures and cropland established on cleared rainforest obviously lack such effects, making not only the cleared lands but neighboring forests hotter and drier. limate models show deforestation becomes irreversible beyond a certain point, and the entire forest turns inexorably into a hotter, drier steppe—the remaining trees, weakened, become more vulnerable to pathogens and invasive species.\n|{K805@A pine forest hit by climate change and bark beetle. Pines produce less resin, so beetles don’t get stuck and can feed without hindrance—the tree becomes defenseless against invasion}|\nForests’ net carbon dioxide emissions can also be triggered by climate change, which affects both photosynthesis and respiration.\n\nRespiration intensity increases proportionally with air temperature—thus further raising atmospheric CO2.\n\nThe decomposition rate of organic matter in soil also increases in a warming climate (though it stabilizes long-term and may return to original intensity), but conditions may arise where respiration/decomposition increases far more than photosynthesis, turning forests into active carbon sources.\n\nThese emissions can far exceed those from burning fossil fuels, so the phenomenon is anything but negligible.\n|{K804@Prolonged drought and extreme heat due to climate change have scorched and burned oak leaves}|\nA study in Science Advances [10] analyzed two decades of eddy-covariance CO2 measurements across Earth’s major biomes and found global-scale critical temperature tipping points beyond which plants’ ability to fix and store atmospheric carbon begins to decline.\n\nCrossing the threshold (18 degrees Celsius for most temperate forests and 28 degrees Celsius for tropical forests), photosynthetic efficiency steadily worsens, while terrestrial ecosystem respiration increases exponentially with temperature up to a point.\n\nThis means that as global average temperature rises, carbon emissions slowly and consistently come to dominate over carbon uptake.\n\n|&K36&[z]In recent decades, terrestrial ecosystems have been able to withdraw and store nearly one-third of the carbon dioxide emitted into the atmosphere by human activities.[-]|\n|&K36&[a]However, it is hot, droughty periods only worsen the situation: they weaken trees’ condition and reduce resilience, leading to even more severe forest die-off, fires, and damage from diseases and pest insects.\n|{K203@Unusually high heat and critical water shortages can ignite forest fires that are very hard to extinguish...and the problems are compounded if buildings are nearby!}|\nThe Amazon OriasKapokFaMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nSince humans have existed on Earth, animal husbandry has always played an important role for us.\n\nIn this way, people could keep livestock at hand, could easily and conveniently satisfy their dietary needs, and could trade them.\n\nMeat is a valuable source of protein, but it is also rich in fats, vitamins A, B, and D, iron, zinc and other minerals, and essential amino acids.\n\nIt has served as a staple food throughout our development and evolution, our digestive system adapted to it, it contributed to our growth and development, and hunting promoted our ancestors’ cooperation in groups.\n\nAlongside these many positives, however, the tradition of meat-eating has greatly changed to this day, and increased meat consumption, besides endangering our health, also has multiple harmful impacts on the planet.\n|{K603@Many people cannot imagine their diet without meat and other animal-derived foods}|\nBreeding certain livestock species—especially cattle—places an extraordinary burden on the environment.\n\nCattle have high feed and water needs, and pasture and agricultural land must also be provided for their upkeep.\n|{K307@Grazing and resting cattle}|\n|{K706@Not all livestock are in a position to live their lives in free-range conditions worthy of animals. The American organization Farm Sanctuary (www.farmsanctuary.org [15]) fights against the catastrophic impacts of animal husbandry on animals, the environment, social justice, and public health through rescues, education, and advocacy}|\nDue to our heightened demand for red meat, the continuous growth in cattle numbers has intensified the demands of animal husbandry and has now become one of the greatest global problems.\n\nIt is not the few cows, goats, and pigs kept on small farms and homesteads that cause the problems, but industrial-scale meat and dairy production.\n\nEnormous—most often forested—areas are cleared and turned into pasture or farmland, and cattle (whose global population exceeded 1 billion in 2021) also contribute to the effects of global warming because their belching during rumination and their flatulence are rich in methane, which enters the atmosphere.\n|{K802@Industrial livestock breeding requires vast grazing areas all around the world}|\n|{K801@Steppes, prairies, and savannas are increasingly used by industrial livestock production. These vast grassy areas with scattered shrubs and trees host unique animal and plant life. African savannas have particularly rich biodiversity; however, on the ever more numerous pastures established there (mainly for cattle), neither predators nor herbivorous wild animals are considered desirable “guests.” To create lusher, greener pasture, dry grass is often set on fire, which can indeed result in temporarily better grazing; but if grass is burned too frequently, the below-ground shoots of turf-forming plants become exhausted and die, causing rapid pasture degradation. These areas then become defenseless against wind and sun—the drying soil is carried away by the wind, preventing vegetation from regenerating, and the formerly grassy, shrubby area turns into desert. A good example is the Sahel belt.}|\n|&K36&[p]Producing a single kilogram of beef results in 27 kilograms of carbon dioxide emissions and requires 15,000 liters of drinking water.[-]|\n\nThat is how much we need from freshwater, this extremely valuable natural asset.\n\nA single 180-gram slice of beef equates to the greenhouse gas emissions of driving a car for 40 kilometers, and 15,000 liters is about what an average family uses in a month for washing, cooking, and bathing.\n\nAnother approach examines carbon-dioxide generation per gram of protein produced: for cattle, producing one gram of protein results in 238 grams of carbon dioxide, for sheep 200 grams, for wild-caught fish 39.5 grams, and for agricultural crops an average of 24 grams [12].\n|{K203@Producing one kilogram of meat comes with enormous land and water requirements and significant carbon-dioxide generation}|\nIt is thought-provoking how greatly humanity dominates the class of mammals: if we take the total body mass (biomass) of all mammals living on Earth, humans account for 36 percent, while livestock account for 60 percent (according to a 2018 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) [19][20]).\n\nThe remaining 4 (!) percent is shared by all other mammals—about 6,500 species—from mice to whales.\n\nResearch published on the “Our World In Data” portal in 2022 [21] paints a similar picture: humans 34 percent, livestock 62 percent, all other terrestrial mammals 4 percent.\n|{K105@An illustration prepared on the basis of data published on the “Our World In Data” portal shows the proportions strikingly}|\n|{K205@The total mass of our livestock is nearly two-thirds of the total mass of all mammals living on Earth. rather, only a stem cell sample is taken from them (although each biopsy is painful).\n\nThe samples are placed in bioreactors and mixed with various nutrients (vitamins, sugars, amino acids), allowing them to develop in a biochemical environment similar to an animal’s body.\n\nIn response to the nutrients, the cells grow into ever larger muscle and fat tissues—according to experts [8], it is possible to cultivate in a few weeks meat that would take three years to raise from cattle.\n\nSo far, only a single country, Singapore, has approved (in 2020) lab-made chicken meat; however, companies prepared to produce cultured meat are awaiting approval worldwide.\n\nWhat advantages would (today still expensive) cultured meat have?\n\nIt would likely reduce water use, land area, and greenhouse gas emissions associated with livestock production (provided that cultured meat facilities use renewable energy); The breed’s unique coat (called PRLR-SLICK) was achieved using gene-editing technology—the process of genetic modification (GMO) involves inserting foreign genes into an organism, creating a being that would not occur in nature. The FDA has previously authorized the application of similar genetic changes—those involving Intentional Genomic Alterations (IGA)—in pigs, chickens, goats, rabbits, and salmon as well. There is also a form of gene editing (called CRISPR) that works with a given breed’s existing gene set; therefore, in theory, organisms created this way could also be produced through traditional breeding methods—it would just take much longer.\n\nConsidering current population growth figures, in a few decades we will be 10 billion people on Earth, and the fact is that the planet will no longer be able to support us for long due to our current production and consumption practices, which are far from sustainable.\n\nWherever possible, we should reduce our ecological footprint—and this applies to meat consumption as well.\n\nTo this end, interest in entomophagy (insect consumption) [11] is growing, and it has become one of the alternatives to meat consumption. DatolyaSzilvaFaNagyToPatakMJNev=Lightning
DatolyaSzilvaFaNagyToPatakMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nA companion of storms, lightning is not only a spectacular phenomenon but also a truly dangerous natural force.\n\nLightning is an electrical gas discharge that can occur between clouds and the ground, within a cloud, or between clouds.\n|{K304@An extraordinary sight—the lightning bolts formed at the same moment both within a cloud and between clouds}|\nThe process begins as the intense movement of air masses and droplet formation inside a thundercloud cause friction and collisions, then charge separation occurs.\n\nAs charges accumulate, areas of differing charge (polarity) create a potential difference that lightning equalizes.\n|{K201@Energy beams illuminating the night sky}|\n|{K402@Not every lightning bolt reaches the ground—this one was absorbed by the cloud cover}|\nIntra-cloud or inter-cloud lightning typically carries less energy and forms between regions of different polarity within clouds.\n\nCloud-to-ground lightning, which affects living beings most, occurs when the electric field strength (potential difference) grows so large between cloud and ground that air can no longer insulate the two oppositely charged points, and a channel forms between them through which the electrical discharge proceeds.\n\nA lightning flash lasts only two-tenths of a second, travels at up to 180 kilometers per second, and currents of up to 30,000 amperes can occur in the lightning channel.\n\nThunder following lightning forms because the electrical discharge heats the air in the channel to around 30,000 Kelvin, suddenly warming the surrounding air by several thousand degrees Celsius; the air expands, collides with surrounding air masses, and this produces a huge crash.\n\nLightning’s bluish color is given by the light of nitrogen decomposing in the suddenly superheated air.\n|{K204@In a storm, every point clearly protruding from the ground’s surface can be considered a lightning-strike zone}|\nWhy lightning and thunder are not simultaneous stems from the different propagation speeds of light and sound.\n\nThe light of a strike—traveling at 300,000 kilometers per second—reaches the observer much faster than sound—traveling at 330 meters per second—so we see the flash first and hear it later.\n|{K307@The intensely moving air masses of thunderclouds are hotbeds of lightning TabortuzMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nAcid rain is an extremely nature-damaging environmental impact, most often caused by human pollution.\n\nIt forms when carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and various nitrogen oxides released into the air undergo chemical reactions with the gases and water vapor of the atmosphere in the presence of sunlight [8].\n\n|{K508@The various types of pollution that adversely affect the atmosphere can be described by complex chemical equations, which could most simply be reduced if we lowered the amount of pollution we release into the air...}|\nAs a result of these chemical reactions, carbonic acid, sulfuric acid, and nitric acid are produced, which precipitation washes out of the air.\n\n|&K36&[p]These acids descend onto vegetation in an extremely polluting way and enter water systems as well, condemning the life that developed there to slow destruction.[-]|\n|{K507@Acidic precipitation forming over heavily polluted areas is harmful to animal and plant organisms as well as to human-built infrastructure}|\nThe process becomes truly destructive when the natural processes that absorb pollution are weakened: the continuous and increasingly rapid industrial and residential pollution can no longer be neutralized by nature, which is already weakened in this respect.\n|{K103@A windstorm swept through a forest weakened by air-pollution impacts, further deepening the problems of the disadvantaged area}|\n|&K36&[k]Where does this astronomical amount of pollution enter the air from?[-]|\n\nVirtually all areas of human activity are involved: coal- and oil-burning power plants, heavy-industry smelters, the chemical industry, fertilizer production, mining, transportation with internal combustion vehicles, and households that use non-renewable energy sources all contribute [8][9].\n\nIn the world’s largest and most polluting industrial regions, heavy metal and other chemical pollution reaches such levels that almost no native plant or animal species can survive—neither on land nor in the surrounding rivers and lakes.\n|{K301@Our industrial sectors face a difficult step: making production cleaner will be a huge pollution, because polluted air can travel long distances—thousands of kilometers—with prevailing atmospheric flows and winds, causing environmental damage far away.\n|{K203@Tourist trail—how would Solutions with a lower pH are called acids, while those with a higher pH are called bases.\n\nWe speak of acid rain when the pH of precipitation is 5 or below.\n\nAcid rain does not mean only rain; any form of wet precipitation can be acidic—snow and fog can also have an acidic pH.\n\nThis environment-damaging phenomenon does not discriminate: it erodes buildings and statues made of sandstone or limestone, corrodes metal structures and bridges, attacks both gymnosperms and angiosperms, ruins and acidifies soils, and poisons lakes and other aquatic habitats.\n|{K104@Even patinated bronze EltorlaszoltPatakMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nOverpopulation is without doubt humanity’s largest and most complex challenge.\n\nNot because other environmental problems are negligible by comparison—on the contrary!\n\n###Earth is becoming overpopulated, and as a consequence every human activity that transforms nature and all environmental pollution linked to us are becoming stronger and more intense.\n\n###Population growth is a natural process for any species, because nature can keep it within bounds.\n\n|&K36&[p]###In our case it works differently, because with our intelligence and technological readiness we have taken over nature’s supervisory role.[-]|\n|{K602@We are present at almost every point on Earth—perhaps with the exception of extremes like the hottest deserts, the highest mountains, the harshest polar points, or the oceans’ lightless depths}|\nThroughout human history, a slow, gradual population increase can be observed, limited by the amount of food producible at the prevailing technological level and in a given environment, as well as by hygiene and health conditions.\n\nWhen the population exceeded the sustainable level, it caused famines and armed conflicts, often accompanied by epidemics with catastrophic effects on a population already weakened.\n\nUntil the 18th century, human activities did not bring about global changes that reshaped Earth’s entire ecosystem.\n\nNatural selection, which characterizes all life on Earth, also functioned effectively for the human species until humanity reached a technological level that enabled it to remove those limiting factors.\n|{K1001@The Dark Ages were not troubled in every respect. At the start of our era, the human population was around 250 million, which by the mid-17th century had grown slowly to 550 million. During this long period, a much smaller human population than today was sustained by far fewer raw materials (stone, wood, and other natural materials) and far less plant- and animal-based food, and it interfered with nature only to a small extent. Transport between settlements was by oxen and horses; sea travel used the wind and human power (rowing). There were indeed striking cases—such as the huge demand for timber by merchant and naval fleets, and the deforestation and related erosion caused by increasing population’s need for farmland—but overall, most activities remained well within sustainability limits.}|\nWith the Industrial Revolution, however, humanity created a qualitatively new production and social system based on fossil fuels—the use of coal and oil—which, even over a short period, led to overloading Earth.\n\nThe most striking change was the increasingly rapid population growth, which immediately brought destruction of nature and environmental pollution on a scale orders of magnitude greater than before.\n\nThe population explosion unfolded very differently in developed and developing countries.\n\nIn developed countries, living standards and quality of life improved markedly thanks to better healthcare, sewerage systems, education, and more abundant and varied diets, which also increased life expectancy.\n\nIn the developed world, however, the population explosion subsided within just a century.\n\nThis happened largely because the earlier female ideal—being a good mother and running the household—changed.\n\nWomen’s rights rose to match men’s; they gained jobs and careers and had fewer children.\n\nMany parents had—and still have—only as many children as allow them to maintain their standard of living; wealth flows from parents to children (and the more it is divided, the more it is fragmented), so having children brings no economic gain to the family.\n|{K1004@In developed societies, only as many children are born as allow the family’s standard of living to be maintained—children are raised from the family’s wealth, which they later inherit}|\nIn developing countries, the starting causes of population growth are the opposite—due to large disparities, the limiting mechanisms of developed countries do not work.\n\nIn the absence of social safety nets, pension systems, and financial security, generations are in strong interdependence.\n\nChildren start working from a very young age (if they can find work), thus having economic value, and they also care for their elderly parents.\n\nWealth flows from children to parents, and poverty can be divided among any number of heirs without limit.\n\nFor survival and the struggle against poverty, the short-term interest of families is to have as many children as they can possibly raise.\n\nWomen typically cannot assert their rights; as a result, they often become mothers already in girlhood, from their mid-teens (and grandmothers by their 30s), thereby generating a much faster population cycle.\n\nWorking children and girls who become mothers lose educational opportunities (in reality, they would have no money for it), the concepts of birth control and family planning remain unknown to them, and thus they are unable to grasp the harmful effects of overpopulation.\n\nUnemployment reaches massive proportions; most men cannot find work, so there is no demand to involve women in production, and the basic expectation of them is childbirth and running the household.\n\nIn these societies, so many children are born that the number of 14-year-olds and younger exceeds one-third of the entire population and, in extreme cases, can reach half.\n\nThe educational system cannot absorb such huge numbers of children, healthcare cannot provide for them, and as adults they have little chance of finding jobs.\n|{K1002@Life is hard in poor regions both in cities and in the countryside. Part of people’s struggle against poverty is that many children are born, because that increases their chances of survival. Often the only way a family can hope to get ahead is if as many children as possible can work—but the children often end up inheriting poverty}|\n|{K1003@In today’s world there are many hungry people. Only those who have experienced hunger and poverty at close range can truly understand this. Feeding poor, malnourished people is an extremely selfless and generous act, but sadly there isn’t enough food every day for everyone}|\nThe root causes of the population explosion are thus poverty, lack of schooling for children, and the absence of gender equality.\n\nThese causes are amplified—and make population growth virtually unstoppable—by agricultural production that has become available even in underdeveloped areas, boosted by every tool (yield enhancers, fertilizers, pesticides); by support and aid from developed countries; by food reaching those in need more or less free and generally predictably (often only in amounts sufficient to avert starvation); and by advances in medicine, which—with drugs and available vaccines—have reduced mortality.\n\nIn addition, due to abysmal healthcare conditions, water scarcity, complete hopelessness, and the enormous internal tensions created by rapid population growth, civil wars erupt, and refugee camps (and the generations growing up there in greater safety) all further fuel a country’s capacity to reproduce its population.\n\nFor now, Earth’s population growth seems unstoppable—the UN and the international community have been unable to persuade the political leaders of countries affected by the population explosion to cooperate in promoting birth control [29].\n\nThis also affects the remaining natural resources: transforming today’s still-dominant linear global economy into a circular one would greatly help manage resources more efficiently (we are still far from this), but we cannot speak of true sustainability so long as a constantly growing population’s needs require ever more natural resources (minerals, farmland, drinking water, energy).\n\nOne conclusion emerges clearly:\n\n|&K36&[p]###Sustainable development is not possible as long as Earth’s population is increasing.[-]|\n\nBecause of regional differences in population growth, in young, rapidly expanding societies high unemployment, water and food shortages, and a general decline in quality of life trigger migration; people in hopeless situations leave their homes and seek their fortunes in other—usually developed—countries.\n\nIn aging, steadily shrinking developed societies lacking young labor, it seems an obvious solution to admit surplus population from elsewhere, bring in migrant labor, and involve them in production—thus labor import helps maintain welfare systems, including social and food systems.\n\nHowever, there are security risks with labor arriving from afar: there is unemployment even in developed countries; cheap migrant labor depresses wages; migrants often arrive in poor health, creating healthcare burdens; and people with different religions and cultures cannot—or often do not wish to—integrate into the community.\n\nDeveloped countries must cope with the steadily increasing and strengthening religious and ethnic diversity resulting from continuous immigration, with frictions arising from different cultures, and with the demands of immigrants for fairer treatment in education, healthcare, and the labor market.\n|{K805@For refugees transported by boats or trucks in the hope of a better life, national borders are serious obstacles—the text on this tent conveys it well: “Help us open the borders”}|\nNow for the numbers...\n\nAt the start of the 19th century, Earth’s population was 1 billion; now, at the start of the 21st century, it is over 8 billion (we passed the mark in November 2022).\n\nEach year the number grows by more than 80 million—160 (!) more people every single minute—which is almost 3 people per second!\n\nIt took more than 10 thousand generations for the first billion people to appear on Earth; reaching 2 billion took half a dozen generations and 130 years; now we add 1 billion in less than 13 years...\n\n|&K36&[p]In the time it takes you to read this sentence, there are 10 more of us![-]|\n\n(The current state of the human population, along with lots of other info, can be viewed on the worldometers.info website [15], and the UN’s World Population Prospects shows past and projected population numbers by continent [19].)\n|{K207@How large is 8 billion as a number? If you could count from 1 to 8 billion at one number per second, it would take more than 250 years... Or, at a lottery like the five-number draw (where five numbers are drawn from 90 and the chance of a jackpot is about 1 in 44 million), more than 180 people would hit the jackpot if you handed each person a ticket with a different pick and, once you ran out of unique picks, you started distributing them all over again...}|\nRegarding sustainability, the biggest problem is not that we have surpassed 8 billion (bearing in mind that at the turn of the millennium we were nearly 2 billion fewer), but that per-capita consumption is rising in parallel, and the harmful emissions and greenhouse gases associated with that consumption are not decreasing.\n\nThere is a formula called IPAT (I = P*A*T) [10], in which I (humanity’s negative environmental impact on Earth) is, simplified, the product of P (population size), A (affluence—average consumption per person), and T (the technology required to achieve and maintain affluence).\n\nIn this equation, I (environmental impact) assumes that the environment is a self-regenerating system that can withstand a certain level of impact. The maximum value of tolerable impact is carrying capacity. As long as I is less than carrying capacity, the P, A, and T components are sustainable without time limit for the environmental system; however, if I exceeds carrying capacity, it can only be a temporary state, because the overshoot can reduce the environment’s tolerance, thereby lowering carrying capacity.\n\nPopulation growth (P) increases land use, resource use, pollution, biodiversity loss, and climate change, among other things.\n\nGrowth in affluence (A) also increases environmental burden, because increased consumption—thus every product consumed or used—has wide environmental implications, from raw-material mining through water use and wastewater generation to soil and air pollution.\n\nTechnology (T) shows how energy-intensive it is to produce affluence and how large the environmental impact is in creating, transporting, and disposing of the goods and services used. Improving technological efficiency can reduce resource intensity, but it does not necessarily reduce environmental impact if efficiency comes with price reductions that spur further resource use.\n\nThe IPAT formula is disputed in several respects: it is considered too simple for a complex problem; it ignores interactions among P, A, and T and political, social, and cultural contexts (differences in individuals’ power, influence, and responsibility over environmental impacts); and it portrays people as merely harmful to the environment, failing to account for conservation and restoration efforts and sustainable resource use achieved by societies.\n\n|&K36&[p]However, it is beyond dispute that per-capita GDP has risen continuously over recent centuries, and in the equation I=P*A*T this increases human impact, which is why, since the 1970s, our environmental burden has tipped into unsustainability.[-]|\n\n###There is no doubt that the human population is already too large in number, but the problem is not only that it is growing; it is also that in its current form it is unsustainable in both the long and the short term.\n\n###(Except for the very poorest and those who truly live environmentally consciously) for our comfort, mobility, and entertainment we use more environmental resources than Earth can reproduce or than we give back.\n\nA serious question is how the mass of people will make a living (both food and energy demand are rising sharply) given the ever-shrinking and fragmenting resources.\n\nHumans—like every other living organism—have a primary goal: survival, which requires eating and drinking.\n\nIn overpopulated countries, however, sustaining an ever larger population requires intensive freshwater and farmland use, which also leads to the destruction of natural resources—and growing food needs take away new areas from native flora and fauna.\n\nEarth is a place with strict limits; therefore, natural resources available for use (freshwater, farmland, minerals) are only available in limited quantities; their amounts do not grow with population—in fact, they tend to diminish and degrade.\n\nThus, on the one hand, the developed world’s pollution, extravagant resource use, and wasteful lifestyle are responsible; on the other, the developing countries’ unwise, self-destructive activities—deforestation, overgrazing, wars, and short-term soil exhaustion—are to blame.\n\n|&K36&[p]###If we continue like this, a direct consequence will be that Earth’s resource stocks will be exhausted.[-]|\n|&K36&[a]###“There’s too many of us. According to Sir David Attenborough, population growth could be stopped following the Japanese model [31]. Japan’s population has been declining continuously since 2005, and its society is aging faster than any other country’s. The reasons: one of the world’s lowest fertility rates and the highest life expectancy. The increase in life expectancy is due to better nutrition, advanced medical and pharmacological technologies, better living conditions, and intensive economic growth. The low fertility rate is the result of complex economic and cultural processes, including higher educational attainment, urbanization, the growth of nuclear (self-sufficient, self-maintaining) family households (instead of large families), poor work-life balance, later and fewer marriages, increased participation of women in the labor market, declining wages and lifetime employment, as well as a large gender pay gap, ever smaller living spaces due to crowding, and the high costs of raising children [32].}|\n###With regard to countries, there are many constraints that limit possibilities: psychological, cultural, educational (or rather lack of education), religious, and views based on old habits, traditions, and beliefs.\n\n###Experts believe that the time of necessity will come and will topple these barriers.\n\nWe should definitely avoid, however, that this be preceded by an enormous overcrowding.\n\n“When in 1972 the groundbreaking bestseller ‘The Limits to Growth’ [23] was published, the impact of humanity on the planet was still within sustainable levels.\n\nThe purpose of writing the book was to slow the pace of growth, not to exceed the Earth’s carrying capacity.\n\nSince then, we have crossed these limits—despite the great interest and the concepts that still influence our thinking, humanity did not heed the book’s conclusions—the fundamental processes of the modern, industry-based world became unsustainable just a few decades later.\n\nDennis L. Meadows, the book’s co-author, said the following in an interview in 2022 on the book’s 50th anniversary [11]:\n\n|&B28&[a]“In 1972 the question was what humanity needed to change to remain within the limits set by nature’s resources. However, like climate change, the depletion of our resources also has long-term effects: this makes it difficult to assess the consequences and respond to them.\n\nOver the course of evolution, focusing on the here and now proved to be a successful survival strategy for Homo sapiens, not worrying about distant dangers. For the first time—and much faster than on an evolutionary timescale, therefore requiring a societal-level change—we should master a new coping mechanism.\n\nThe challenge is made even harder by the fact that the current way of operating is profitable for significant groups; it is the source of money and power. In the case of decision-makers, it was not a lack of understanding that prevented them from drawing conclusions from their work or addressing climate change. They simply plan for the short term. By the time problems of such magnitude reach sufficient weight to trigger the level of concern necessary for action, the resources needed to solve them may no longer be available.”[-]|\n|&K36&[a]“In 1972 we were still queuing at the cash desk of the roller coaster. TornadoMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nThe tornado is a natural force of extremely intense and destructive character.\n\nThis rotating, swirling atmospheric formation develops from the pressure difference between the rising warm air (convective updraft) and the colder air mass aloft [1].\n\nThe warm air that reaches higher altitudes cools; its humidity condenses and creates cumulus cloud cover.\n|{K501@The rotating atmospheric formation that later strengthens into a rampage begins with increasingly dense and darkening cumulus clouds}|\nDue to the pressure difference that develops between the cloud and its surroundings, a swirling motion starts from the top of the cloud toward the cloud base.\n\nIf a sufficiently large temperature and pressure difference develops, this swirling air movement exits the cloud and starts downward, toward the ground.\n\nIf this elongated, funnel-shaped air vortex reaches the Earth’s surface, we speak of a tornado; if not, its name is a funnel cloud (tuba).\n|{K308@At this moment, the funnel is still just a funnel cloud—imagine you live nearby and watch petrified, praying it won’t reach the ground...}|\n|{K303@###The beginning of destruction: the air vortex has reached the surface—now it’s a tornado!}|\nDue to the Coriolis force, the air vortex rotates counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.\n\nTornadoes can be multi-vortex (with satellite funnels forming around or within the main funnel, amplifying the tornado’s power), waterspouts (forming over water), or dust devils/landspouts (forming over land).\n|{K301@A tornado forming over the sea, i.e., a waterspout}|\nA tornado’s movement is fast (it can reach 50–100 km/h), its average diameter is 400–600 meters (some are only a few meters, while the largest can be several kilometers), and it often changes direction (sometimes one even forms that spins in place).\n\nMost tornadoes exist for only a few minutes, but rarely their mature phase after ground contact can exceed one hour—then their track can be over a hundred kilometers long, depending on forward speed.\n|{K505@The tornado struck very fragments far and wide!\n|{K206@###An unimaginable magnitude of rampage}|\nTornadoes can develop anywhere in the world where conditions are suitable, yet they most frequently occur in the central and KidontottFaMJLeiras=|&K45&[s]Impact[-]|\n\nAs Earth’s climate changes, weather extremes occur ever more frequently.\n\nClimate change also favors the formation of increasingly intense, raging hurricanes and windstorms, which are sometimes accompanied by hail that damages or destroys everything.\n\nA hurricane, typhoon, or tropical storm (its name depends on whether it forms over the Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, or the region of Australia) is a circular or spiral-shaped, rotating ensemble of thunderstorms forming over a warm ocean, whose diameter can be several thousand kilometers [3].\n|{K102@A huge hurricane formed over the ocean}|\n|{K101@We are curious about the nature of storms—understanding their formation conditions and behavior can help us prepare for and defend against them}|\nDue to its enormous extent, it can take several days for it to pass over a given area with gusts exceeding 200 km/h, and its total lifespan can be several weeks.\n\nTo understand how hurricanes form, we must first understand how cyclones form.\n\nAir always flows from areas of high pressure toward those of low pressure—until equilibrium is achieved at the end of the process.\n\nThe flow does not occur in a straight line but in a spiral along the Coriolis force present due to Earth’s rotation.\n\nMoreover, wind blows downward and outward in high-pressure systems, and inward and upward in low-pressure systems—the latter are called cyclones.\n|{K405@A cyclone threatening the region of Iceland}|\nCyclones form where relatively warm, moist air rises from Earth’s surface—aloft, when cold and warm air meet, the high-speed, continuously rising air creates terrifying air vortices, and the warm, humid air results in thunderclouds.\n\nAs a result of higher temperatures, more water evaporates into the air, and the storm sucks in this water vapor.\n\nThen, when rain forms, heat is released, which further increases the storm’s intensity.\n\nHurricanes form in summer and autumn months, most often under the tropical climate zone but farther from the Equator (typically between the 10th and 20th parallels), over intensely warming oceans.\n\nThese formations can form only at certain latitudes and do not cross the Equator because the Coriolis force is zero at the Equator, yet its rotational effect is necessary to spin the rising warm, humid air.\n\nA sea surface temperature of 26 degrees Celsius is considered the threshold—if the average temperature of the upper 50 meters of seawater reaches this, it provides enough heat energy for hurricanes to form [4][5][6].\n|{K108@###Greenhouse gases contribute to climate warming and thus to more intense ocean warming as well. Researchers are not yet certain whether warming causes more hurricanes (though a 2022 study [1] says extreme Atlantic hurricanes are twice as likely as in the 1980s), but it is certain that forming storms reach greater intensity; destructive hurricanes are becoming stronger. Analyses support this: in some regions, including the North Atlantic, the intensity of the strongest hurricanes has increased over the past two to three decades}|\nThe thunderclouds created by the continuously rising warm air from the sea transform into huge supercells, which the Coriolis force also spins.\n\nAs the cloud’s rotation accelerates, a pressure drop develops in its center due to the intensifying updraft.\n\nAs a result, an eye forms—a cloud-free, downward flow that can reach a width of 40 kilometers—also called the eye of the hurricane.\n|{K502@The eye of a hurricane is highly deceptive: the weather is clear and calm in the center, while the strongest winds rage around the eyewall}|\nA hurricane’s wind speed depends on how strongly pressure increases outward from the hurricane’s center.\n\nHurricanes are categorized by wind strength on the Saffir–Simpson scale, where Category 5 denotes the most destructive hurricanes.\n\nWhen a hurricane moves from sea to land, its enormous winds push a water column several meters high ahead of it.\n|{K305@Waves crash against breakwaters with tremendous force}|\n|{K203@Seawater rushes onto the land and floods everything}|\nThis vast amount of water inundates coastal areas, and the hurricane’s rampage destroys everything: buildings collapse, hundreds or thousands of objects fly through the air, vegetation is wrenched from the ground, branches snapped, leaves torn off.\n\nAs a result of downpours, sewage covers everything; there is no drinking water, roads are impassable, power is cut, information is absent—scenes worthy of a horror film everywhere.\n|{K204@}|\n|{K201@}|\n|{K304@}|\nEnormous storms, cyclones can form not only in equatorial regions but also in extratropical (outside the tropics) areas (at the boundary of the tropics and the temperate zone).\n\nThey often develop in the cooler part of the year (from September to May) in the North Atlantic.\n\nIn the temperate zone, west–east zonal flow is generally dominant for most of the year, temperature differences are moderate, weather is predictable, and there are no sudden changes or extreme events.\n\nHowever, when the difference between polar cold and equatorial warmth is large and the energy seeks to equalize with huge force, a very intense north–south meridional flow develops, causing sudden, significant changes and extreme weather.\n\nA cyclone forms where, at the boundary between the tropics and the temperate zone, cold and warm, moist air collide; locally, the most favorable conditions for this are over the much warmer-than-before Gulf Stream area—the warm air above the current mixes with cold air arriving from Canada or the Arctic.\n\nFrom then on, only the direction of the emerging “superstorm” is in question: heading east, it can hit Europe with the strength of a medium hurricane; moving west, it can dump a huge snowstorm on North America.\n\nResearchers have observed that meridionality not only intensifies, it also forms more often and persists longer—the process is complex, because the transformation of ocean currents, the warming of the seas, and the melting of northern ice also influence the formation and intensity of meridional flow.\n|{K705@###A supercell approaching with hail threat and strong gusts}|\nAccording to the WMO (the UN’s World Meteorological Organization), the main causes of increasingly frequent extreme weather events worldwide are changes in the atmosphere’s jet streams.\n\nThe fast-moving winds in the planet’s upper atmosphere have a major impact on climate through the subtropical and polar jets—and these air currents can reach farther south than usual.\n\nAs a consequence, unusually mild or extremely cold weather, hurricane-force winds, torrential rains accompanied by avalanche danger in mountains, or suddenly falling several meters of snow can occur.\n|{K707@Weather extremes can also result in unprecedented amounts of snow. In the Western Italian Alps, the huge amount of snowfall already in the winter of 2008–2009 caused numerous catastrophic avalanches, whose damage, comparable to deforestation, severely threatened forest heritage}|\nBut what causes the jet streams to reach farther south?\n\nAccording to climate researchers, among other things, the Arctic is warming faster than the tropics.\n\nSome studies [2] suggest that the ice melt caused by global warming and the warmer-than-usual Arctic air weaken the northern polar vortex (the enormous cyclone rotating over the North Pole), which affects its associated jet streams as well; they lose stability: warmer southern air can flow north, and colder polar air can break south—disrupting the weather.\n\nThis would not occur with a strong polar vortex and a stable jet stream: those cyclones keep cold air over the poles and do not let it escape.\n|{K706@Climate change makes weather extremes more frequent}|\nIn 2023, record sea temperatures were measured in the Mediterranean in July (even though maximum temperatures typically occur in August) [8].\n\nThe sea surface temperature was well above 20 degrees Celsius everywhere, and in some places even reached 30–32 degrees Celsius (up to 5 degrees Celsius warmer than average).\n\nWhat does this mean? With higher temperatures, intensified evaporation increases the atmosphere’s water vapor content; as a result, the water cycle accelerates, leading to intense, highly extreme weather events.\n\nHalf-kilogram hailstones of extreme size and deluge-like precipitation causing flash floods may affect not only the Mediterranean region: the precipitation band of Mediterranean cyclones And we have not yet talked about the hundreds of millions of people who are forced to live next to polluted water and do not have clean drinking water...}|\n|{K603@###Why is municipal wastewater treatment an extremely difficult task? Because it is unpredictable what ends up in our toilets and other drains...}|\n|{K506@###Wastewater treatment plant: extremely complex chemical process chains are necessary for the extremely difficult task of achieving an acceptable level of water purification. Wastewater treatment generally has three stages: mechanical, biological, and disinfection. The decomposition of pollutants is primarily carried out by bacteria active in biological treatment, whose enzyme systems determine the breakdown of organic pollutants, including pharmaceutical residues. However, the biological degradation of many pharmaceutical residues is inhibited (among others, diclofenac—an active ingredient in anti-inflammatories and painkillers—is such), therefore a fourth stage is globally needed to remove organic micro-pollutants (its implementation has already taken place—with adsorption using activated carbon and 80 percent efficiency—in 2015 in Switzerland, and then in Germany at a wastewater treatment plant near Ulm) [2]}|\n###Some wastewater treatment plants occasionally hold open days, when anyone can go and observe their work and ask about their activities.\n\n###We already know very well how to pollute water; on open days, however, we could also learn how to clean water and, as far as possible, avoid polluting it...\n\n|&K36&[a]###When you turn on the tap, remember that a great deal of energy is used to make drinking water from wastewater—therefore use only as much drinking water as you absolutely need![-]|\n|{K701@###In addition to the solvents, surfactants, and phosphate-containing ingredients of the many chemicals that end up in the toilet, medicines also resist wastewater treatment processes and thus enter natural waters! At more than a quarter of the sampling sites, the concentration of at least one pharmaceutical active ingredient reached a level that is no longer safe—i.e., toxic—for aquatic organisms, and it may also contribute to the development of antimicrobial resistance. According to the WHO and the UN, antibiotic resistance is one of the greatest dangers facing humanity; it could lead to the next pandemic. The contamination of the world’s rivers with pharmaceutical chemicals is a global problem that requires coordinated worldwide efforts to remedy.}|\n|{K804@###We are consuming antibiotics at an alarming rate [3]. As a consequence, the number of deaths caused by antibiotic-resistant infections has become so high (currently 700,000 per year) that it could increase tenfold within a generation and become one of the leading causes of death in the world. What is antibiotic resistance? When bacteria and other microorganisms (e.g., pathogenic fungi, single-celled parasites) resist the antibiotics intended to destroy them. What facilitates the global spread of resistant bacteria? Incorrect, uncontrolled, and excessive antibiotic use in human and veterinary medicine; international tourism; and international trade in animal products. What can we do at the individual level?
