FenntartK32V11=As part of your shopping strategy, instead of visiting several smaller local shops by bicycle or on foot, you buy everything in one place at a larger store—even if this means you have to go by car.
FenntartK32V12=You prefer organic and sustainable products—producing such products burdens the environment less, as they use fewer chemicals and fertilizers.
FenntartK32V13=You choose energy-efficient electrical and household appliances—these devices consume less energy, so they are more eco-conscious and contribute to long-term energy savings.
FenntartK32M=Environmentally conscious shopping is a consumer practice in which the buyer considers the environmental impacts of a product or service and, through their choices, supports sustainability and minimizes negative effects on the environment.\n\nIt has numerous advantages: it helps reduce environmental pollution, protects natural resources, supports sustainable production and eco-friendly businesses.\n\nIt also helps you choose healthier products and has positive effects on social and economic change.\n\nEco-conscious shoppers thus lay the foundations for a sustainable future.\n\nEvery purchase you make is also a vote showing which companies matter to you.\n\nVote with your money for companies that operate sustainably and produce environmentally conscious products!

FenntartK33=Wash more sustainably! How can you do this? Select the relevant points!
FenntartK33V01=You try to help ensure fewer chemicals end up in waters—under normal circumstances there is no need for chlorine bleaches and disinfectants, so for disinfecting kitchen tools and surfaces you use boiling or alcohol.
FenntartK33V02=Among store-bought detergents you choose one that contains as few chemicals as possible (and is phosphate-free, because phosphate is harmful to natural waters), and you only use as much as is absolutely necessary.
FenntartK33V03=You wash at 30 degrees or in cold water—this helps preserve the shape and color of washed clothes, extends their lifespan, and reduces the amount of harmful dyes and microfibers released into the environment.
FenntartK33V04=You buy garments made from organic materials and produced ethically, and you wash and dry them according to the information on their labels (the listed washing temperature is not the recommended but the maximum value).
FenntartK33V05=You don’t wash clothes that aren’t dirty, just worn or lightly used—you air them out in the open air.
FenntartK33V06=You wash only slightly dirty clothes at low temperature on a short program, and you don’t even wash clothes with just a small spot—you use a dampened sponge to remove the stain.
FenntartK33V07=You don’t use store-bought fabric softener; instead you apply an eco “softener” consisting of washing soda, vinegar, water, and essential oil (indeed, the combination of vinegar and natural laundry perfume is often enough).
FenntartK33V08=You try to skip machine drying and ironing—you always dry clothes outdoors, smoothing them and arranging the edges; you place blouses, shirts, and thicker T-shirts on hangers so they crease less.
FenntartK33V09=You wash according to old, entrenched habits, so besides washing powder, bleach, and softener you always have disinfecting bleach at home, and you choose a high-temperature program on the washing machine, because only this makes clothes clean.
FenntartK33V10=To remove more stubborn, dried-in dirt effectively, you dissolve a little washing soda in warm water and soak the clothes in this mixture—this is time-consuming, but the result will be clearly visible on the clothes.
FenntartK33V11=Each season you pack away and take out clothes from the wardrobe and wash everything, whether necessary or not—the clothes will be freshly washed and fragrant.
FenntartK33V12=Your iron, washing machine, and dryer are at least energy class “A,” but the latter are only energy efficient if you always run them with a full drum.
FenntartK33V13=You replace washing powder with a laundry egg or natural substances containing saponins (soap nuts, horse chestnut kernel), or with a homemade laundry gel made from hot water, laundry soap, and washing soda.
FenntartK33M=Your clothes may be made of strictly controlled and certified organic cotton without chemicals, yet the largest share of a garment’s ecological footprint arises after you buy it.\n\nSo you cannot sit back thinking that by purchasing an ethically produced garment made of organic material you have done everything possible for Earth.\n\nHow you handle, wash, dry, and how long you wear your clothes has a much greater impact on the environment than you might think.\n\nOnly part of this is the energy and water consumed in the processes; the detergents and softeners used, and the dyes and microplastics released from clothes are all environmentally hazardous factors.\n\nTherefore, environmentally conscious handling of clothes requires care from you—if you strive for it, every step can be sustainable.\n\nDetergents and softeners, for example, can be replaced with eco-friendly agents that can be made at home:\n\nHomemade laundry gel: 4 liters of hot water, 150 grams of laundry soap grated, 250 milliliters of washing soda.\n\nOn the stove you stir the laundry soap into the hot water until it dissolves completely, then gradually add the washing soda, after which you bring it briefly to a boil. Stir the cooled, gel-like liquid, and it’s ready to use. For one load of laundry (4-5 kg) you need about 100 milliliters. n\nEco “softener”: one cup washing soda, one cup household vinegar, one cup water, 5-10 drops essential oil.\n\nMix the washing soda, vinegar, water, and essential oil and put this into the softener compartment. For essential oil you can choose lavender, because it also has disinfectant properties, or lemon oil, which has a refreshing effect. With these natural substances you protect not only our skin but the environment as well.

FenntartK34=Eco-friendly vinegar can be an extraordinary help in the household if you know when and where to use it. Select its uses!
FenntartK34V01=For carpet cleaning—you spray carpets with diluted vinegar, then clean them with a dry brush.
FenntartK34V02=For cleaning and polishing cutlery—you rub water spots off cutlery with a soft cloth dipped in vinegar; you remove coffee stains from your teaspoon and mug by soaking them in vinegar water.
FenntartK34V03=To remove limescale in the bathroom and kitchen—you add 1 cup of vinegar to 1 liter of water and bring it to a boil in the limescale-coated kettle; for the shower head and tap you soak the limescale deposits in vinegar water.
FenntartK34V04=Against mold on walls—you thoroughly spray the moldy area with 20% vinegar in a spray bottle, let it sit for a few hours, then scrub the spots with a brush (tea tree oil and baking soda are also effective against mold).
FenntartK34V05=Ant deterrent—you regularly wipe the windowsill and door frame with vinegar—you can add a little peppermint essential oil, since ants don’t like that either.
FenntartK34V06=Disinfection—white vinegar is a natural and safe disinfectant, helping you avoid harsh, harmful chemicals.
FenntartK34V07=Removing stains and odors—you spray stains with a mixture of 1 teaspoon baking soda, 1 tablespoon white vinegar, and 2 cups of water; for tougher stains you add a pinch of baking soda, then scrub with a brush dipped in vinegar.
FenntartK34V08=Natural cleaning spray—its acidity and grease-cutting ability make it an excellent cleaner—so it can be used to clean the oven, refrigerator, microwave, and dishwasher.
FenntartK34V09=Against clogs—you put 1/3 cup baking soda into the drain, flush it with a generous amount of vinegar, then pour hot water over it all—be careful not to inhale the gas released.
FenntartK34V10=For refurbishing lime-based materials—the acidic vinegar cleans granite, marble, or natural stone surfaces well, especially if the surfaces can be in contact with vinegar for a longer time.
FenntartK34V11=For washing dishes—because white and apple cider vinegar are excellent natural degreasers—bringing vinegar to a boil in a greasy pan also restores the pan’s original nonstick state.
FenntartK34V12=To remove bacteria from vegetables and fruits—you mix vinegar and water in a 1:3 ratio in a spray bottle, spray the produce, then rub it clean with your hands and finally rinse with cold water.
FenntartK34V13=For water softening—hard water makes bed linen or towels rough—to avoid this you add half a cup of vinegar to the wash cycle.
FenntartK34M=Vinegar can be used in very versatile and economical ways in the household.\n\nWith its help, harmful chemicals can often be dispensed with.\n\nUse it boldly, but with care, especially when using vinegar and baking soda together.\n\nVinegar dissolves lime-based materials, so do not use it on granite, marble, or natural stone surfaces, as it can etch them; it may also leave stains on hardwood floors or cast-iron cookware.\n\nOn the other hand, it is very effective for cleaning windows, glass, mirrors, drains, trash cans, ceramic tiles, laminate floors, and bathroom steel fixtures when you want to remove limescale, soap scum, or dirt.\n\nVinegar can even be used for soil care, as it can help restore soils with unbalanced pH values, but before applying it you must carry out precise tests and calculations.

FenntartK35=Lemon isn’t just a fruit and vinegar isn’t just a condiment—both can help effectively with household tasks as well. Select these activities!
FenntartK35V01=Cleaning a glass shower cabin—you make a vinegar–baking soda paste, apply it to the glass surface, leave it on for fifteen minutes, then wipe it off with a damp cloth.
FenntartK35V02=Natural home deodorizer—you cut a lemon in half and place it near unpleasant odors—for example on a coffee table or in the kitchen.
FenntartK35V03=Upholstery cleaning—you make a solution of vinegar, water, and dish soap, pour it into a spray bottle, spray the upholstery, then scrub it well; if necessary, sprinkle with baking soda too, then vacuum.
FenntartK35V04=Cleaning a cutting board—you rub the board with a halved lemon.
FenntartK35V05=Removing ink stains—you mix milk and vinegar in a 2/1 ratio and soak the ink-stained fabric in this solution overnight, then wash it the usual way the next day.
FenntartK35V06=Cleaning the microwave—you place a mixture of a glass of water and a few tablespoons of lemon juice in the microwave, run a short program to bring the water to a boil, wait fifteen minutes, then wipe off the residue with a cloth.
FenntartK35V07=Cleaning a blender—if its jar has turned cloudy, fill it with half a liter of warm water, a few drops of dish soap, and vinegar, then run the machine for one minute.
FenntartK35V08=Deodorizing plastic containers—you rub the surfaces with lemon; the containers will not only be odorless, but their stains will be removed too.
FenntartK35V09=Cleaning the freezer—before you start, spray the freezer with a warm-water-and-vinegar solution; the mixture is food-safe and effectively removes built-up grime.
FenntartK35V10=Eliminating odors from the trash can—you scrub the bin with a combination of ice cubes, coarse salt, and lemon peel.
FenntartK35V11=Window cleaning—you mix distilled water with vinegar, pour the mixture into a spray bottle, and clean the windows with it.
FenntartK35V12=Removing sweat stains from clothes—before putting garments in the washing machine, you rub the underarm areas with lemon juice.
FenntartK35V13=Cleaning the dishwasher—before starting the appliance, place a bowl of vinegar on the top rack; this not only disinfects it but also removes limescale.
FenntartK35M=Lemon is good for more than baking; thanks to its properties, besides removing limescale it can be used in many other areas around the home.\n\nVinegar is an exceptional tool in your household that can help you in every room.\n\nReplace household chemicals and use natural, eco-friendly solutions!

FenntartK36=You can maintain your wardrobe sustainably as well. How? Select these activities!
FenntartK36V01=You look for quality—the quality of buttons, seams, finishing, lining, zipper, and cuts, in addition to the materials, all help you see whether you’re holding a quality garment.
FenntartK36V02=You “shop” your closet—you start wearing your long-forgotten, previously worn garments again.
FenntartK36V03=You source your clothes second-hand—thus you keep them in circulation longer, so you visit thrift stores, consignment shops, second-hand clothing stores, and flea markets.
FenntartK36V04=You learn to sew—this way you can repair your clothes, and every self-made garment brings rightful joy and pride and also makes an excellent gift.
FenntartK36V05=You organize clothing swaps—you exchange garments with family members, friends, and colleagues, since each other’s clothes may still be treasures.
FenntartK36V06=You avoid impulsive, spur-of-the-moment clothing purchases—to do this you get to know your current wardrobe so you know which items you truly need.
FenntartK36V07=You build a wardrobe where every piece can be combined with every other—this way less will be enough, yet you won’t feel like you have nothing to wear.
FenntartK36V08=Your appearance is different at every important event and even on the street—to this end you constantly tour the latest fashion brand stores—there’s no way you’ll be seen in the same outfit twice.
FenntartK36V09=You know what suits you—you learn which colors, cuts, patterns, and materials truly flatter you and you only buy such pieces, because you’ll certainly wear them.
FenntartK36V10=Before buying you examine what material the garment is made of—the most eco-friendly materials are hemp, linen, wool, certified (e.g., GOTS, OEKO-Tex) organic cotton, and recycled synthetics.
FenntartK36V11=When you buy new clothes you mainly look for those made in your country or in neighboring countries, and you ensure that the garments are produced under ethical conditions with minimal environmental impact.
FenntartK36V12=You have your clothes repaired and altered—a good seamstress can do great work even with out-of-fashion pieces.
FenntartK36V13=You acquire the smallest number of clothes necessary to meet your needs—overconsumption is the biggest problem, so for you the focus is on quality rather than quantity.
FenntartK36M=Clothing and clothes shopping usually aren’t among the headline topics of environmental protection, yet the apparel industry is among the most polluting industries.\n\nIf you dress more consciously, you both reduce your own footprint and influence how the clothing industry operates.\n\nOne of the most eco-conscious solutions is to obtain clothing second-hand—besides thrift stores, visit consignment shops, charity shops, curated second-hand stores, flea markets, vintage sources, used-clothing webshops, Facebook groups, and Facebook Marketplace as well.

FenntartK37=You can reduce your eco-footprint in many ways in everyday life. Select the points that fit here!
FenntartK37V01=You don’t waste food—you plan the weekly menu in advance and go shopping with a list, leaving you with more money, throwing away less food, and making fewer later trips to the store for forgotten items.
FenntartK37V02=You grow vegetables—produce you grow yourself doesn’t need transport, cooling, or packaging, so you save a lot of energy, and your own produce tastes better and is richer in vitamins.
FenntartK37V03=If there’s an alternative, you don’t use the car—you choose public transport, cycling, or walking instead.
FenntartK37V04=You switch to a vegetarian diet—with this one change you can reduce your eco-footprint by as much as 40 percent, because meat consumption has huge land and water demands.
FenntartK37V05=You buy used items instead of new ones, or borrow what you need—this way your home won’t be filled with objects you’ll only use a few times over their life.
FenntartK37V06=For reasons of cost and energy saving you hardly use your kitchen at all—whenever possible you eat in restaurants or pizzerias, or order food delivery.
FenntartK37V07=You make your home energy efficient—with insulation, replacing windows and doors, modernizing the heating system, and using energy-saving appliances.
FenntartK37V08=You set the temperature lower (i.e., to a comfortable level with a sweater) at home—you don’t heat unnecessarily, and in rooms you’re not in you turn the heat down; besides saving energy, this also reduces your carbon dioxide emissions.
FenntartK37V09=If you need a car, you prefer a smaller one and drive it as little as possible—smaller, lower-displacement cars are more energy efficient than big ones and their taxes are lower.
FenntartK37V10=You reduce the waste you generate—a lot of waste is produced in the household; to prevent this you avoid single-use and overpackaged products.
FenntartK37V11=You don’t fly on vacation—you discover the beauties of your own country, or take the train to neighboring countries.
FenntartK37V12=You recycle whatever you can—you look at waste with a creative eye and try to give it a new life, and you donate surplus but still usable items, e.g., to charities.
FenntartK37V13=You buy locally produced organic foods—seasonal, unprocessed produce from organic farming doesn’t need to be transported far or overpackaged to keep it fresh.
FenntartK37M=Every year there is a peculiar day: Earth Overshoot Day.\n\nIt is ultimately a benchmark showing which day of the year humanity begins to consume beyond Earth’s regenerative capacity.\n\nWe crossed this threshold in 1970 and have consumed more and more ever since; by 2025 we would already need 1.8 Earths to avoid consuming its resources on credit.\n\nThis means humanity uses up long before year’s end the natural resources available for that year that ecosystems renew year after year.\n\nBy the 2020s humanity was consuming in seven months what would be available for a whole year if we respected the planet’s regenerative capacity.\n\nIf we do not change our consumer habits, this will lead to a large decline in resources and, eventually, their depletion.\n\nTo prevent this, reduce your footprint, change your lifestyle, and step onto the more sustainable path!

FenntartK38=A sustainable life requires a lifestyle change. How can you live with a smaller footprint? Select the relevant points!
FenntartK38V01=You don’t overcool/overheat the home—you stay in the comfort zone—you define the comfort zone by correctly setting the trio of temperature, humidity, and ventilation, i.e., the range in which you feel good.
FenntartK38V02=You reduce the time spent using TV, computer, and phone—you’ll have much more free time you can use meaningfully (e.g., for exercise, reading, hobbies) and your electricity consumption will also decrease.
FenntartK38V03=You dress appropriately at home—insulation and an efficient heating system are very important, but the cheapest, easiest, and fastest solution against the cold is simply to put on more clothes.
FenntartK38V04=You eat less red meat—thus your carbon footprint and diet-related pollution will be smaller; you’ll be healthier and slimmer and even save money.
FenntartK38V05=You adopt a fully nomadic lifestyle—you practically never leave the house: you have work you can do from home, you have someone else do the shopping, and you have other material needs delivered to your door.
FenntartK38V06=You insulate your home—proper insulation is one of the best ways to reduce energy use; good insulation (and good ventilation) helps maintain comfort in every season.
FenntartK38V07=You live in a community, settlement, or neighborhood where you can reach everything on foot and/or by bicycle—this saves a lot of fuel and less of your time goes to commuting and daily travel.
FenntartK38V08=You eat local and seasonal foods, grow your own produce through gardening, shop at local markets, and preserve whatever you can for winter.
FenntartK38V09=You live a minimalist life—you strive for fewer belongings and get rid of everything you don’t need.
FenntartK38V10=For longer trips you take the train—it’s much greener than flying, more eco-friendly than driving, offers more legroom, lets you move around freely, and the view is enjoyable.
FenntartK38V11=You buy energy-efficient products—using lower-consumption appliances is better for the environment and for your wallet.
FenntartK38V12=You get a bicycle and ride it, and you walk a lot—both are extremely eco-friendly, cost-saving, healthy, make you more athletic, and improve brain function.
FenntartK38V13=You eat more vegetables and fruit—their cultivation requires far less water, energy, and land than dairy and meat animal husbandry; by consuming them you’ll be healthier and you’ll spare animals as well...
FenntartK38M=If you strive for a sustainable life, you must see and feel that there is a big difference between prosperity that prioritizes quantity and the far more important well-being that focuses on a quality life.\n\nStrive for well-being!\n\nIf you do it right, a quality life will have great positive side effects: health, more free time, friends with similar interests, and the joy and satisfaction of being on the best path—the sustainable path!

FenntartK39=An important part of saving energy at home is not leaving household appliances in standby mode, but turning them off. Select the statements/actions that apply!
FenntartK39V01=You always unplug chargers from the outlet when you’re not using them, because they can draw power even when they’re just plugged in.
FenntartK39V02=With a switched power strip placed in an easily reachable, visible spot you eliminate the standby consumption of connected devices—you also won’t forget to switch them off.
FenntartK39V03=Smaller devices don’t necessarily consume less in standby than larger ones; a simple battery charger can use multiples of a modern TV—so it’s best to cut the power to all of them when not in use.
FenntartK39V04=Devices almost considered “furniture,” quietly standing most of the time (e.g., the washing machine, dryer, and dishwasher) can also consume power if you leave them plugged in—so you only power them when in use.
FenntartK39V05=You cut power to hard-to-reach, hard-wired devices (e.g., oven, dishwasher) with a remote-controlled outlet, so you can switch them off/on from a distance.
FenntartK39V06=Before bed you walk through the rooms of your home and switch off any devices in standby that you won’t need overnight.
FenntartK39V07=You check your electrical devices (or their manuals) to see if they contain a transformer, because these can consume power even when the device is switched off—so you disconnect them from the mains when not in use.
FenntartK39V08=If you have a TV set-top box, you cut its power when you’re away from home—this is one of the most power-hungry devices typically waiting in standby.
FenntartK39V09=You keep computer- and game-console-free weekends (even one or two days a month helps), and if you travel for the weekend or longer, you switch off the router too.
FenntartK39V10=You use a simple or programmable timer switch for every device that only needs power intermittently (e.g.,: Wi-Fi router, aquarium lighting, circulation pump for the heating and domestic hot water systems).
FenntartK39V11=You try to avoid standby by leaving devices fully on: e.g., while you cook or clean, the TV is on and you also listen to music from a hi-fi or computer.
FenntartK39V12=For devices with peripherals (e.g., computer, TV) you use an energy-saving master-slave power strip, so when you switch off the primary device, the others switch off automatically.
FenntartK39V13=You research the power-management options of your computer and monitor and set them up to run more efficiently while meeting your needs.
FenntartK39M=In an average household, all devices left in standby can account for 8–10 percent of electricity consumption.\n\nYour devices are in standby when they’re ready for use but you aren’t actively using them.\n\nThe more appliances you keep plugged into the mains, the more unnecessary electricity you use—so you need to pay that much more attention to disconnecting them after use.\n\nAccording to calculations by the European Environmental Bureau, limiting standby mode could save up to 80 TWh (terawatt-hours) of consumption annually in the EU.\n\nThat amount equals the output of 11 power plants!

FenntartK40=Amid the climate crisis it’s becoming clearer what counts as a real need and what doesn’t. Which needs aren’t strictly necessary for a more sustainable life?
FenntartK40V01=Luxury comfort—you forgo stripping to the waist thanks to a 26 degrees Celsius winter room temperature or warming up under a 20-minute shower—20–22 degrees Celsius is enough at home in winter, and a shower should only be 5 minutes.
FenntartK40V02=Hoarding used stuff—your home isn’t a warehouse, so you take time to inventory and get rid of unnecessary items (sell or donate)—fewer possessions don’t mean deprivation; they’re liberating.
FenntartK40V03=The latest gadgets—the constant production of trendy new things demands huge resources, so you don’t let ads dictate and don’t want a new phone every six months when the previous one still works perfectly.
FenntartK40V04=Daily commuting to work and daily shopping—if you can, you work from home and only shop once or twice a week, and you bake pastries at home.
FenntartK40V05=A new car—it has a high selling price and manufacturing it carries a heavy environmental burden—so if you need a car, you opt for a good-quality, properly serviced used one from a reliable dealer.
FenntartK40V06=Store credit—beyond the cash you have, you don’t daydream—burdensome installments will follow you like a “shadow” for a long time, especially if you pay several each month (home, car, furniture, washing machine...).
FenntartK40V07=Never-used gifts—you get rid of things that only collect dust—to do so, you organize gift swaps with family and friends, so previously neglected products find use and you avoid new purchases.
FenntartK40V08=Window-shopping and shopping as a pastime—the result is tons of unnecessary stuff, so you only buy when you truly need something and you write a list; you don’t let yourself be diverted.
FenntartK40V09=Old light fixtures—you review the light sources at home and replace as many as possible with energy-saving ones, preferably LED bulbs—efficient bulbs can consume up to 80 percent less energy.
FenntartK40V10=Television, cable TV—you reduce TV time or even give it up—without TV you have more time to read, pursue hobbies, meet friends, and your electricity bill will be lower.
FenntartK40V11=Newspapers and magazines—in the internet age you don’t need paper media; but if you still crave the rustle of paper, you use the library or subscribe with others and circulate the issues.
FenntartK40V12=Ready-to-eat and convenience foods—instead of pre-cooked, pre-fried, and ready meals from refrigerated and freezer counters, you choose homemade food from fresh ingredients, often cheaper and much healthier.
FenntartK40V13=“Carpe diem” lifestyle—you don’t live only for today, so you don’t waste; you save water, electricity, and money in general, because tomorrow’s consequences of today’s carelessness won’t be kindly covered by yesterday...
FenntartK40M=During any crisis (economic, pandemic, climate) it becomes clear what belongs to our true needs and which desires are dictated by the greed of consumer society.\n\nIn the midst of the climate crisis the time has come to experience that less is truly more.\n\nWith lower consumption everyone gets more of life’s real flavor, and the ecosystem that sustains nature—and us—has a better chance to at least partially regenerate.

FenntartK41=How can you save drinking water at home? Select these activities!
FenntartK41V01=You keep a bottle of water in the fridge for when you get thirsty, instead of running the tap for a long time to get cold water.
FenntartK41V02=You sweep paths, paving, and patio stones with a broom instead of using a hose.
FenntartK41V03=You don’t rinse or wash dishes before putting them into the dishwasher—you remove food residue with a used paper napkin.
FenntartK41V04=You repurpose shower and bath water, and the rinse water after dishwashing for hand washing, soaking, mopping, toilet flushing, or cleaning shoes.
FenntartK41V05=You use cooled cooking water (e.g., from boiled eggs) and the used water drained from the aquarium after water changes for watering plants.
FenntartK41V06=You collect rainwater in a concrete tank, because the water won’t stagnate and its acidity decreases; alternatively you use a plastic or stainless container with a pre-filter.
FenntartK41V07=You try to reduce household water consumption by buying as many soft drinks, bottled waters, beers, and wines as your family wants.
FenntartK41V08=You plant less water-demanding plants in the garden and place mulch under them—the best ground cover; with it you can save a lot of water.
FenntartK41V09=When washing clothes you prefer the water-saving eco program, and you wait to wash until you have a full load.
FenntartK41V10=You water plants in the morning or evening so they can use the water efficiently and make do with less.
FenntartK41V11=Indoors you use collected rainwater and greywater (used water from washing and bathing) for toilet flushing and even for laundry; for laundry you purify it with a three-stage activated-carbon filtration system.
FenntartK41V12=You use a programmable smart irrigation system that accounts for the weather (doesn’t water when it rains) and the plants’ needs.
FenntartK41V13=At your weekend plot you set up a barrel on a stand, painted black, and use the collected rainwater for occasional showers.
FenntartK41M=Managing Earth’s freshwater resources wisely is an ever-growing global challenge, made harder by the uneven distribution of water, which may become even more extreme with climate change.\n\nWater is a vital treasure—each of us is responsible for not wasting it!\n\nIt’s easy to see the luxury of using drinking water for toilet flushing, laundry, cleaning, and irrigation, even though in many cases we could replace it with greywater (lightly polluted water already used once in the household) or even rainwater.

FenntartK42=In the spirit of energy saving, you decide to turn the thermostat down in winter. Select how you can help your home feel comfortable with virtually no cost!
FenntartK42V01=You lay warm rugs in the rooms you use most so less heat escapes and the soft material pampers your feet.
FenntartK42V02=In the morning you raise the blinds, draw the blackout curtains aside, and let the daylight in all day.
FenntartK42V03=You warm yourself first, not the space—so you wear a warm sweater and thick socks, and add a blanket for reading or watching TV.
FenntartK42V04=You ensure furniture doesn’t block free airflow or the operation of heaters.
FenntartK42V05=If you can’t afford new windows and doors, you use self-adhesive silicone strips for gaps, and for drafty doors and windows you make a DIY draft stopper—an old pair of tights filled with fabric scraps.
FenntartK42V06=Several times a day you drink hot beverages (mainly tea, maybe hot chocolate or coffee) and eat warm soup.
FenntartK42V07=You surround yourself with plants, because they increase humidity (40–60 percent is ideal in winter), which improves thermal comfort.
FenntartK42V08=You turn the thermostat down so much that you can only tolerate the indoor temperature with gloves and a coat—you risk catching a cold, but this saves the most.
FenntartK42V09=You place heat-reflective foil behind radiators mounted on exterior walls, or make your own from cardboard and aluminum foil.
FenntartK42V10=At night you draw the curtains, lower the blinds, and close the shutters.
FenntartK42V11=If you feel a bit cold, you do some exercise or take a walk—the activity refreshes you and warms you up.
FenntartK42V12=You air out several times a day but for short periods (just a few minutes each time), preferably when it’s warmest (or least cold) outside.
FenntartK42V13=The colors of walls and artificial light also affect how warm the air feels, so you choose warmer shades.
FenntartK42M=Most household energy use goes to heating, which is why it’s typically the biggest area for savings too.\n\nEnergy use can often be reduced without sacrificing comfort—and there are many practices that cost almost nothing!

FenntartK43=What are easy-to-implement, energy-efficient baking/cooking practices? Select these points!
FenntartK43V01=Whenever possible you use a pressure cooker or other pressurized steamer—you can save up to 70 percent of the energy needed for cooking.
FenntartK43V02=If the bottoms of your pots start to blacken from use, cooking efficiency drops—so you keep cookware clean.
FenntartK43V03=You always put food into a preheated oven—this cooks it through better and makes the top crispier.
FenntartK43V04=Where possible you cook multiple dishes in the oven at once—beyond saving energy, this also saves time.
FenntartK43V05=You buy good-quality nonstick and cast-iron cookware—the former is easy to clean; the latter retains heat well.
FenntartK43V06=You make sure pot size always matches the hob or burner size.
FenntartK43V07=When baking you don’t keep opening the oven door, and if visibility is poor you clean the glass before baking.
FenntartK43V08=Instead of buying the latest electric kitchen gadgets, you take out a hand whisk that works without power, the old one-arm grinder, and use good sharp knives for slicing.
FenntartK43V09=You cut ingredients into smaller pieces so they cook faster—this also applies later when reheating in the microwave—smaller pieces heat up more quickly.
FenntartK43V10=To avoid heat loss you use a lid that matches the diameter of the pot or pan.
FenntartK43V11=You don’t defrost frozen foods in the microwave; instead you take them out the night before and let them thaw on their own.
FenntartK43V12=You also use tiered cookware so you can prepare multiple dishes or courses at once (e.g., the main course and its sides).
FenntartK43V13=You switch the oven off a few minutes before the end of baking, keep the door closed, and use the residual heat to finish cooking.
FenntartK43M=Cooking accounts for roughly 7 percent of household energy use—after space heating and hot water, it’s where we spend the most energy.\n\nCooking-related energy use can be reduced if you work in the kitchen consciously and thoughtfully.\n\nIt’s also very important not to throw food away, as this significantly increases your CO2 emissions!\n\nPackage leftovers, write the date on them, and freeze them so you can use them later.\n\nIf you don’t generate food waste, you reduce the carbon footprint of your meals by an average of 25 percent.

FenntartK44=There are many kitchen activities that lead toward sustainability. Select these activities!
FenntartK44V01=You plan in advance what and how much you’ll eat during the week—this is the most efficient way to save energy and food.
FenntartK44V02=You like to make one-pot meals, because they allow quick, complete dishes.
FenntartK44V03=You use quality pots and pans with good heat transfer, such as Teflon-coated or stainless steel with a sandwich base.
FenntartK44V04=You match the size of tools to the amount of food—an oversized pot for a small portion or firing up the oven for just a few bites wastes a lot of energy.
FenntartK44V05=You often cook dishes that are quick to prepare, e.g., pasta and rice dishes.
FenntartK44V06=You include raw foods or those requiring little cooking/baking in your diet.
FenntartK44V07=You place meat, fish, vegetables, and fruit in the fridge’s dedicated drawers, and you store less perishable foods (drinks, sauces) in the door—this reduces spoilage.
FenntartK44V08=You try to buy ready-made meals in stores, because then you don’t have to spend time in the kitchen and you’ll have more money left in your wallet.
FenntartK44V09=You eat leftovers no later than the next day (or the third day if they keep longer), or you freeze them. You pay close attention to making sure no food ends up in the trash.
FenntartK44V10=If possible, you create a pantry next to the kitchen to store vegetables, fruits, and staples—this reduces what needs refrigeration and allows a smaller fridge.
FenntartK44V11=You don’t buy pasta at the store; you make it yourself—this saves on ingredients and can shorten cooking time.
FenntartK44V12=Industrial meat production has a large carbon footprint, so you reduce meat-based menus and have meat-free days every week.
FenntartK44V13=Where possible you buy local, seasonal, and organic foods—their production and transport are more energy-efficient than products coming from far away.
FenntartK44M=The kitchen is one of the most important rooms of daily life—we use it every day and spend a lot of time there.\n\nThe benefits of conscious organization and sustainable eating methods show up quickly: you’ll work faster and use less energy, saving time and money.\n\nA key part of a conscious kitchen is sourcing: buying local produce through short supply chains supports local production and reduces transport-related carbon footprint, while seasonality helps avoid high-energy (and thus high-carbon) greenhouse produce.\n\nMany households already strive to operate frugally: not having every light on everywhere all the time, not heating rooms that aren’t in use—and the list could go on.\n\nPay attention—in the kitchen and in the rest of your home—to save as much energy as you can, because that’s how you spare the environment the most!

FenntartK45=There are many kitchen practices that can speed up tasks while also saving energy. Choose these!
FenntartK45V01=Before switching on electric appliances (e.g., blender, oven) you make sure all ingredients are properly prepped so they don’t run unnecessarily while you finish preparations.
FenntartK45V02=Before cooking or baking you always fully defrost ingredients—e.g., you don’t start soup with frozen meat or frozen vegetables.
FenntartK45V03=You heat pasta together with the water rather than dropping it into already boiling water—this way it cooks faster and needs less energy.
FenntartK45V04=You often use a wok for cooking—it’s energy-efficient and lets you prepare fresh, healthy meals.
FenntartK45V05=You use the dishwasher as a sous-vide cooker (low-temperature cooking)—e.g., you put diced vegetables into a sealed jar, and when the dishwasher cycle ends, the vegetables are tender—and they retain their vitamins and nutrients.
FenntartK45V06=In the oven you use ceramic or oven-safe glass dishes—they retain heat better than metal ones, so they work more efficiently, and food will cook just as fast at a lower oven temperature.
FenntartK45V07=You soak whatever you can—besides legumes (e.g., beans, lentils, chickpeas) you also soak baked and layered pastas to soften them; this saves energy and time during baking.
FenntartK45V08=You coordinate baking and oven use so you can bake multiple items at once—e.g., under the main dish you toast small bread cubes on another tray for the soup.
FenntartK45V09=You choose the pan that best fits the dish and desired speed—copper-bottomed pans heat up faster than steel, while cast-iron pans retain heat more effectively.
FenntartK45V10=After baking you use the oven’s remaining warm air to keep sides or soup warm for the upcoming lunch or dinner.
FenntartK45V11=A common trait of vegetables is that they always cook quickly, so instead of slicing thinly or into small cubes, you throw them into the water whole.
FenntartK45V12=Where possible you cook efficiently with steam—you use less water for cooking, e.g., 1–2 cm of water is enough for potatoes, eggs, or steaming vegetables.
FenntartK45V13=You cook food only as long as necessary; you look up the softening times for ingredients—overcooked food falls apart and you waste a lot of energy.
FenntartK45M=Put proper emphasis on frugality in the kitchen, too, since baking and cooking involve significant energy use—which your bill clearly shows.\n\nAnd the time you spend in the kitchen matters as well—careful planning can save you lots of time that you can then spend meaningfully, for example with a good book while the food cooks or bakes :)

FenntartK46=With a pre-planned shop and the consciously organized cooking that follows, you can save a lot. What are these activities?
FenntartK46V01=For shopping you take reusable freezer bags, storage containers, boxes and cloth bags with you, and you avoid disposable packaging.
FenntartK46V02=You pay attention to shelf life, so you always search food packages for the best-before date and/or the use-by date.
FenntartK46V03=You process the more expensive ingredients first rather than the older (but still usable) ones, because if something spoils and you have to throw it away, your loss will be smaller.
FenntartK46V04=You choose wholesalers’ more affordable own-brand, good-quality products and larger pack sizes, because this saves more.
FenntartK46V05=You’re always aware of the per-kilogram prices and you compare prices during shopping.
FenntartK46V06=You don’t set leftover vegetables aside or throw them away; with a quick idea you cook a soup from them, or a skillet vegetable dish.
FenntartK46V07=You always buy fresh fruit and vegetables and avoid pre-cut products.
FenntartK46V08=You choose good plant protein sources, such as soy, lentils, beans, mushrooms, etc.—you don’t always need meat to be on the table.
FenntartK46V09=You avoid store-bought ready meals—these cost more than cooking yourself and often contain lots of unnecessary additives.
FenntartK46V10=Instead of dried spices you keep ever-growing potted kitchen herbs, so you always have fresh herbs.
FenntartK46V11=Your fridge and freezer are almost empty, you always store only enough food for one cooking—this way nothing spoils and the appliances also operate energy-efficiently.
FenntartK46V12=You shop once a week instead of going to the supermarket every day—this takes planning, but you save a lot of time and fuel.
FenntartK46V13=You go shopping when you’re full—people who are hungry often buy less effectively and less cost-consciously.
FenntartK46M=Cooking begins with shopping, where the key mottos are: reusability instead of disposability, and fresh ingredients instead of ready-made foods.\n\nOnly bring home the quantity of fresh food that’s truly necessary, preferably in your own basket and containers, without unnecessary packaging.\n\nThink and plan before you shop, stock up for a whole week so you don’t have to visit the store every day.\n\nCareful planning pays off in the kitchen, too: cooking time shortens and you save energy.

FenntartK47=It’s very hot in summer, but for climate-protection and savings you don’t want air-conditioning. What options do you have to cool yourself?
FenntartK47V01=You mist cold water into the rooms, onto houseplants, on the curtains and on yourself, because evaporating water removes a lot of heat.
FenntartK47V02=In the evening you water the lawn and plants around the house, splash down the pavement and pavers in front of the house, and sometimes even the house wall.
FenntartK47V03=You drink plenty of fluids, because a hydrated body tolerates heat better.
FenntartK47V04=During the day you don’t open doors and windows unnecessarily, and you bake and cook less.
FenntartK47V05=You hang a wet sheet where air circulates in the flat, and you put a cold, wet towel on yourself.
FenntartK47V06=You go walking or hiking in shade-giving parks and forests.
FenntartK47V07=You prevent heat from getting into your home and you shade: on the sunny side you use shutters, heat-protective blinds, blackout curtains and parasols.
FenntartK47V08=You spend a lot of time in the sun, because shade will feel much better afterwards.
FenntartK47V09=You drink very little, because that way sweating will hit you later and less often.
FenntartK47V10=You use a ceiling fan—it consumes little and makes the room feel more pleasant and cooler.
FenntartK47V11=You plant many trees in your garden and create a garden pond, because these temper extreme heat.
FenntartK47V12=You go down to the nearest riverbank or lakeshore and take a dip.
FenntartK47V13=At night you open the windows and before sunrise you air the house with a cross-draft.
FenntartK47M=Heating is the biggest household energy consumer, but in the age of air-conditioners, cooling also takes an ever larger share of total consumption.\n\nWith advancing climate change this share will likely keep growing, even though we should be reducing the use of ACs.\n\nWe all feel the summers getting ever hotter and drier, and the summer heat is harder to bear.\n\nFortunately, many cooling options can help even if you don’t want—or can’t afford—home air-conditioning.

FenntartK48=You’re preparing to travel for vacation (or business). You know the environmental impact of flying, but within the given time you can’t reach your destination any other way. How can you make your trip more sustainable?
FenntartK48V01=You research eco-hotels that respect nature and eco-tourism options in advance, and with conscious planning you use these.
FenntartK48V02=From the airport to your lodging you take a taxi (or rent a car) only if unavoidable—instead you walk or use the more eco-friendly public transport—this also helps you get to know local life better.
FenntartK48V03=Instead of disposable mini cosmetics you bring refillable travel bottles from home pre-filled with your favourite creams—so your host country faces less waste.
FenntartK48V04=When planning the trip you use Google’s flight search (Google Flights, which includes CO2 data) and Google Travel’s services that promote more sustainable tourism.
FenntartK48V05=To save water and detergents you request linen or towel changes at the hotel only when really necessary—you check at reception what their convention is for signalling laundry.
FenntartK48V06=You make sure souvenirs and keepsakes don’t come from endangered animals—you ask what the item is made of.
FenntartK48V07=You don’t take local flyers and paper maps packed with ads, because they end up in the trash at the end of the trip—instead you download a digital map (that works offline) to your phone.
FenntartK48V08=You eat foods made from locally produced ingredients that require less transport, and you don’t choose dishes made from endangered species.
FenntartK48V09=You offset the CO2 emissions from your trip—you support tree-planting and biodiversity protection programs, and if the airline offers carbon offsetting, you use it.
FenntartK48V10=When planning a package tour you research travel agencies and use only those whose services apply responsible tourism and strive to minimize the environmental and ethical impacts of their activities.
FenntartK48V11=You plan your trip based on brochures and flyers and choose the cheaper, on-sale option from competing offers; you don’t get lost in the details—that’s the provider’s job.
FenntartK48V12=Because of the waste it generates you don’t drink bottled water—if the local tap water poses health risks, you bring a portable filter and a reusable bottle—so you’ll always have clean water.
FenntartK48V13=You only visit zoos and parks that respect the environment, provide refuge and a chance of survival for animals, and bring wildlife protection closer to people.
FenntartK48M=Travel is wonderful because we can see the world; the downside is we inevitably contribute to several environmental problems: CO2 emissions, water waste, wildlife exploitation, waste generation.\n\nWe overconsume not just in shops but on our trips; we’re hugely wasteful. We “devour” countries, sights and kilometres because “we deserve it.”\n\nFew ask whether ecosystems can withstand all this globetrotting.\n\nJust as the pandemic forced us to slow down and rethink our daily lives, we should plan our travel with a slower, more thoughtful, more modest approach.\n\nIf you have no choice but to fly and stay in hotels, choose services with the smallest possible environmental impact, and offset the carbon emissions from your trip!

FenntartK49=You’re going on vacation and want to spend it as an eco-tourist, more consciously. Which factors do you consider in your decision?
FenntartK49V01=Mode of travel—plane, ship, car, long-distance bus or train—undeniably, the train is the transport mode with the smallest environmental burden—you always consider this when planning.
FenntartK49V02=Accommodation—large properties and huge hotels impact the environment more than smaller guesthouses or B&Bs—but of all options, camping in a tent has the smallest footprint.
FenntartK49V03=Travel distance—the biggest impact usually comes from the travel itself—the farther you go, the bigger the impacting—so you most often choose a domestic destination.
FenntartK49V04=Ethical and sustainable activities—whether the hotel or the area offers programs that don’t endanger or disturb local wildlife and local communities’ lives.
FenntartK49V05=Trip frequency—if you’ve already travelled this year (short or long distance), now you choose a destination closer to home to reduce your annual travel burden.
FenntartK49V06=Waste generation—whether the chosen lodging offers selective waste collection and pays attention to minimizing waste (e.g., do they hand out lots of waste-creating cosmetics and gifts).
FenntartK49V07=Meals—how food gets to the hotel restaurant table, where ingredients come from—do they prefer local, seasonal, organic products and cook from these.
FenntartK49V08=Sewage handling—what steps the accommodation takes to save water, where wastewater goes, what happens to it, how it’s treated.
FenntartK49V09=Community tourism—whether programs involve the local community, build on local culture and customs, let visitors join daily life and support green projects.
FenntartK49V10=Energy for cooling, heating and lighting—how energy-efficient the lodging is—whether heating/cooling and lighting can be controlled per room; whether natural ventilation is possible; and it’s a plus if they use renewables.
FenntartK49V11=Transport options at the destination—don’t consider only the car—it’s far less sustainable than rental bikes, scooters, EVs or local public transport.
FenntartK49V12=Souvenirs and keepsakes to bring home—buying as many and as exotic mementos, decor and household items as possible, collecting souvenirs from nature.
FenntartK49V13=Offsetting—whether the carrier and the accommodation offset their environmental burden by financing sustainability projects (e.g., tree-planting, ecosystem protection, biodiversity conservation, solar parks).
FenntartK49M=A 2018 study estimated tourism accounted for 8 percent of global CO2 emissions (with aviation the largest emitter).\n\nThis share fell (forcibly) during the pandemic, but has since surged and surpassed the record-setting levels of 2019.\n\nThe problem isn’t only travel-related carbon; it’s also how we behave while away—we leave traces everywhere: we litter, make noise, disturb protected places, and collect rare natural treasures as souvenirs.\n\nBut we can be eco-tourists: we can vacation more consciously so our rest leaves the smallest possible carbon footprint and the least environmental harm.\n\nBe an eco-tourist!\n\nSustainable vacations depend on you, but also on the carrier (if you don’t drive) and on the host. With conscious planning and choices, nudge them toward more sustainable services and steps to offset their operational impacts.

FenntartK50=There are many things—some easier, some harder—that can effectively help slow the accelerating climate change. What are these?
FenntartK50V01=You reduce and selectively collect your waste, compost what you can, and don’t buy any disposable, single-use packaging.
FenntartK50V02=You drive an energy-efficient car, and you strongly limit car use, mainly choosing public transport and human-powered modes.
FenntartK50V03=On trips, vacations and business travel you avoid polluting road, air or water transport with a large environmental impact.
FenntartK50V04=You give up industrial meat; instead you seek backyard-raised meat, eggs and dairy, and you prefer a plant-based diet.
FenntartK50V05=You set up for a self-reliant life: you grow key food and herbs, keep animals, and practice soil-regenerating gardening.
FenntartK50V06=You insulate your home, install rooftop solar, heat/cool with renewables, and among modern technologies (home, entertainment, mobility) you choose energy-efficient, durable, high-quality options and plan for the longest possible use.
FenntartK50V07=Every year you plant as many trees as you can—fruit trees or any kind, primarily native species suited to the local climate—and you support afforestation and nature-restoration activities.
FenntartK50V08=You don’t buy or order products from far away that require long-distance shipping or have high environmental impact or large resource needs (e.g.,  water, land).
FenntartK50V09=You avoid overconsumption; you don’t waste food, drinking water or energy; you aim to buy repairable things and, if they break, you repair or have them repaired.
FenntartK50V10=You protect the natural world and the animals and plants living in it—Earth is their planet, too, not just ours.
FenntartK50V11=You keep drinking water, air and soil as clean as you can—you buy consciously and use your money to support sustainable production.
FenntartK50V12=You support environmental organizations, and by expressing eco-conscious views you try to influence decision-makers to enact climate-protection measures.
FenntartK50V13=You choose to have fewer children—having one fewer child cuts emissions by nearly 60 tons of CO2 per year; it’s a very personal decision, but it protects the planet more than any other green effort.
FenntartK50M=To cut pollution effectively and address climate change, we need genuine, sustainable solutions.\n\nWe must abandon overconsumption and waste, because natural resources are dwindling on every continent.\n\nWe must review everything that drives overuse of resources, including drinking water and land.\n\nWe need to reduce non-renewable energy use and finance and expand renewables.\n\nWe should move to a sustainable, preferably self-reliant lifestyle, which is far gentler on the environment than industrial production.\n\nA few decades ago there was less waste, overuse and pollution; we can still learn from people for whom a more eco-conscious life was natural.\n\nLet’s listen to them and follow old examples—the good news is that many changes don’t worsen quality of life at all; in fact, cleaner air and cleaner human environments make nature—and us—healthier.

FenntartK51=To spare nature and forests we need to reduce paper consumption and thus paper waste. Select the applicable actions!
FenntartK51V01=You print only when unavoidable; you use both sides of the paper, use thinner paper, print multiple pages per sheet, reduce font size (and use refillable ink cartridges).
FenntartK51V02=You join the library, you lend out your finished books at home, and you read on a digital device (e-book).
FenntartK51V03=You switch to e-billing—most providers already offer alternatives to paper bills—you don’t have to count bills mailed to you or stand in line at the post office to pay them.
FenntartK51V04=You store your paper waste in cartons in the attic, because in winter they’re excellent fire starters and burn well by themselves in a mixed-fuel boiler.
FenntartK51V05=You unsubscribe from newsletters you never read—digital junk is still junk and it increases your ecological footprint—servers with serious operating costs run because of them.
FenntartK51V06=Instead of sticky notes and notepads you use your phone for notes and shopping lists; you don’t accept flyers, ads or business cards, you just photograph the latter and save it to your phone.
FenntartK51V07=You cancel subscriptions to newspapers you don’t read, and for the ones you do, you switch to digital papers and journals.
FenntartK51V08=You collect cardboard boxes, old newspapers and papers selectively, tie them up and turn them in for recycling.
FenntartK51V09=Instead of disposable paper towels, napkins and tissues you use cotton or hemp kitchen cloths, cloth napkins and cloth handkerchiefs; they can be washed together with clothes.
FenntartK51V10=You choose online tickets—with several benefits: some providers give discounts, you don’t have to go to the venue, you don’t queue and you’re not tied to a time.
FenntartK51V11=You use a digital calendar—paper ones either end up in the bin at the new year or clog desk drawers.
FenntartK51V12=You choose digital gift vouchers instead of printed ones—which you then use and give digitally.
FenntartK51V13=You reuse printed papers that don’t contain confidential data for notes or drawing, or you donate them to a kindergarten.
FenntartK51M=A conscious lifestyle includes cutting paper use, because responsible use not only saves forests from being cut down but also reduces the ecological footprint generated in daily life.\n\nPaper production and recycling have high environmental impacts, with manufacturing processes consuming a lot of water and energy.\n\nDon’t waste paper in any form; use it only when you truly need it!

FenntartK52=Printing is part of everyday home life and office work. Select the activities that point toward sustainability!
FenntartK52V01=Before printing you always check print preview—you see how the document will look; if it’s not right, you can still intervene and modify the content.
FenntartK52V02=You set print permissions: allow/deny printing, quota limits—this reduces waste and forces users to review their print jobs.
FenntartK52V03=You use paper quality and thickness just sufficient for the purpose—for everyday home, school and office printing, premium, expensive papers are usually unnecessary.
FenntartK52V04=You do all internal communication online—email and instant messaging are often enough to replace printed paper.
FenntartK52V05=You store documents in the cloud or on a local server—users can access and edit files digitally, so printing is often unnecessary.
FenntartK52V06=You print in draft mode—usually fine for everyday prints, as it reduces ink use with minimal drop in appearance and can increase print speed.
FenntartK52V07=You choose an economical printer—beyond quality and speed, you consider cartridge price and size, device energy efficiency, and whether you truly need colour printing.
FenntartK52V08=You don’t crumple misprints or unneeded documents into the general bin; you collect them selectively or use a shredder—the paper stays recyclable either way.
FenntartK52V09=You print on both sides (duplex), or on the blank side of paper previously used for printing that has since become unnecessary (if the document isn’t official).
FenntartK52V10=You print every document because it might be needed decades later, and ring-binders make them easier and faster to retrieve than digital storage.
FenntartK52V11=You print multiple pages or slides per sheet (for handouts)—text remains legible and paper use drops greatly.
FenntartK52V12=You print in black-and-white whenever possible—colour can cost five to ten times more because colour cartridges are pricier than black.
FenntartK52V13=You reduce font size and choose economical typefaces—fonts that use less ink and paper include Times New Roman or Century Gothic.
FenntartK52M=In many areas of life printing is necessary and sometimes unavoidable, so it’s important to steer it firmly toward sustainability.\n\nConscious printer use has several components: energy efficiency, reduced paper use, optimized ink use.\n\nDon’t forget the printer itself: choose an energy-efficient, high-quality device; use it as long as possible; don’t leave it in standby overnight; switch it off; have broken printers repaired; and treat dead devices responsibly as hazardous waste.\n\nCost-conscious offices, schools and households take care of their printers and pay attention to printing; that way they save money and use Earth’s resources more gently.

FenntartK53=Building an eco-conscious lifestyle and conscious shopping habits are key parts of sustainability. Which actions fit here?
FenntartK53V01=Home energy efficiency—you insulate your house, use energy-efficient appliances, run LED lighting, and regulate indoor temperature frugally.
FenntartK53V02=Green transport—you cycle and walk a lot, use public transport, car-share, and use electric vehicles.
FenntartK53V03=Resource-frugal consumption—you eat less meat, switch to a plant-based diet, buy seasonal goods from local producers, grow key foods yourself, and save drinking water.
FenntartK53V04=Home energy sources—you install solar panels or buy energy from green suppliers, heat water with solar thermal or use an energy-efficient boiler.
FenntartK53V05=Mindset shift—you shop and consume consciously, learn products’ life cycles and repairability, get informed and inform others about the importance of cutting CO2 footprints.
FenntartK53V06=Waste generation—you aim for as little waste as possible, sort selectively, and compost food scraps and garden waste.
FenntartK53V07=Shopping—you use your own containers, visit zero-waste stores, choose larger pack sizes that create less waste, look for eco labels on products, and buy second-hand too.
FenntartK53V08=Reusable products—you use returnable or refillable bottles, seek washable and reusable alternatives to paper-based products, and avoid plastic cutlery.
FenntartK53V09=Homemade products—from natural ingredients you make your own cleaners (e.g., from vinegar, baking soda, lemon) and your own cosmetics (e.g., from coconut oil, shea butter).
FenntartK53V10=Digital solutions—you switch to electronic bills and mail instead of paper communication, and you use digital devices for note-taking and reading.
FenntartK53V11=Conscious consumption—before buying anything you ask yourself whether you really need it; you repair broken items and seek new uses for things you no longer use.
FenntartK53V12=Eco-friendly products—you look for items from natural, renewable, biodegradable materials, free of toxic substances.
FenntartK53V13=Manufacturing process—you support producers who use renewable energy, provide ethical work conditions and pay fair wages.
FenntartK53M=Eco-conscious living matters because every single action you take helps the Earth and the future.\n\nWhat’s special is that most steps are easy to learn and cost almost nothing, they just need a bit of attention.\n\nImplement as many steps as you can and be part of the change!

FenntartK54=Coupling a plant-based diet with conscious food sourcing and storage is among the most effective ways to shrink your ecological footprint. Which actions fit here?
FenntartK54V01=You don’t switch to a plant-based diet overnight—at first you have one meat-free day a week, then you gradually raise the share of plant-based meals.
FenntartK54V02=You cook plant-based meals at home and discover the variety of vegetables, legumes, grains, seeds and nuts.
FenntartK54V03=You buy fresh vegetables and fruit at local farmers’ markets, which supports the local economy and cuts transport-related carbon emissions.
FenntartK54V04=You try plant-based alternatives to your usual animal-based foods, such as meat substitutes, plant milks and cheeses.
FenntartK54V05=You’re mindful of food waste, so you plan ahead and use up leftovers.
FenntartK54V06=You learn the plant-based protein sources such as lentils, beans, mushrooms, buckwheat, millet and soy-based tofu.
FenntartK54V07=You eat seasonal vegetables and fruit, which—unlike exotic foods—don’t need extra energy for growing and transport.
FenntartK54V08=You constantly track markdowns in stores and stock up heavily on discounted meats, and if you don’t have time to spend long in the store, you choose fast food.
FenntartK54V09=You grow your most important vegetables, fruit and herbs—you get the best quality and flavour without packaging or transport.
FenntartK54V10=You set up a cellar or cool pantry and learn proper storage for purchased or home-grown produce so you can keep them fresh longer.
FenntartK54V11=You master and use preservation methods (e.g., drying, canning, dehydrating, pickling) to turn surplus produce into special foods.
FenntartK54V12=You join online communities where you can share and find favourite plant-based recipes.
FenntartK54V13=You make sure you get enough iron, calcium, omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin B12, because these need special attention on a plant-based diet.
FenntartK54M=A plant-based diet isn’t just an eating style; it’s a sustainable way of life that respects the planet and its resources.\n\nThis shift goes hand-in-hand with conscious shopping and with learning proper storage and preservation of produce.\n\nChange isn’t always easy, but the positive impacts on the environment and your health are worth the effort.\n\nStart today and take a step toward a conscious and sustainable lifestyle!

FenntartK55=Single-use plastics don’t fit a sustainable lifestyle. Select the actions that reduce single-use plastics in your environment!
FenntartK55V01=You ask for bread and pastries in your own cloth bags—this spares you loads of paper and plastic; at home you keep bread in a breadbox with a lid or in a large drawer so it doesn’t dry out.
FenntartK55V02=You say no to cosmetics containing microbeads, because microplastics pollute the environment on a shocking scale—you look for words starting with “poli” or “poly” in the ingredients.
FenntartK55V03=You refuse any plastic dining item that you’d toss after eating—such as plastic straws, cups, bottles, plates, sauce tubs and cutlery.
FenntartK55V04=You brush your teeth with a replaceable-head toothbrush and use a metal safety razor that lasts a lifetime—you only replace the blade—and shaving with soap isn’t necessarily required.
FenntartK55V05=You’re surrounded by lots of single-use plastics, but you collect them all selectively so several sacks fill up weekly—it’s the collection and processing system’s responsibility what happens to plastics, not yours.
FenntartK55V06=You never release balloons—balloon releases cause the death of many animals, who eat them, and the strings tangle and hinder or strangle them.
FenntartK55V07=You choose glass or aluminum packaging—their recycling preserves value, unlike plastic whose recycling is down-cycling to lower quality material.
FenntartK55V08=When ordering online you ask the shop in the notes not to use plastic void fill—if padding is needed, it should be from recycled cardboard pieces.
FenntartK55V09=You use tools from natural materials sourced from sustainable operations—e.g., a wooden brush or comb with coconut-fiber bristles, or a loofah gourd dish sponge.
FenntartK55V10=You look for bulk, package-free goods in shops and bring jars, boxes and cloth bags for storing them.
FenntartK55V11=You give up single-use coffee, tea and ice-cream cups and coffee capsules—most takeaway cups contain plastic, and most capsules end up in the trash.
FenntartK55V12=You take your own cutlery—you get a practical metal spork or take washable metal or wooden cutlery from the kitchen drawer.
FenntartK55V13=For moving house or organizing items in cupboards and drawers—toys (wooden instead of plastic), etc.—you use foldable cardboard moving boxes instead of plastic crates.
FenntartK55M=The biggest problem with single-use plastics is their very low social perceived value, so people pick them up easily and discard them just as easily.\n\nThey’re cheap to produce and buy, light and strong enough to serve briefly—which made them popular and led to massive production to this day.\n\nThat scale can’t be processed; in many places they don’t want to, or the technology isn’t available, especially in developing countries.\n\nRecycling (when available) is expensive and often not worthwhile given the cheapness and low quality of the materials, so many single-use items (not just plastic) are burned, landfilled or end up somewhere in nature or the seas.\n\nWhat’s the solution? Reduce single-use plastics—and disposable items in general—as much as possible.

FenntartK56=As a conscious consumer you decide responsibly how you obtain the things around you and whether you need them at all. Select the sustainable activities!
FenntartK56V01=You take care of your things (any usable tool, electrical device or clothing), and if you no longer need them you sell them (e.g., garage sale, online marketplaces) or donate them.
FenntartK56V02=You borrow or rent—you don’t buy new items you’ll use only a few times a year, because they’d just sit around, take up space and depreciate.
FenntartK56V03=You shop less often and buy less—you use what you have as long as possible and only acquire what’s truly necessary, paying attention to products’ life-cycle environmental impacts.
FenntartK56V04=You always choose the leading products of the latest trends, because outdated, six- to twelve-month-old clothes, phones and other cast-off things wouldn’t maintain the prestige you’ve built in front of others.
FenntartK56V05=You often buy tools or clothes second-hand, and you avoid “fast fashion” clothing and accessory brands because they generate huge greenhouse-gas emissions, wastewater and waste.
FenntartK56V06=You don’t shop on an empty stomach, because you’re more likely to deviate from your shopping list and buy unnecessary things—a few nuts, an apple or a roll already eases hunger.
FenntartK56V07=Everything that still works but you deem obsolete—after buying a new one—you carry up to the attic—because “it’ll be good for something,” and if later it isn’t, “after all, it didn’t ask for food.”
FenntartK56V08=You learn to say no to an offer, product or service if you don’t need it.
FenntartK56V09=You repair what you can—if something breaks, tears, wears or cracks, you try to fix it or have a professional fix it—and you aim to buy repairable things.
FenntartK56V10=You shop consciously and don’t fall for flashy “two for the price of one” deals if you don’t need the products and/or they come with poor quality.
FenntartK56V11=Before buying something, you always ask yourself whether you really need it and will use it.
FenntartK56V12=You buy carefully—you always prioritize quality, durability and long use—you only consider replacing an item when it’s irreparably broken.
FenntartK56V13=You learn to avoid greenwashing—companies and products that, with false, misleading messages, present themselves as greener and try to deceive the buyer.
FenntartK56M=A conscious shopper pays attention to many factors: environmental conditions, social aspects and their own wallet.\n\nWhen shopping it’s far from enough to watch promotions: if you buy something cheaper, are you truly better off?\n\nBecause it matters what environmental cost the product was made at, how it reached you and what happens to it when you no longer need it.\n\nAlso, do you really need it? If yes, is it good quality and durable so you can use it for a long time?\n\nAnd is it sure you always need new things? Isn’t a used but flawless item enough?\n\nThere are many questions, but one thing is certain: today’s consumer society is extremely wasteful.\n\nImmersed in the huge selection, yielding to promotions and advertising, we overconsume—leading to massive raw material use, mountains of waste and accelerating climate change.\n\nBut there’s another way—see the line between unsustainable consumption and eco-friendly, cleaner future-focused conscious shopping habits.

FenntartK57=Education and community engagement are the engines of change. What options do you have if you’d like to help popularize sustainability?
FenntartK57V01=Lifelong learning—you organize talks and courses on eco-conscious living for all age groups.
FenntartK57V02=Community-based tourism—you encourage local community-based tourism providers to respect the local environment and culture.
FenntartK57V03=Social media—you use social media to inform and mobilize the community on environmental issues.
FenntartK57V04=Building partnerships—you work with local businesses to support the development of eco-friendly products and services.
FenntartK57V05=Support networks—you create support networks where people can share experiences, resources and ideas for environmental sustainability.
FenntartK57V06=Mentoring—as someone experienced in sustainability, you mentor younger generations in environmental initiatives.
FenntartK57V07=Campaigns—you launch or join community initiatives and information campaigns that highlight environmental problems and possible solutions.
FenntartK57V08=Community influence—you use your local influence to encourage decision-makers to adopt eco-friendly policies and practices.
FenntartK57V09=Volunteering—you take part in local environmental projects (e.g., tree planting, shoreline cleanups, or creating community gardens).
FenntartK57V10=Environmental education—you help ensure environmental education is part of the curriculum at every level so students understand the importance of sustainability.
FenntartK57V11=Global movements—you join global movements (e.g., Earth Hour, World Cleanup Day) that bring people together worldwide for environmental protection.
FenntartK57V12=Forums and debates—you organize forums and public debates where community members can discuss environmental issues and shape solutions together.
FenntartK57V13=Digital platforms—you use digital platforms and social media to share information and best practices related to sustainability.
FenntartK57M=An eco-conscious lifestyle can’t be achieved only through individual decisions; education and community participation are also key tools for its popularization.\n\nRaising awareness and supporting community projects are indispensable steps in advancing environmental consciousness.\n\nBy sharing knowledge and resources and actively participating in community activities, you contribute to building a more sustainable and liveable future.\n\nBecome an active participant in environmental change using the tools of education and community engagement!

FenntartK58=Protecting and preserving the oceans and seas is an important part of sustainable living. How can you contribute? Select these actions!
FenntartK58V01=Conscious purchasing—you make sure products are eco-friendly when shopping and avoid those that harm the oceans, e.g., fishing practices that damage marine life.
FenntartK58V02=Reducing fossil energy use—you curb your non-renewable energy demand, because rising carbon-dioxide concentrations increase ocean acidity and endanger marine ecosystems.
FenntartK58V03=Ocean-friendly products—you choose items made sustainably that don’t harm the oceans (e.g., cleaners made from environmentally friendly ingredients).
FenntartK58V04=Avoiding seas and oceans—you believe you best protect the oceans by keeping away from them, so you don’t need to change your lifestyle or daily habits.
FenntartK58V05=Cutting plastic use—you avoid unnecessary plastic packaging and single-use plastic products; instead you seek durable, recyclable, biodegradable alternatives.
FenntartK58V06=Sustainable clothing—you avoid plastic-based (polyester) garments because of microplastic pollution, and you choose clothing made from natural materials under ethical conditions with minimal environmental impact.
FenntartK58V07=Raising awareness—you educate yourself and others about the dangers of marine pollution, the oceans’ importance, vulnerability and the need for protection; you share your knowledge with your community and on social media.
FenntartK58V08=Support—you donate to or volunteer with civic and environmental organizations and initiatives that aim to safeguard the oceans and actively work for their protection.
FenntartK58V09=Cleanup actions on coasts and in your area—you organize or join cleanup initiatives where volunteers collect and remove trash from nature.
FenntartK58V10=Sustainable seafood—you choose sustainably caught and farmed fish and seafood when shopping (labels: MSC—sustainable fishing, ASC—sustainable aquaculture) and you support laws and regulations that limit overfishing.
FenntartK58V11=Water sports and mindful leisure—during water-based hobbies (e.g., sailing, diving, fishing) you behave responsibly, look after the aquatic environment and don’t litter.
FenntartK58V12=Waste management—you reduce all types of waste, choose proper (selective) disposal methods and ensure you don’t dump trash into the oceans or onto coasts.
FenntartK58V13=Encouraging marine research and expanding protected areas—you support scientific projects, organizations and measures that assess and understand ocean conditions and sustain and strengthen marine populations.
FenntartK58M=The oceans are fundamental to life.\n\nThey produce oxygen, regulate climate, provide food and jobs, and are home to cultures and communities worldwide.\n\nThey also absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide, helping to mitigate climate change.\n\nOcean health therefore directly affects human quality of life and the well-being of the entire planet.\n\nBuilding and following a sustainable lifestyle contributes not only to protecting the oceans but to the health of the whole Earth.\n\nRespect and care for the oceans are everyone’s responsibility and help preserve sustainable oceans for future generations.

FenntartK59=Waste management and waste treatment are among the most critical topics. Select the factors through which you help make them more sustainable and eco-friendly!
FenntartK59V01=Recycling—you sort glass, paper, plastic and metal correctly and selectively, because efficient recycling reduces the need for virgin natural resources.
FenntartK59V02=Composting—you compost kitchen and garden waste; compost serves as excellent soil and reduces transport of organic waste to landfills.
FenntartK59V03=Energy recovery—you reduce and carefully sort non-recyclable and non-compostable municipal waste; waste-to-energy plants and anaerobic wastewater treatment can generate energy from waste.
FenntartK59V04=Handling electronic waste—electrical and electronic waste often contains hazardous substances, so you collect it with special care and drop it off at a recycling center.
FenntartK59V05=Awareness, education and information—these are key to building sustainable mindsets, so you share your waste-management practices and eco-lifestyle habits with others.
FenntartK59V06=Donating or repurposing used items—you sell or donate still-usable items to charities instead of throwing them away.
FenntartK59V07=Sharing and borrowing—you rent and share items via online platforms and create a local sharing-economy community to jointly use household and garden tools and machines.
FenntartK59V08=Conscious purchasing—you consider product lifespan, durability and repairability; quality products last longer and generate less waste.
FenntartK59V09=Reusable products—you use items that can be reused many times (e.g., shopping bags, water bottles, cutlery) to help cut single-use plastics.
FenntartK59V10=Low-waste packaging—when shopping you choose products with less packaging, or packaging that is recyclable or reusable.
FenntartK59V11=Raising awareness—you learn products’ and services’ life cycles and research companies that practice sustainability.
FenntartK59V12=Eco-friendly alternatives—you look for greener alternatives to products like paints and cleaners that are less harmful to the environment and health.
FenntartK59V13=Conscious eating—by avoiding food waste you reduce organic waste and support the minimization of food waste overall.
